wave1.lens_self_description: I answered purely as an outside-view reference-class historian: every number is a historical frequency over the widest defensible window, adjusted only for the mechanical/arithmetic content of the locked priors (PPP weights, basket weights, labour-force arithmetic, starting levels), and I forbade myself any reasoning about AI capability trajectories, scaling, model releases, diffusion mechanics, or any episode-specific causal story.
wave1.cq1_reasoning:
CONJUNCT 1 - OECD-38 harmonized unemployment 5-yr average <=5.5% (2032-36). Reference class: OECD Total Area harmonized unemployment, annual, 1960-2025 (OECD MEI / FRED LRHUTTTTO1A156S; note the FRED OECD-total series runs 1999-2016 only and Eurostat's Sept-2000 definition change breaks pre-2000 comparability - search did not confirm 1970/1980/1990/2024 values, so pre-1999 levels are reconstructed from OECD Employment Outlook historicals). Non-overlapping 5-yr windows, 1960-2024 (13 windows): <=5.5% in 1960-64, 65-69, 70-74 and marginally 75-79; NOT in any window 1980-2019 (1980-84 ~7.6%, 2010-14 ~8.1%, 2015-19 ~5.9%); 2020-24 ~6.0% on the COVID spike. Unconditional base rate ~4/13 = 31%. Two mechanical adjustments I am permitted: (i) the starting level is ~4.9-5.0%, below the threshold, not above it; (ii) 2A's old-age ratio arithmetic (31% -> 39-41%) means OECD labour-force growth is near zero or negative 2032-36, which mechanically tightens the market independent of any AI story. Against: the base rate that a 5-yr window contains at least one OECD-wide recession is ~45% (8 negative-growth OECD years in 65 -> 1-exp(-5*0.12)), and OECD unemployment rises ~2pp peak-to-trough in recessions, which alone lifts a 5-yr average starting at 5.0% to ~5.6-5.8%. So conjunct 1 collapses to roughly "no material OECD recession in 2032-36 plus continued tightness": MARGINAL = 0.50.
CONJUNCT 2 - ISIC F+Q real median hourly wage growth beating J+K+M by >=10.0pp cumulative 2025-2036 (~0.87pp/yr for 11 years). Reference class: 11-year real wage growth differentials between broad sector groups, OECD, 1960-2025. Divergences of >=10pp between broad sector pairs do occur in roughly 25-35% of pair-windows (e.g. US finance vs manufacturing 1980-1991, ~15pp), but the DIRECTION is the binding constraint: in ~80% of 11-year OECD windows since 1970 the skill/cognitive premium WIDENED, not narrowed. The documented exceptions are the US Great Compression (1940s) and the post-COVID low-wage catch-up (US 2020-2024, leisure/hospitality and care beating professional services by ~5-8pp over 4-5 years, i.e. ~1.3pp/yr, then stalling by 2024-25). Directional base rate therefore ~15-20%. One mechanical discount from 2A: ISIC Q is predominantly publicly funded in OECD-38, and 2A locks a binding fiscal constraint (gross public debt >100% of GDP by 2029, net interest 2%->3% of GDP, China pension subsidies already 10.1% of fiscal expenditure). Public pay settlements are the transmission channel for care wages, and a fiscally squeezed state is the historically reliable suppressor of them (UK/Italy/Spain public pay 2010-2019: real declines of 5-15% during tight labour markets). MARGINAL = 0.17.
CORRELATION: positive but weaker than it looks. Positive channel: tight labour markets are the only historical condition under which manual/care relative wages rise. Negative channel: a 10pp+ care-wage surge historically coincides with inflation and policy tightening, which raises unemployment. Net assumed rho ~ +0.20, giving P(conjunct2 | conjunct1) ~ 0.17 * 1.3 = 0.22.
JOINT = 0.50 * 0.22 = 0.11 -> 11.
wave1.cq2_reasoning:
CONJUNCT A - OECD-38 GDP-weighted core CPI/PCE >=2.50%/yr average 2027-2036. Reference class 1 (full history, non-overlapping decades since 1960): 1960-69 ~2.3% no; 1970-79 ~7% yes; 1980-89 ~5.5% yes; 1990-99 ~3.2% yes; 2000-09 ~2.0% no; 2010-19 ~1.6% no -> 3/6 = 50%. Reference class 2 (the regime-relevant one: inflation-targeting era, overlapping 10-yr windows starting 1995-2016, n=22): only the windows starting 2014-2016 clear 2.5%, and only because they contain the 2021-23 spike -> 3-5/22 = ~18%. The resolution window 2027-2036 EXCLUDES that spike, so reference class 2 governs. Base rate ~20%.
RELATIVE-PRICE SKEW vs LEVEL, carried with explicit weights (my effort's core requirement): the inflationary impulses my brief names are mostly OUTSIDE the stated measure. US core CPI and core PCE and euro-area HICP core all EXCLUDE household electricity and gas, so 4-6% electricity inflation reaches core only as a second-round business input cost. Construction cost inflation reaches core only through shelter rent/OER, which tracks rents and incomes, not build cost - and 2A's demographics mechanically suppress household formation in Japan, Korea, Italy and Germany. Arithmetic composite on US-style core PCE weights for 2027-2036: shelter 18% x 3.0 = 0.54; health/care services 17% x 3.3 = 0.56 (this is the one large, genuinely demographic channel); other services 30% x 2.7 = 0.81; financial/insurance 8% x 2.0 = 0.16; core goods 23% x 0.3 = 0.07 (China export deflation). Sum ~2.14%. Euro-area and Japanese core run below the US, so the GDP-weighted OECD-38 central path is ~2.1-2.4% - BELOW the 2.50 bar. A regime where electricity, construction and care run 4-6% while software, media, professional services and tradable goods run 0-1% is exactly the configuration that leaves the CORE AGGREGATE unremarkable, because the hot items are either excluded from core (energy), weight-light, or publicly price-administered. MARGINAL A = 0.27 (20% base rate nudged up for fiscal deficits, the 17% health weight, and the financial-repression incentive at >100% debt).
CONJUNCT B - China headline CPI <1.50%/yr average 2027-2036. Reference class: China NBS CPI 10-yr averages - 1995-2004 ~1.0%, 2000-09 ~2.0%, 2005-14 ~3.0%, 2010-19 ~2.4%, 2015-24 ~1.4%, 2020-25 ~0.8%, 2023-26 ~0.0-0.4%. Closest single reference class: post-property-bust aging East Asia. Japan's rolling 10-yr CPI averages were below 1.5% continuously from the window ending 2002 through the window ending ~2021 (1993-2002 ~0.3%, 1998-2007 ~-0.1%, 2003-12 ~-0.1%) - roughly two decades of consecutive hits. Taiwan 2000-2020 ~1.0%. Counter-cases: Korea post-1997 ran 2-3%. That reference class alone supports ~0.70-0.75. Discounts: AMRO (Jan 2024) concludes China's deflationary risks are "rising but not as severe as Japan's case in 1990s", and China's policy rate is materially higher than Japan's was, leaving easing room; headline (not core) is also food/pork/energy-levered over a 10-year window and an RMB devaluation is reflationary for headline. MARGINAL B = 0.58.
CORRELATION: slightly NEGATIVE, rho ~ -0.20. Chinese deflation is exported into OECD core goods (23% of core PCE weight), which makes conjunct A harder; the 2014-2019 and 2023-2026 episodes of Chinese disinflation both coincided with OECD core undershooting target. So P(B|A) = 0.58 * 0.85 = 0.49.
JOINT = 0.27 * 0.49 = 0.133 -> 14.
wave1.cq3_reasoning:
Reference class: non-overlapping 5-year windows of PPP-weighted real GDP growth for OECD + China since 1960 (13 windows; OECD MEI, Penn World Table / Maddison for China pre-1980, IMF WEO PPP weights). Reconstructed window averages: 1960s ~5.0-5.5%; 1970s ~3.8%; 1980-84 ~1.8% (the historic low, OECD ~1.0% plus China 9% at a then-6% weight); 1985-89 ~4.0%; 1990s ~3.2-3.5%; 2000-04 ~3.3%; 2005-09 ~2.8%; 2008-12 ~2.4% (OECD ~0.5%, China ~9.3% at ~22% weight); 2015-19 ~3.75% (OECD 2.3%, China 6.7% at ~33%); 2019-24 ~2.6%. UNCONDITIONAL DISTRIBUTION: mean ~3.4%, SD ~1.1pp, minimum ~1.8%, maximum ~5.5%. Fraction of windows below 2.0%: ~1/13. Below 1.7%: 0/13. Above 2.6%: ~11/13.
Mechanical adjustments (the only ones my lens permits): (i) WEIGHTS. OECD-38 PPP GDP ~$80T, China ~$40T; China's share of the combined aggregate is ~33% in 2025 and ~34% by 2032. This is the single most important arithmetic fact, because the historical high averages were produced by a small-weight, double-digit-growth China; a 34%-weight China growing <3% cannot do that job. (ii) OECD ARITHMETIC. 2A locks per-capita baseline 1.0% -> 0.6%/yr; OECD-38 population growth 2032-36 is ~0.15-0.25%/yr, so baseline OECD aggregate growth is ~0.8%/yr, ~1.0-1.3% with a modest productivity offset. (iii) CHINA ARITHMETIC. 2A locks a ~60M population decline 2026-2035, worker/retiree 4.4->2.8, and a -2.7pp/yr aging drag; from a ~5% base that lands near 2.5-3.0% for 2032-36.
Central: 0.66 x 1.15 + 0.34 x 2.80 = 0.76 + 0.95 = 1.71%; with a 1.3% OECD / 3.0% China variant, 0.86 + 1.02 = 1.88%. I set P50 = 2.00%, deliberately ABOVE the mechanical point estimate, because the outside view says 12 of 13 historical windows beat 2.0% and growth-decline forecasts have systematically overshot the downside (the "Japanification of everything" and "secular stagnation" 5-year-ahead calls of 2013-2019 undershot realized OECD growth).
P10 = 1.05%: the base rate that a 5-yr window contains at least one global recession is ~45%; a 2032-36 window with one OECD recession and China at 2% lands near 1.0%. P90 = 2.95%: requires OECD ~1.9% (per-capita ~1.7% vs the locked 0.6% baseline, i.e. a +1.1pp productivity offset, which is beyond AI-Q1's >=+0.50pp at 23%) plus China ~4%. Distribution is left-skewed - the right tail is thinner than normal because the demographic denominators are near-deterministic over 10 years while the recession risk is not.
wave1.cq4_reasoning:
STARTING LEVEL, computed from the locked prior. 2A gives US 10y TIPS ~2.60% (FRED DFII10, 30 Oct 2026). G7 nominal GDP weights (US ~$30T of ~$50.5T = 59%; Japan 8.3%; Germany 9.3%; UK 7.3%; France 6.3%; Italy 4.8%; Canada 4.6%) applied to current real 10y yields (US 2.60, Germany ~0.6, UK ~1.5, France ~1.2, Italy ~2.2, Japan ~0.2, Canada ~1.8) gives a GDP-weighted start of ~1.98%, i.e. ~2.0%. Note the measure is US-dominated, so this is 60% a US TIPS question.
REFERENCE CLASS: G7 GDP-weighted 10y real yields by decade (reconstructed; my search did not return a confirmed decade-average series - the Bursa.ro G7 linker chart and the Jorda-Knoll-Kuvshinov-Schularick-Taylor long-run dataset are the sources that would settle it, so treat these as approximate): 1970s ~-1.5% (deeply negative ex post); 1980s ~+4.5%; 1990s ~+4.0%; 2000s ~+2.2%; 2010s ~+0.3%; 2020-2025 ~+0.3% average, ending ~+2.0%. Long-run 1960-2025 mean ~+2.0-2.5%.
BASE RATE OF STAYING NEAR THE STARTING LEVEL: low. Of the 5 decade-to-decade transitions since 1970, only 1980s->1990s stayed within ~0.5pp; the other 4 moved >=1.5pp. So P(a decade average within +/-0.5pp of its start) ~ 20%. This forces a WIDE distribution, which is the main thing my lens contributes here.
P50 = 2.15%. Two reasons to sit essentially at the starting level despite the low "stays put" base rate: (i) 2.0-2.2% IS the long-run 1960-2025 mean, so the starting point and the mean-reversion target coincide - the one configuration in which a flat central forecast is the base-rate answer rather than a lazy one; (ii) the locked 2A arithmetic is directionally upward (debt >100% of GDP by 2029, ~142% US and ~127% China by 2031, net interest 2%->3% of GDP, 3-yr P95 Debt-at-Risk ~117% and +2.4pp under a 20% AI-led equity shock, eroding convenience yields, levered basis-trade absorption) while the IMF's own aging result is that (r-g) worsens ~+1.0pp mainly through g falling ~1.1pp "even where a frictionless r* eases". Those roughly offset in the level and both widen the tails.
P90 = 3.60%: the 1980s/1990s term-premium regime, reachable from a 2% start by a 1.5pp move - smaller than 4 of the 5 historical decade transitions. P10 = 0.70%: the financial-repression / post-bust / flight-to-quality regime, which has a 2-in-6 decade base rate (1970s negative, 2010s ~0.3%) and is the regime a capex bust plus the BIS Box C demand deficit would produce. Mildly right-skewed because the debt arithmetic is one-directional and the zero lower bound is no longer the binding floor it was in the 2010s.
wave1.cq5_reasoning:
CONJUNCT A - ICE BofA MOVE averages >=105 over 2027-2036. Reference class: MOVE since inception 1988. One source puts the inception-to-date mean near 103 and another informal chart commentary treats ~85 as "average"; the discrepancy is itself informative, because the ~103 full-sample mean is inflated by 1988-1994, when nominal yields were 5-9% and MOVE (a basis-point, not normalized, vol measure) routinely printed 100-140. Reconstructed calendar averages: early 1990s ~105-130; 1994 ~130; 1995-2004 ~95-115 (2003 ~115); 2004-2006 ~65-80; 2007-08 ~110-180; 2009-12 ~85-105; 2013-2021 ~60-75; 2022 ~120; 2023 ~125; 2024 ~105 (Bloomberg: ~99 at end-2024); 2025 opened 96.67 and closed 63.96 - the steepest annual drop since 2009 and one of the steepest since 1988. Overlapping 10-yr windows starting 1988-2016 (n=29) averaging >=105: roughly the 1988-1990 and 1993-1994 starts, ~6-8/29 = 20-25%.
Decisive mechanical adjustment: the STARTING LEVEL. The window begins from a MOVE in the 60s-80s. The two historical analogues of a 10-yr window starting from a compressed-vol base both failed the bar (start 2004 at ~70 -> 2005-2014 avg ~90; start 2017 at ~60 -> 2017-2026 avg ~85), while the window starting 1994 from ~100 cleared it. Offsetting upward: MOVE scales with the yield LEVEL, and 2022-2024 averaged ~117 with 10y nominal ~4%, so a 2030s at 4-5% nominal plus 2A's Debt-at-Risk, convenience-yield erosion and basis-trade leverage supports a structurally higher mean than the 2010s. Net MARGINAL A = 0.33.
CONJUNCT B - at least one MSCI World >=25% peak-to-trough drawdown in 2027-2036 WITH G7 10y nominal failing to fall >=50bp (or rising >=25bp) in the window. Sub-part 1: base rate of a >=25% MSCI World drawdown in a 10-year window. Episodes since 1970: 1973-74, 1980-82, Oct 1987 (~-24%), 1990 (~-25%), 2000-02 (~-47%), 2007-09 (~-57%), 2020 (~-34%), 2022 (~-26%) - ~7 in 56 years, so 1-exp(-10/8) = 71% per 10-yr window; by decade, 5 of 6 decades contained one (2010s is the miss). Use 0.80. Sub-part 2: CONDITIONAL on such a drawdown, the historical frequency that bonds failed to rally >=50bp. Correlated/failed-to-rally: 1973-74 (yields rose), 1980 (rose), Aug-Oct 1987 (rose ~100bp into the crash), Jul-Oct 1990 (rose ~40bp on the oil shock), 2022 (rose ~250bp) = 5. Flight-to-quality: 1981-82 (ambiguous, yields fell after the peak), 2000-02 (-200bp), 2007-09 (-200bp), 2020 (-100bp) = 4. So ~5/9 = 55%. THIS IS MY LENS'S MAIN CONTRIBUTION: the "bonds always rally in an equity crash" prior is a 1995-2020 artifact; across the full 1970-2025 record the correlated regime is close to a coin flip and dominates high-inflation, high-term-premium, high-debt eras - which is the environment 2A locks. Keep 0.55 rather than raising it, to avoid double-counting the locked priors. MARGINAL B = 0.80 x 0.55 = 0.44.
CORRELATION: strongly POSITIVE, rho ~ +0.55 - both conjuncts are the same latent regime (high rate vol and positive stock-bond correlation co-occur in 1973-74, 1980-82, 1987, 2022). P(A|B) ~ 0.50.
JOINT = 0.44 x 0.50 = 0.22 -> 22.
wave1.cq6_reasoning:
Applied the lexical priority lock, first match wins, using my own CQ3 (P10 1.05 / P50 2.00 / P90 2.95; modelled as left-skewed with implied sigma ~0.74) and my own OECD-38 GDP-weighted core inflation path for 2032-36 (central 2.1-2.4%, from the explicit basket-weight arithmetic in my CQ2 reasoning).
STEP 1 - A (growth >=2.6%). Normal approximation on my CQ3 gives P = 1-Phi(0.6/0.74) = 21%; trimmed to 17% for the left skew (demographic denominators are near-deterministic, so the right tail is thinner than Gaussian). Outside-view tension noted and deliberately not resolved to zero: 11 of 13 historical 5-yr windows since 1960 exceeded 2.6%, so A is the HISTORICALLY NORMAL outcome and only the weight/labour-force arithmetic argues it away. Mechanically, A needs OECD ~1.9% (per-capita ~1.7% vs the locked 0.6% baseline, a +1.1pp offset) with China ~4% - beyond AI-Q1's >=+0.50pp at 23%. A = 17.
STEP 2 - C (core >=2.7% AND growth <2.0%). P(OECD-38 GDP-weighted core 2032-36 >=2.7%) = 0.20 from my CQ2 decomposition (a 5-yr average has more variance than the 10-yr average that drove my 0.27 at the 2.50 bar, but 2.7 is a higher bar and 2032-36 is the back half, where my brief's disinflationary forces - capex digestion, excess capacity, China export deflation, the BIS Box C demand drag - dominate). P(growth<2.0) = 0.50 from my CQ3 P50. Stagflation correlation rho ~ +0.15 (supply-wall regime), so P(growth<2.0 | core>=2.7) ~ 0.58 -> 0.116. STEP 3 - D (growth <1.7% AND core <2.0%). P(growth<1.7) = Phi(-0.41) = 34%, ~37% with left skew. P(core<2.0 | growth<1.7) ~ 0.55 (positive correlation; this is the demand-shortfall cell) -> 0.20. HARD outside-view constraint applied: NO 5-year window of OECD+China PPP growth since 1960 has come in below 1.7% - even 2008-2012 was ~2.4% - so the unconditional base rate for D is ~0/13. D is live only because of the never-before-seen arithmetic (China at 34% weight growing under 3% while OECD labour force shrinks). I pull D from 0.20 down to 0.17 to respect the zero base rate without discarding the arithmetic. D = 17.
STEP 4 - B = residual = 100 - 17 - 13 - 17 = 53. Sum = 100 exactly.
CONSISTENCY CHECK PERFORMED. (i) vs CQ3: my P50 of 2.00% falls squarely inside B's residual cell (growth 1.7-2.5% with core 2.0-2.6%), and A at 17% matches P(growth>=2.6) read off my own distribution rather than being set independently. (ii) vs CQ2: I put 14% on OECD core >=2.50% over 2027-36 jointly with China <1.50%. C requires a HIGHER inflation bar (>=2.7%) over a SHORTER, LATER window and does not require the China conjunct; dropping the China conjunct raises it, the higher bar and later window lower it, and 13% sits consistently alongside 14%. (iii) The relative-price skew central to my effort - electricity, construction and care at 4-6% while software, media, professional services and tradable goods run 0-1% - is definitionally the B cell: it produces an unremarkable CORE aggregate precisely because the hot items are excluded from core (household energy), weight-light, or publicly administered. That is why B carries the majority of my mass while C stays low despite extreme dispersion in the underlying prices.

hypothesis_critique.a: "SMOOTHLY" carries the entire failure, and the base rate for it is effectively zero. Reference class: cross-occupational reallocation after a sectoral labour shock. US manufacturing displacement 1979-2010 (Autor-Dorn-Hanson, and the earlier displaced-worker literature) shows 5-15 year adjustment lags and 15-20% PERMANENT earnings losses for displaced workers; coal and steel regions in the UK, Germany and the US never reallocated at all within a generation. Add three mechanical blocks that no historical episode has ever cleared smoothly: care work is licensed (nursing registration, certification hours), geographically non-substitutable (physical presence at the point of care), and publicly price-administered, so the wage signal that would pull a displaced analyst into it is set by a fiscal authority that 2A locks as constrained. Even in the single most favourable observed case - US 2020-2024, when low-wage and care sectors outpaced professional services by ~5-8pp - net cross-sector FLOWS from cognitive to care occupations were small and the gap stalled by 2024. Score 4.
hypothesis_critique.b: "BLOCKS" and "SEVERELY" both fail, and they fail for different reasons. "Blocks" conflates the two channels the scope lock deliberately separates: PHYSICAL labour migration (nursing, elder care, construction, domestic work, seafaring) is demographically PULLED by exactly the 2A old-age arithmetic - 31% to 39-41% by 2036 - and nothing in that channel is technologically displaceable within the horizon, so the larger of the two export channels is strengthened, not blocked. Only the VIRTUAL channel is exposed. "Severely" fails on magnitude: Indian IT/BPO services exports are ~$200B against a ~$4T economy (~5% of GDP), and Philippine BPO is ~7-8% of GDP with remittances another ~8-9% - but remittances flow overwhelmingly from physical migrants, so the two shocks do not stack. Reference class: technology shocks to a single export sector of a large diversified economy (telephone operators, UK textiles 1960s-80s, Caribbean offshore data entry 1990s-2000s) almost never produce severe AGGREGATE damage; they produce a concentrated distributional shock inside one city or occupational cohort. Score 11.
hypothesis_critique.c: No single word fails - the SHAPE is the historically modal pattern, which is why this is the only plank I score above 50. Base rate: 10-year and 5-year inflation averages mean-revert in roughly 70% of windows; the post-shock reversion from a spike is the single most reliable regularity in the OECD inflation record (1951-55, 1975-79, 1981-86, 1991-95 all reverted). My own basket-weight arithmetic independently produces this shape: the inflationary impulses are front-loaded (grid and power capex crowding, tariff and fragmentation pass-through as a LEVEL shift that fades out of the rate by 2029-2030, construction and care wage scarcity) and the disinflationary forces are back-loaded (capex digestion and post-bust excess capacity, China overcapacity export deflation into the 23% core-goods weight, the BIS Box C labour-income demand drag). The weak word is "HOT": core is already near 2.5-2.8% rather than accelerating, so 2027-2030 is better described as sticky-above-target than hot, and "falls in the 2030s" is likelier to mean settling at 2.2-2.4% than at 1.5%. The plank is right about direction and wrong about amplitude at both ends. Score 58.
hypothesis_critique.d: "EVENTUALLY" is the word that makes the plank unfalsifiable, and "WINS" is the word that makes it wrong by Dec 2036. On "eventually": with no date the claim cannot resolve, so I score the only testable reading - aggregate real GDP growth beating the demographic drag within the horizon. Base rate for "technology will offset demography" claims resolving true: low. Japan ran the world's most aggressive robotics and ICT deployment 1995-2020 and did NOT offset its demography (per-capita growth held up, aggregate growth averaged ~0.8%); the US "new economy" delivered exactly one 8-9 year TFP burst (1995-2004) and then faded; the Solow productivity paradox and David (1990) on electrification put the general-purpose-technology lag at 20-40 years before TFP registers. Within a 10-year horizon the base rate is ~15-20%. The locked arithmetic agrees: aging is -1.1pp/yr globally (-2.7pp China), and AI-Q1 gives 23% to a TFP lift of merely >=+0.50pp - a third of what offsetting would require. "Wins" also smuggles in an aggregate claim from a per-capita mechanism: an "exponential" productivity term multiplied by a shrinking labour input is still arithmetic, and my CQ3 P90 of 2.95% is where that arithmetic tops out. Score 13.

key_drivers: PPP WEIGHT ARITHMETIC. China is ~33% of the OECD-38+China aggregate in 2025 and ~34% by 2032. Every historically high 5-year window was produced by a small-weight, double-digit-growth China; a 34%-weight China growing under 3% with a 60M population decline cannot reproduce it. This single fact drives my CQ3 P50 down to 2.00% and is the only reason CQ6-D is live at all against a ~0/13 historical base rate.

CORE-BASKET WEIGHT COMPOSITION, which is the decisive separation of LEVEL from SKEW. US core CPI/PCE and euro HICP core EXCLUDE household electricity and gas, and reach construction only through shelter rent/OER. So the 4-6% inflating items touch core mainly via health/care services (~17% of core PCE) and shelter (~18%), while China's overcapacity deflation hits the full ~23% core-goods weight. The arithmetic composite lands at ~2.1-2.4%: extreme relative-price dispersion with an unremarkable aggregate. This is why my CQ2 is 14 and my CQ6-C is only 13 despite a genuine supply-wall story.

MEAN REVERSION OF 10-YEAR INFLATION AVERAGES UNDER INFLATION TARGETING. Only ~3-5 of 22 overlapping 10-year windows starting 1995-2016 averaged >=2.5% OECD core, and those only because they contain the 2021-23 spike that the 2027-2036 window excludes. The full-history base rate (3/6 decades) is a pre-targeting artifact and I weight it down.

THE FULL-SAMPLE (not 1995-2020) STOCK-BOND CORRELATION RECORD. Of the ~9 MSCI World >=25% drawdowns since 1970, ~5 came with G7 yields flat or rising (1973-74, 1980, 1987, 1990, 2022) and ~4 with a flight-to-quality rally. The correlated regime is a coin flip, not a tail - this is what keeps my CQ5 at 22 rather than single digits, and it is offset only by the compressed MOVE starting level (2025 closed at 63.96, the steepest annual drop since 2009).

DIRECTIONAL ASYMMETRY OF THE HISTORICAL SKILL PREMIUM, plus public funding of ISIC Q. >=10pp broad-sector real wage divergences happen, but in ~80% of 11-year OECD windows since 1970 the cognitive premium WIDENED. Care wages are set by fiscal authorities that 2A locks as constrained (debt >100% of GDP by 2029, net interest 2%->3%). This is the binding constraint on CQ1's second conjunct and caps it at ~17%.

DISPERSION OF DECADE-TO-DECADE REAL YIELD TRANSITIONS. wave1.coupling_tension:
THREE TENSIONS, IN THREE DIFFERENT DIRECTIONS.

(1) AI-Q3 IS TOO HIGH ONCE 2A's FINANCING ARITHMETIC IS ENDOGENOUS - DOWNWARD. AI-Q3's P50 of 998.2 TWh is ~2.7x the ~365 TWh 2024 base, and it must be financed through exactly the window (2029-2033) in which 2A's demographics bind hardest: gross public debt >100% of GDP by 2029, net interest 2%->3% of GDP, 3-yr P95 Debt-at-Risk ~117% (+2.4pp under a 20% AI-led equity shock), eroding convenience yields, and ~$1.4T of circular vendor/cloud/chip commitments on ~$300B equity and ~$650B debt. Data centres are the longest-duration, most capital-intensive asset in the 2B set, so they are the most hurdle-rate-sensitive; my CQ4 P50 of 2.15% real with a P90 of 3.60% raises that hurdle precisely when the second and third capex waves need funding, and AI-Q4 already puts 66% on impairment or revenue shortfall. The joint distribution of AI-Q3 and AI-Q4 as stated is internally slack: a 66% impairment probability is barely compatible with a 998 TWh median of STRICT OPERATIONAL capacity. Direction: AI-Q3's P50 should fall to roughly 850 TWh, and its P10 should fall further than its P50 (596.8 -> ~500), because an impairment event plus grid-interconnection queues and electricity-price crowding truncate the LEFT tail downward while leaving the right tail roughly intact.

(2) AI-Q5 IS TOO LOW ONCE AGING IS A DEMAND PULL - UPWARD, AND THIS IS THE SIGNATURE TENSION OF MY EFFORT. AI-Q5 (38.2%) was elicited with demographics exogenous, so it misses two mechanical channels. First, a shrinking OECD labour force raises the scarcity wage of the physical/care worker, which raises the relative payoff to substituting away from cognitive labour - aging is an automation demand pull, not only a drag to be offset. Second, and more important for the accounting: the LABOUR COMPENSATION SHARE of J+K+M GVA can fall purely through denominator growth. Hyperscaler rents inflate sector J's GVA with no cognitive wage decline at all, and aging mechanically feeds this by pushing a growing retirement-asset pool into intangible-rent sectors as the safe-asset r* is compressed. So AI-Q5 should read ~46%. Note this moves in the OPPOSITE direction from tension (1) and is only weakly coupled to AI-Q2 (21.3%): the ensemble's implied correlation between adoption BREADTH and FACTOR-SHARE shift is too tight. The consistent joint is narrow, deep automation inside J/K/M plus wide compensation-share compression - which is precisely CQ6-B, and is why B carries 53 of my 100.

(3) AI-Q1 AND 2A JOINTLY STARVE THE INFLATION CELL - DOWNWARD ON CQ6-C, AND THIS IS WHERE MY LENS'S ANSWER IS MOST UNCOMFORTABLE. If the TFP lift does not arrive (77% per AI-Q1), then 2A's aging drag plus the BIS Box C labour-income demand deficit plus China's overcapacity export deflation make OECD core UNDERSHOOT, not overshoot. The stagflation cell therefore cannot be demand-driven at all: its inflation must come entirely from supply walls in grid, care and construction. But those walls sit mostly OUTSIDE the resolution measure - US core CPI/PCE and euro HICP core exclude household electricity and gas, construction enters only through rent/OER, and ISIC Q prices are administered by fiscal authorities that 2A locks as constrained. The honest finding is that the coupled world can deliver a genuinely severe relative-price crisis (electricity, care and construction at 4-6%) while the LOCKED CORE AGGREGATE never reaches 2.7%. A measure-dependent resolution gap, not a forecast disagreement: CQ6-C is suppressed by basket construction as much as by economics, and anyone resolving these questions in 2037 on a headline or energy-inclusive measure would get a materially different answer from the same world.

wave1.lens_self_description: I answered purely as a Fermi structural decomposer on the inflation-path/relative-price-skew effort: every number is built from an explicit arithmetic identity (basket weights x sub-component rates, growth-accounting sums, conjunct marginals x stated correlations), and I forbade myself any appeal to historical base rates or frequency-of-occurrence reasoning — where I would normally have reached for "how often has X happened", I instead decomposed X into a quantity, a weight and a shadow price.
wave1.cq1_reasoning:
REFUSED from the model: the adapter self-reports "not representable - no unemployment, no ISIC sectors, no sectoral median wage". No figure below touches the simulation.

CONJUNCT A: OECD-38 harmonized u <= 5.5% avg 2032-36. Marginal 0.60. Decomposition, not base rate: u = 1 - E/LF. The locked 2A old-age ratio move (31% -> 39-41%) withdraws labour supply. OECD labour force contracts ~0.3%/yr from 2030; over 5 years that is -1.5% of LF, which at unchanged E lowers u by ~1.4 pp off a ~4.9-5.0% 2025-26 level. The demographic mechanics alone drive u toward 4%. The failure channel is arithmetic on recession-years: one high-u year at 7.0% plus four at 4.8% averages (7.0+19.2)/5 = 5.24% (PASSES); two high-u years gives (14.0+14.4)/5 = 5.68% (FAILS). So conjunct A reduces to P(fewer than two badly-slack years in the five), plus an AI-mismatch term from AI-Q5 (38%) adding frictional unemployment concentrated in J/K/M. I put P(>=2 slack years) at ~0.30 and residual measurement/definition risk at ~0.10 → A = 0.60.

CONJUNCT B: cumulative real median hourly wage growth F+Q minus J+K+M >= +10.0 pp over 2025-2036. Marginal 0.20. 10 pp over 11 years = +0.87 pp/yr differential. Care-side quantity build: OECD 65+ rises ~29% in 11 yr (~+2.3%/yr) and 80+ faster (~+3.5%/yr). Care-worker supply grows with the working-age base (~-0.2%/yr) plus migration plus wage-elastic entry; excess demand growth ~3.5 pp/yr against a labour-supply elasticity of 1.5-2.5 implies a required relative real care wage of +1.4 to +2.3 pp/yr, i.e. +15 to +25 pp over the window — IF FUNDED. ISIC Q is 60-80% publicly financed and the locked 2A has net interest going 2% -> 3% of GDP with debt past 100%. ASSUMPTION (stated, not proven): a fiscally constrained Baumol sector resolves excess demand as QUANTITY RATIONING (waiting lists, thinner staffing ratios, informal family care) rather than as a measured wage. That single assumption is what collapses B. Realistic path: F+Q ~+1.15%/yr real (= +13 pp over 11 yr, care +1.3, construction +1.0, construction haircut because AI-Q4's 66% bust lands in ISIC F during exactly 2032-36); J+K+M +0.6 to +1.0%/yr real (= +7 to +11 pp). Differential +2 to +6 pp, short of 10. To clear 10 pp you need J+K+M real median essentially FLAT for 11 years, which requires displacement at the median AND above it — but the composition/selection effect runs the other way: if AI removes junior and median cognitive roles, the surviving MEDIAN wage mechanically rises. M also receives a positive demand pull (engineering, architecture, project management for the grid/DC build). Add resolution fragility: ISIC-level median hourly wage at F/Q/J/K/M granularity exists only in the 4-yearly Eurostat SES and a few national series, so a clean >=10.0 pp read is itself uncertain. B = 0.20.

CORRELATION: +0.15. Two offsetting channels. A tight labour market (low u) is the same labour-scarcity state that bids up F+Q wages (positive). But the AI-displacement state that compresses J+K+M wages raises mismatch unemployment (negative for A). They nearly cancel; small net positive.

MULTIPLICATION: P(A n B) = 0.60 x 0.20 + 0.15 x sqrt(0.60x0.40x0.20x0.80) = 0.120 + 0.15 x 0.196 = 0.120 + 0.029 = 0.149 → 15.
wave1.cq2_reasoning:
REFUSED from the model: adapter reports "not representable - the model has no price level". Nothing below is model-derived.

This is my effort's core question, so I carry the weights explicitly.

CONJUNCT A: GDP-weighted OECD-38 core CPI/PCE >= 2.50%/yr avg 2027-2036. Marginal 0.55.
US-style core basket build (US is ~45% of the GDP weight):
- Shelter, 44% of core CPI, at 3.0%/yr. Aging cuts household formation (-) but raises single-occupancy and cuts mobility (+); immigration restriction (-); grid/DC crowding of construction labour and copper raises new-supply cost (+).
- Core services ex-shelter, 35% of core, at 2.48%/yr. Sub-split carried explicitly: care/health/personal services 15 pts of core at 3.5%/yr; AI-exposed professional/financial/information services 12 pts at 1.0%/yr; other services (transport, insurance, education) 8 pts at 2.8%/yr → (15x3.5 + 12x1.0 + 8x2.8)/35 = 86.9/35 = 2.48%.
- Core goods, 21% of core, at +0.3%/yr. Underlying -0.3%/yr (China/Vietnam overcapacity export deflation plus AI manufacturing productivity). Tariff pass-through is a LEVEL shift, not a rate: a 10% effective tariff passing 60% through to a 21%-weight basket is 0.10x0.6x0.21 = 1.26% of core LEVEL, which spread over a 10-year average adds only ~0.13 pp/yr (I use +0.6 pp/yr on the goods line, concentrated 2027-29).
US core = 0.44x3.0 + 0.35x2.48 + 0.21x0.3 = 1.32 + 0.868 + 0.063 = 2.25%/yr.
OECD-38 GDP weighting: US 0.45x2.25 = 1.013; euro area 0.22x2.0 = 0.440; Japan 0.09x1.6 = 0.144; UK 0.055x2.5 = 0.138; Canada 0.04x2.1 = 0.084; Korea 0.035x2.0 = 0.070; Australia 0.025x2.5 = 0.063; high-inflation members (Turkiye, Mexico, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica) 0.085 x ~6.5% = 0.552. SUM = 2.503%/yr.
That lands EXACTLY on the threshold, and the decisive term is the 0.55 pp contributed by five high-inflation members at an 8.5% weight. Drop them and the aggregate is 1.95%. So conjunct A is substantially a measurement-convention question (market vs PPP weights — PPP raises Turkiye/Mexico further, pushing it UP) rather than a US/euro-area inflation question. Time profile: 3 years at 2.9% (tariffs, electricity pass-through, care wages, grid capex crowding) plus 7 years at 2.35% = (8.7+16.45)/10 = 2.52%. Front-loading is what clears the bar. A = 0.55.

CONJUNCT B: China headline CPI < 1.50%/yr avg 2027-2036. Marginal 0.48. Treated as a semi-independent object per the effort brief, not an OECD mirror. Disinflationary structure: (i) property adjustment suppressing the housing/rent component (~16% of the basket) and household wealth through ~2030; (ii) household income share of GDP ~44% and consumption ~39%, the deliberate suppression that is the structural source of deficient domestic demand; (iii) deliberate supply-side industrial policy — overcapacity and "involution" price wars across the new-three and 20+ sectors, PPI negative for years; (iv) aging acts disinflationary HERE despite labour scarcity, because the pension system is thin (subsidies already 2.9T RMB, 10.1% of fiscal expenditure) so precautionary saving dominates the wage channel. Inflationary risks: one hog cycle can add 1-2 pp to a single year and so move a 10-year average by 0.1-0.2 pp; a successful consumption-rebalancing pivot; RMB pass-through; and the genuine upside — services wage pass-through as the workforce shrinks, which grows monotonically through the 2030s. Split-window arithmetic: 2027-2030 at ~0.8%/yr, 2031-2036 at ~1.9%/yr → (4x0.8 + 6x1.9)/10 = 1.46%/yr. Knife-edge, just under. B = 0.48.

CORRELATION: -0.10. Two channels fight. Direct linkage: China export deflation is an INPUT to OECD core goods — a China export price fall of 3%/yr at 30% pass-through into a 21%-weight basket is -0.19 pp/yr on OECD core, so B true pushes A false (negative). Decoupling channel: tariff/fragmentation walls mean China's overcapacity deflates domestically while OECD goods prices rise, making them positively correlated — and that is the regime the locked 2A describes. The wall is leaky (Vietnam/Mexico transshipment, commodity and capital-goods prices) and a global BIS-Box-C demand shortfall would drag both down together, so I take a small net negative.

MULTIPLICATION: 0.55 x 0.48 + (-0.10) x sqrt(0.55x0.45x0.48x0.52) = 0.264 - 0.10 x 0.2486 = 0.264 - 0.025 = 0.239 → 24. I am ABOVE a naive conjunction discount here precisely because my weight-carrying work pushes both conjuncts toward 0.5 rather than toward 0.3.

USE: I take only one thing from the model — its PPP weight split (OECD-core proxy 0.629 / China 0.371 at 2031), as a cross-check on my own weights.

hypothesis_critique.a: The failure word is SMOOTHLY, and secondarily SUPPLY. Arithmetic: OECD ISIC J+K+M employment is ~15-18% of total employment, so a 10% displacement releases ~1.6% of the workforce. Care demand: health+LTC is ~11-13% of OECD employment and must grow ~25-35% by 2036 to hold staffing ratios against an 80+ cohort growing ~3.5%/yr, i.e. an additional +3 to +4% of total employment is needed. The released pool is roughly HALF the required inflow at its most generous, so even a frictionless transfer does not clear the gap — the quantities do not match before any friction is considered. Then SMOOTHLY fails on four independent non-substitutabilities: occupation (a paralegal is not a nursing aide), licensure (care work is credentialed and the credential takes 1-3 years), geography (cognitive jobs are metro, care demand is dispersed and rural-heavy), and wage (care pays ~50-65% of the displaced cognitive wage, so the transfer requires a voluntary real income cut). The clearing price is a large real care-wage premium, and that premium is unfunded because ISIC Q is 60-80% publicly financed while the locked 2A has net interest going 2%->3% of GDP. SUPPLY also fails: in a fiscally rationed Baumol sector the excess demand resolves as quantity rationing — waiting lists, thinner ratios, informal family care drawn from the same working-age base — not as workers supplied.
hypothesis_critique.b: The failure words are BLOCKS and SEVERELY, in that order. BLOCKS conflates two exports with opposite signs. VIRTUAL services exports are AI-exposed; PHYSICAL labour migration is AI-COMPLEMENTARY and is pulled HARDER by the same aging that motivates the AI. Philippines: OFW remittances ~$38-40B is ~8-9% of GDP and rises with the OECD care wall; IT-BPM revenue ~$38B is ~7-8% of GDP but perhaps only 25-40% of that stock is genuinely automatable by 2036, so the AI-exposed slice is ~2-3% of GDP against an aging-expanded slice of 8-9%. The net sign for the Philippines is plausibly POSITIVE. India: IT services exports ~$200B is ~5% of GDP; an AI-exposed slice of ~30% is ~1.5% of GDP, against domestic demand that is ~80% of the economy. BLOCKS is also wrong mechanically: AI raises output per offshore delivery worker, which DECOUPLES export revenue from export headcount — the dollar value can grow while employment falls, which is a distributional shock inside the sector, not a blocked export. SEVERELY is the wrong magnitude word at the GDP level for either country, though it would be the right word for the specific 2-3 million-person entry-level BPO cohort.
hypothesis_critique.c: The failure word is FALLS, with HOT as a secondary offender for being unquantified. My own build is hot-then-cooler: GDP-weighted OECD core ~2.9%/yr over 2027-2030, ~2.35%/yr over 2031-2036. So the plank's SHAPE is right and it is the closest of the four to my effort's central path — hence the high score. But FALLS implies a return to something like target, and the arithmetic says a persistent ~0.35 pp overshoot instead. The reason is a weights-and-shadow-price point: the disinflating leg (software, media, professional services, financial services, tradable goods) is only ~33 of 100 points of core, while shelter (44) and care/health/personal services (15) carry a non-substitutable labour input whose shadow price RISES monotonically with the 80+ cohort through 2036 and beyond. Software deflating at 0-1% cannot pull a 59-point shelter-plus-care bloc running at 3.0-3.5% down to 2.0%. The plank is directionally correct and quantitatively wrong in the same direction most forecasters err: it mistakes the fading of the one-off impulses (tariff level shift, grid capex crowding) for the fading of the structural relative-price skew, which does not fade.
hypothesis_critique.d: The failure words are EVENTUALLY and WINS, with EXPONENTIAL carrying a category error. The 2036 arithmetic: the locked aging drag on the OECD-38+China basket is 0.68x(-0.4) + 0.32x(-2.7) = -0.27 - 0.86 = -1.136 pp/yr. The AI offset, computed from AI-Q6's own regime probabilities, is 0.162x0.75 + 0.472x0.35 + 0.365x0.06 = +0.309 pp/yr of TFP, plus my capital-deepening estimate of +0.10 pp/yr, = +0.41 pp/yr. The offset is 36% of the drag, short by a factor of 2.8. EVENTUALLY concedes exactly this by refusing to name a horizon; at the Dec 31 2036 resolution date the answer is arithmetically no. EXPONENTIAL is a category error: compute and parameter counts are exponential, but the GDP contribution is bounded by the Hulten weight of the automatable task share and by the Baumol share of the non-automatable remainder, so an exponential input maps to a roughly logarithmic output in measured GDP — and the measured-output mapping gets WORSE as aging shifts the composition toward sectors whose output is measured by their input. WINS is undefined: against which counterfactual, and in levels or in growth rates? AI can raise the level of GDP permanently while the growth RATE still falls, which is the most likely outcome and which the plank would score as a loss.

wave1.coupling_tension:
THREE TENSIONS, EACH WITH A DIRECTION.

(1) THE SHARPEST: AI-Q4 (66%) is in severe tension with AI-Q3's P50 of 998 TWh and P90 of 1,574 TWh once demographics and fiscal space are endogenous. AI-Q4 says there is a two-in-three chance that >=20% of announced hyperscaler buildouts are impaired or cancelled, OR that net external AI revenue runs below 0.5x compute D&A for two consecutive years. AI-Q3's P50 says STRICT OPERATIONAL OECD-38+China datacenter electricity reaches 2.74x its 2024 level of ~365 TWh. These cannot both be comfortably true: a 2.74x operational load requires the build to substantially complete AND to be energized AND to be paid for, which is close to the complement of AI-Q4. Arithmetic: AI-Q3 P50 implies +633 TWh over 12 years = ~53 TWh/yr of new load = 9.3 GW/yr of firm capacity at a 65% load factor (53,000 GWh / 8,760 h / 0.65), claiming ~10-18% of OECD+China net firm-capacity additions, with interconnection queues at 4-7 years and HV transformer lead times at 2-4 years — physical constraints that a 66%-probability financing shock interacts with multiplicatively, not additively. DIRECTION: I resolve it against AI-Q3. Coupled, I would put the 2036 OECD-38+China strict operational figure at a P50 of ~820-860 TWh, roughly 14-18% below the locked 998, with the P10 barely moving (the already-committed 2026-2029 tranche is energized regardless) and the P90 falling to ~1,350. The adapter's own output is an independent flag in the SAME direction being violated: the model's WORLD 2036 datacenter load is 1,884 TWh (baseline) and 4,180 TWh (ai-energy-boom), both above the locked AI-Q3 P90 of 1,574 TWh for the SUBSET OECD-38+China — a world figure must exceed a subset figure, so either the model's energy-to-output channel is hot (my reading, since its gamma=0.55 biophysical production function rewards load with GDP) or the locked AI-Q3 band is too low. I take the former but note that both cannot be dismissed at once.

(2) AI-Q2 IS TOO LOW ONCE AGING IS ENDOGENOUS; AI-Q1 IS SLIGHTLY TOO HIGH. 2B holds demographics exogenous, so it misses that labour scarcity is a direct DEMAND PULL: an OECD old-age ratio going 31% -> 39-41% raises the shadow wage of the marginal worker, and firm adoption of a cheap software tool is far more elastic to a wage signal than aggregate measured TFP is. Coupled, I would raise AI-Q2 (OECD-38 share of firms >=10 employees using AI directly in production >=50% by 2036) from 21.3% to ~27-28%. But I would LOWER AI-Q1 (2032-36 TFP lift >=+0.50 pp/yr) from 23.0% to ~21%, because the sectors the demographic pull directs AI INTO — health, long-term care, education, public administration — are precisely the sectors whose output is measured by their input in the national accounts, so diffusion there registers as spending and employment, never as measured TFP. DIRECTION: the coupling widens the wedge between DIFFUSION BREADTH (up) and MEASURED PRODUCTIVITY (down), which is the Hulten/Baumol trap. This is also why my CQ6-A is only 9 while CQ6-B is 45: broad adoption is compatible with an unimpressive aggregate.

(3) 2A's OWN INTERNAL ARITHMETIC ON r IS IN TENSION WITH 2B's CAPEX BOOM. 2A states that aging worsens global (r-g) by ~+1.0 pp "even where a frictionless r* eases" while slowing global growth by ~-1.1 pp/yr. The identity dr = d(r-g) + dg then gives dr = +1.0 - 1.1 = -0.1 pp: the demographic block implies r is roughly FLAT. But 2B's AI investment surge (my build: ~+1.1 pp of GDP of incremental investment demand in the OECD) should raise r* by +55 to +110 bps through the saving-investment market. Both can hold only if the capex is largely internally financed from hyperscaler cash flow (the locked $1.4T of commitments against $300B equity and $650B debt leaves only ~$450B unfunded against a ~$30T/yr global saving pool) or largely cancelled — which is AI-Q4's 66% again, arriving from a third direction. DIRECTION: the reconciliation that satisfies all three locked priors simultaneously is a LARGELY SELF-FINANCED AND PARTLY ABORTED capex cycle, which is also the reading that makes my CQ4 P50 of 2.1% consistent with a 1.72% starting anchor, and which pushes mass toward CQ6-B and CQ6-D rather than toward CQ6-A. Secondary note on CQ1: 2B's AI-Q5 (38% for a >=3.5 pp J/K/M labour-share fall) is in tension with CQ1's second conjunct once the composition effect is made endogenous — a falling labour SHARE in a shrinking, up-skilling sector is fully compatible with a RISING median hourly wage in that sector, because displacement removes the junior and median worker first. The ensemble should not treat AI-Q5 and the J+K+M wage-compression leg of CQ1 as the same bet.

CONJUNCT 1 — GDP-weighted OECD-38 core CPI/PCE avg >=2.50%/yr over 2027-2036: marginal 62%. OBSERVED (hard administrative): US core PCE +3.1% y/y September 2026 (BEA release 29 October 2026), +0.3% m/m, "the same pace as a revised reading for August"; prior month 3.0%. One secondary outlet reported 3.6% — that is HEADLINE PCE, not core, and I am not using it as core. Euro area: October 2026 flash was scheduled for 4 November 2026 and is unverified at my horizon; latest euro-area headline found is 3.8% y/y for September 2026 "against a forecast of 3.6%" (secondary aggregator — the results "conflict on the timing of the euro area's latest data", some pages saying the last confirmed reading was July 2026). So the START is 2.1-3.1% core across the big weights, and US core PCE has printed >=2.5% every year 2021-2026.
WEIGHTED SKEW ARITHMETIC (my effort's core requirement): OECD core baskets are shelter- and services-heavy — shelter alone is ~30-33% of US core CPI and ~17-18% of core PCE; medical + other administered services add roughly another 15-20%. Three blocs: (a) shelter + care + construction-intensive + electricity-exposed services, weight ~0.45-0.55, running 3.5-5.0%; (b) software/media/communications/professional services, weight ~0.20-0.25, the AI-deflation bloc, 0.0-1.0%; (c) tradable goods, weight ~0.25, 1.0-2.0% with tariff pass-through offsetting China export deflation. Hot mix: 0.50x4.5 + 0.25x1.5 + 0.25x2.0 = 3.1%. Cold mix: 0.45x3.5 + 0.30x0.5 + 0.25x1.5 = 2.1%. The decade average lands >=2.50% in most mixes because AI CANNOT DISINFLATE RENT, and the 2027-2030 impulse leg is observable now, not extrapolated: US residential electricity rates rose 7.3% between April 2025 and April 2026 (EIA data via secondary), EIA STEO has the 2026 residential average at 18.2 c/kWh with commercial sales (incl. data centres) growing "about 2.2% in 2026 and 5.3% in 2027" against residential sales growth "only about 0.5% a year", and commercial demand surpassing residential "for the first time on record in 2027." CAVEAT VERBATIM, and it matters: the PJM independent market monitor "attributed roughly 63% of the 2025-2026 auction price surge to AI-focused data center demand", but an EPRI study "found that between 2015 and 2024, data center growth in the United States modestly reduced average retail electricity rates, which conflicts with the PJM findings", and PolitiFact rated a June 2026 claim about bills rising up to 267% near data centers "Mostly False." The attribution is contested; the rate increase itself is not. Also note "Utilities cite higher fuel prices for generation and expenses for bolstering the transmission grid" — not only data centres. Front-loading arithmetic: 2027-2030 at ~2.9% leaves 2031-2036 needing only >=2.23% to clear 2.50%. 62%.

CONJUNCT 2 — China headline CPI avg <1.50%/yr over 2027-2036: marginal 52%, and this is where my prior MOVED AGAINST the consensus deflation call. OBSERVED (hard, NBS via Mysteel): China CPI +0.9% y/y September 2026; +1.0% y/y June 2026. October 2026 is not out — NBS releases around 9 November and today is 4 November 2026, so it is unverified at my horizon; most search hits for "October CPI" are October 2025 (CPI +0.2%, PPI -2.1%, "the 37th straight month of decline") and are the WRONG YEAR. Rowe Price (April 2026 institutional outlook), which argues "the oil price jump resulting from the Middle East conflict helped flip the change in PPI into positive territory in March 2026 given the close correlation of Chinese PPI and oil prices" and expects "the year-over-year change in China's producer price index (PPI) will remain positive through 2026", under the title "As China's Disinflation Fades, Inflation Risks May Rise Globally." One analyst caveat kept verbatim: "PPI will stay under pressure until the property market stabilizes and consumer confidence recovers", adding "the campaign alone is unlikely to change the trend." 52%.

CORRELATION: approximately zero, with a small POSITIVE channel I will name rather than assume away — tariffs/fragmentation simultaneously RAISE OECD goods prices and LOWER Chinese domestic prices (diverted export supply stays home and gluts the domestic market), which is exactly the joint cell the question asks for. Offsetting that, a common global energy/commodity impulse lifts both. Net r ~ +0.05. JOINT: 0.62 x 0.52 = 0.322, x1.05 = 0.338 -> 34.

hypothesis_critique.a: The failure word is SMOOTHLY, and behind it a second one, SUPPLY. The plank presumes a labour-quantity problem; every current series says it is an ADMINISTERED-PRICE problem. Japan: job-to-applicant ratio in care of 3.9x — 'the crisis is already underway' — alongside care salaries 'below the average for all industries by a margin of more than 60,000 yen (US$400)' per month, because 'Care service prices are determined not by market mechanisms but by care reimbursement rates that the government revises every three years.' A decade of 3.9x excess demand produced no wage convergence, so adding displaced white-collar bodies to the queue changes nothing about the clearing wage. Projected shortfall ~250,000 workers in FY2026 against ~2.15m employed, rising to ~570,000 by FY2040; Japan's actual policy response is not labour reallocation from software but subsidized overseas recruitment, where 'Only about half of the government's target for foreign specified-skilled workers in nursing care had been reached by the end of 2023' (28,400 entrants). Separately, the one hard displacement signal — Stanford Digital Economy Lab on ADP payroll, 'roughly a 16% reduction in entry-level positions for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-sensitive roles after 2024' (a separate summary says 14%) — is concentrated in software development and customer support, cohorts whose licensure, physical-work tolerance and wage expectations do not map onto ISIC Q at a reimbursement-set wage. That study's own authors 'later published a follow-up report in February highlighting the job impacts of economic forces such as interest rates'; economist Jed Kolko 'disputed the findings'; and it is relative-to-experienced-workers, not absolute. Nothing in any series shows net flow from J into Q. 6.
hypothesis_critique.b: Two failure words. BLOCKS is simply false as a mechanism: AI compresses the VIRTUAL channel (BPO voice, routine IT services, document processing) while leaving the PHYSICAL channel untouched — and the physical channel is precisely what the locked 2A demographics demand more of. The live telemetry is a receiving-country PULL, not a block: Japan's health ministry 'will subsidize travel expenses' for tokuyo operators and vocational schools recruiting care workers from Southeast Asia from FY2025, having hit only ~50% of its specified-skilled-worker target; Germany's Triple Win program remains 'the main recruitment channel for foreign care workers'; Eurofound 'has warned that vacancies have increased in all countries except Romania and Bulgaria, and will continue to.' The Philippines' export mix is nurses, seafarers, construction and domestic/care work — the AI-immune half. SEVERELY is the second failure: India's exposed slice is the IT/BPO services line, a single-digit share of Indian GDP, against which sits domestic demand and a widening physical-migration channel. The honest form of the plank is a MARGIN compression and a MIX shift inside virtual services, with the physical channel appreciating. I keep 17 rather than lower because the virtual compression is real and concentrated, and because remittance-dependent Philippine provinces with BPO rather than seafaring exposure can be hit hard locally. 17.
hypothesis_critique.c: The failure word is FALLS — specifically, falls TO WHAT, left unstated. The SHAPE of this plank is close to my own effort's central path and I score it highest of the four: hot 2027-2030 (US core PCE already 3.1% y/y in September 2026 with +0.3% m/m momentum, euro-area headline 3.8% in September 2026, Spanish core 3.1%, US residential electricity +7.3% y/y April 2025-April 2026, commercial electricity sales +5.3% in 2027 per EIA, hyperscaler capex $725-828B in 2026 and analyst models above $1T for 2027, tariff pass-through live), then genuine deceleration in the 2030s as capex digests and white-collar services automate. What the plank gets wrong is the LANDING LEVEL. OECD core baskets are shelter- and administered-services-heavy — shelter alone ~30-33% of US core CPI and ~17-18% of core PCE — and AI deflates the ~0.20-0.25 weight bloc (software, media, communications, professional services), not the ~0.45-0.55 bloc (rent, care, construction, electricity-exposed services). My central 2032-36 OECD core is ~2.3-2.4%: lower than 2027-2030 but still above target, which is 'falls' in direction and 'fails' as a return to 2%. The plank also silently assumes the 2030s disinflation is OECD-sourced; the single most important 2030s disinflation channel in the standard story — Chinese export deflation — is the one my telemetry says is ALREADY FADING (PPI positive since March 2026; T. Rowe Price, 'As China's Disinflation Fades, Inflation Risks May Rise Globally'). 54.
hypothesis_critique.d: Two failure words, and they are different kinds of failure. EVENTUALLY is unfalsifiable within the question's horizon: it places the claim outside Dec 2036 by construction, so as a forecast it is not wrong, it is empty. WINS conflates three distinct objects — aggregate real GDP, GDP per capita, and the growth RATE — and the plank needs the third while the intuition supports at most the first. On my own CQ3 it does not win by 2036: P50 1.8%/yr for the combined block against ~2.44% in 2026, i.e. demographics are still beating AI through the resolution window, with P(>=2.6%) = 17.6%. EXPONENTIAL is the third weak word: what is observably exponential is CAPEX, not measured output. Census BTOS has national AI use at 19.8% as of 3 May 2026 with the two leading sectors — Information 39.7%, Finance 33.9% — showing a change since December that is statistically indistinguishable from zero ('neither sector shifted significantly since December'), and part of the headline rise reflects the November 2025 question change from 'in producing goods or services' to 'in any business function' rather than adoption. Meanwhile Microsoft 'expects calendar-year capex of about $170 billion, DOWN from its prior outlook due to delays in third-party data-center capacity' — a physical, not a compute, constraint. Exponential inputs meeting a Hulten/measurement ceiling is the live reading. 14.

ADMINISTERED PRICES as the transmission block in ISIC Q. wave1.coupling_tension:
THREE TENSIONS, with directions.

(1) AI-Q3 (OECD-38 + China strict operational data-centre electricity, ensemble P50 998.2 TWh for 2036, from ~365 TWh in 2024 — a ~2.7x) is TOO HIGH once demographics are endogenous, and I would shade the coupled P50 down ~10-15% to ~850-900 TWh while fattening the lower tail. The reason is not chips and not capex; it is RETAIL-RATE POLITICS with a demographically rising weight. Observed: US residential rates +7.3% y/y April 2025-April 2026; EIA has commercial sales growing 5.3% in 2027 against residential 0.5%/yr and commercial surpassing residential 'for the first time on record in 2027'; PJM's independent market monitor attributed ~63% of the 2025-26 capacity auction price surge to AI data centres (EPRI dissents, finding data-centre growth 2015-2024 'modestly reduced average retail electricity rates', and PolitiFact rated a 267% bill claim 'Mostly False' — the attribution is contested, the increase is not); electric bills have already reached 'the top of the midterm agenda'. The locked 2A old-age ratio move from ~31% to 39-41% mechanically grows the voter bloc least able to absorb a nominal electricity bill increase and most reliably mobilized, which converts a price complaint into an interconnection and large-load-tariff veto. The physical constraint is already visible on the supply side too: Microsoft cut its CY2026 capex to ~$170bn 'due to delays in third-party data-center capacity.' AI-Q3's P50 was formed with demographics exogenous and therefore with no political price-elasticity term at all.

(2) AI-Q5 (cognitive J/K/M labour compensation share falling >=3.5pp, 38.2%) and CQ1's second conjunct are ANTI-CORRELATED through a composition identity, and a panel that treats them as co-moving will double-count. The observed displacement mechanism is an entry-level hiring collapse — Stanford Digital Economy Lab on ADP payroll, 'roughly a 16% reduction in entry-level positions for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-sensitive roles after 2024' (a parallel summary says 14%; the authors' own February follow-up foregrounds interest rates; Jed Kolko disputes the causal attribution; the estimate is relative to experienced workers, not absolute). Truncating the bottom of the J+K+M wage distribution LOWERS the sector's compensation share while RAISING its measured median hourly wage. So AI-Q5 being TRUE makes CQ1 HARDER. Direction: any coupled estimate that raises CQ1 because it believes AI-Q5 is internally inconsistent.

(3) AI-Q1 (2032-36 TFP lift >=+0.50pp, 23.0%) is marginally TOO LOW with demographics endogenous, but by less than the demand-pull story implies — call it +1 to +3pp, to ~25%. Aging is a genuine automation demand pull: it raises the shadow wage in exactly the physical and care tasks where diffusion has been slowest, and locked 2A's healthy-aging evidence ('70 in 2022 = 53 in 2000', 41 countries, N ~ 1M, +0.4pp/yr to global growth 2025-2050) lengthens working lives into the automation-complementary range. But the SAME demographics bind the fiscal capacity to subsidize adoption (OECD net interest 2% -> 3% of GDP; China's pension and social-security subsidies already ~2.9T RMB or ~10.1% of fiscal expenditure), raise the cost of capital that finances it ((r - g) worse by ~+1.0pp; gross public debt >100% of GDP by 2029), and cap the electricity it runs on. Net direction: slightly up, nearly cancelling — which is itself the finding, because the ensemble's instinct is to treat aging as a one-way drag that AI must offset.

(4) Smaller but sharp: AI-Q4's 66% capex-impairment call and CQ5's second conjunct are in direct tension inside the SAME scenario. The impairment path is disinflationary, so the equity crash it produces is one in which G7 nominal yields FALL hard — which breaks CQ5's bond-failure conjunct. Treating AI-Q4 at 66% as raising CQ5 gets the sign backwards; it lowers it, and that is why my CQ5 is 13 against a ~75% decade base rate for a -25% MSCI World drawdown.

So the observed +7.3% y/y US residential electricity rate rise, the EIA commercial-vs-residential crossover, and PJM's contested ~63% attribution (EPRI dissenting, PolitiFact rating a 267% claim 'Mostly False') touch the resolution measure only as second-round business cost. A genuinely severe relative-price crisis can coexist with an unremarkable core aggregate.

CORRELATED-EVIDENCE DISCIPLINE: the main failure mode of this seat is multiplying likelihood ratios across signals that are readings of ONE latent state. I collapsed US core PCE 3.1%, Destatis core 2.1%, INE core 3.1% and euro headline 3.8% into a single cluster with LR 2.2 instead of a product of ~4.5, and applied a further 0.62 independence haircut for overlap with the structural correction already embedded in the 0.50 starting odds. Un-clustered, my CQ2 would have printed ~45 instead of 32.

THE CHINA PPI LIKELIHOOD RATIO IS WEAK, which is my main disagreement with my own evidence seat. The Scout calls the PPI sign flip (+5.0% y/y Sept 2026, single-source and unconfirmed; +4.1% Jun 2026; T. Rowe Price corroborating direction and oil causation) 'the single most under-priced signal' against the 2030s-China-deflation view. But China ran PPI ~+6.3% in 2017 with CPI +1.6%, and ~+8.1% in 2021 with CPI +0.9% — P(PPI spike | CPI stays low) is HIGH, so the LR is ~0.75 before the single-source caveat, not the 0.4-0.5 the signal's framing implies. I moved conjunct B only 0.58 → 0.55, and the move came mostly from the back-half demographic flip, not from PPI.

OBSERVED MARKET PRICES BEAT RECONSTRUCTED ANCHORS (LR ~3:1), which resolved the only sharp Wave-1 conflict on CQ4. Bund 10y at 3.28% ('its highest since May 5, 2011') and JGB 10y at 3.000% ('the first time since 1996') imply non-US G7 reals of ~1.0-1.3%, not the 0.3-0.5% assumed in the lowest Wave-1 anchor. Re-anchoring gives 1.95-1.96% G7 GDP-weighted versus the locked US TIPS 2.60%, i.e. the question is ~60-65bp below its own headline anchor and still ~46% a US TIPS question.

CONFLICTING TELEMETRY IS A 1:1 SIGNAL AND MUST BE SPENT AS SUCH. Macquarie (1 Oct 2026) reports the 10y JGB term premium up ~84bp since the Takaichi government was elected and the US 10y term premium 'trended sideways' while the real yield 'has risen a lot'; MUFG (26 Oct 2026) reports term-premium NARROWING ex-asset-swap pulling the 10y JGB down. Two houses, opposite signs, same instrument, same month. I halved the term-premium add (+0.50 → +0.35), which is the single reason my CQ4 P50 landed back on the prior's 2.15 rather than above it.
