wave_audit.wave1_spread: Two places, both diagnostic rather than random. CQ2 had a 20-point spread (Historian 14, Fermi 24, Scout 34) and it was ENTIRELY about what the measure contains, not about inflation: Historian built a US-style CORE-OECD basket and got 2.14%, Fermi added the five high-inflation OECD-38 members and got 2.503% on an 8.5% market-GDP weight, and the Scout started from the observed 3.1% y/y US core PCE of September 2026 and worked forward. Three lenses, one question, three different baskets. CQ5 had an 18-point spread (Scout 13, Historian 22, Fermi 31) and it reduced to one unobservable conditional, P(G7 bonds fail to fall >=50bp | a >=25% MSCI World drawdown): 0.38 / 0.55 / 0.425, on which no 2026 telemetry exists at all. The three lenses AGREED remarkably on CQ4's P50 (2.10/2.15/2.10) while disagreeing by 26bp on the anchor they each computed, which is the opposite pathology — convergence on an output while disagreeing on the input. And all three converged on CQ6-B as modal (42-53) citing each other's independence as support, which the red team correctly identified as three lenses inheriting one measurement assumption from the effort brief's own phrasing.
wave_audit.what_wave2_changed: THE RED-TEAMER LANDED FOUR REAL HITS AND I MOVED ON ALL FOUR. (i) He killed Fermi's aging-drag arithmetic, including Fermi's own certification of it ('a no-aging China counterfactual of ~4.9% minus 2.7 = 2.2%. The two routes agree') as the same subtraction performed twice against a no-aging counterfactual while the realized 4.4-4.5% of 2026 already embeds the drag since China's 2012 working-age peak. I moved China's 2032-36 leg from Fermi's 2.2-2.4% to 2.65%, worth +0.15pp on my CQ3 P50, though I did not go to his 3.0-3.4% because the -2.7pp intensifies across 2025-2050 and convergence deceleration is additive. (ii) He killed Fermi's CQ5 claim that a decade MOVE mean of 105 'requires seven years at ~112, not spikes' with the arithmetic that one 18-month crisis at 175 on a ~100 baseline clears it — scope insensitivity on a fat-tailed average. (iii) He killed Fermi's -100bp Japan repression wedge using the Scout's own observed 3.000% JGB (first time since 1996), a ~22bp swing on the G7 aggregate from one leg. (iv) He killed the Historian's shelter argument as wrong-signed: aging RAISES households per capita through widowhood and single occupancy and suppresses turnover, and Japan's household count rose for roughly two decades past its population peak. HE ALSO RESCUED ONE THING, and it is the best move in Wave 2: he rescued CQ1's second conjunct from the Bayesian's 0.11 by supplying the symmetric composition effect nobody had priced — a fast-expanding care workforce dilutes the F+Q median with low-wage entrants, cancelling the entry-level-truncation argument Fermi and the Scout had run only on the J+K+M side. That removed the entire basis of the Bayesian's -3 move and took my CQ1 to 16. WHERE HE MERELY CONTRARIAN-POSED AND I DID NOT MOVE: the dr = d(r-g) + dg identity. He substituted his own TOTAL growth decline for the locked DEMOGRAPHIC partial to get dr = +0.4pp instead of -0.1pp. That mixes two counterfactuals and is a category error, not a hit; the locked block states what demographics do to (r-g) and to g specifically, so the demographic contribution to r is -0.1pp by construction. I also only half-moved on his AI-Q3 inversion and on his core path of 2.88%, where he stacks three one-directional corrections (full imputation, shelter at 3.5, PPP EM weights) as independent and ignores that euro HICP core carries ~7% rent rather than 44%. THE BAYESIAN UPDATER contributed the two highest-quality items in the effort. He rescued the CQ4 anchor with observed market prices (Bund 3.28% at a 15-year high, JGB 3.000%) against Fermi's reconstructed 1.72%, landing at 1.95-1.96% — I adopt it wholesale. And he killed the Scout's 'single most under-priced signal' on China's PPI flip with the right precedents (PPI ~+6.3% in 2017 with CPI +1.6%; ~+8.1% in 2021 with CPI +0.9%), so P(PPI spike | low CPI) is high and the likelihood ratio is weak — which is why I took China's conjunct B down on the property-stock and back-half-labour arguments instead of on PPI. His correlated-evidence clustering (four hot core prints collapsed into one LR-2.2 cluster rather than a product of ~4.5, plus a 0.62 independence haircut) is the discipline that keeps my conjunct A at 0.64 rather than the Red Team's 0.72. WHERE I DOWN-WEIGHTED HIM: his CQ1 of 8, now defunct, and his halving of the term-premium add on Macquarie-versus-MUFG, which is a 1:1 signal about one month in one instrument being spent against a one-directional decade-long structural case.
wave_audit.unresolved: FOUR THINGS, and the first is the largest. (1) The resolution convention for 'GDP-weighted OECD-38'. Market weights put the five high-inflation members at ~7-8.5%; the constant-2025-USD-PPP basis Section 3 locks puts them at ~11%. That is ~0.25pp on the aggregate — nearly the whole distance between CQ6-B and CQ6-C — and the question text does not settle it, because CQ2 names a local-CPI index, which triggers the lock's own exception clause for the price measure without saying anything about the WEIGHTS. Fermi found this and called it a convention question; the Red-Teamer asserted PPP as settled; neither is right, and I carry ~10% as an expectation over conventions while flagging that my CQ2 and CQ6-C are the two numbers most sensitive to a definition nobody can pin down from the brief. (2) P(G7 bonds fail to rally | >=25% equity drawdown). The full-sample 1970-2025 frequency of ~5 of 9 and the capex-bust-is-disinflationary argument of ~0.38 are both defensible, the spread is 17 points of CQ5, and no 2026 observable discriminates between them. I sit at 0.43 without conviction. (3) Whether the ISIC Q care-labour excess demand resolves as a statutory wage LEVEL JUMP or as quantity rationing. This is the whole of CQ1's second conjunct, it moves the conjunct between 0.12 and 0.33, and the resolution quantity is literally unmeasured at the horizon — the Scout states verbatim that he found no 2026 year-over-year panel broken out for the four sector groups, and ISIC F/Q/J/K/M median hourly at this granularity lives mainly in the 4-yearly Eurostat SES. (4) The deflator treatment of imputed versus market-priced professional and financial services in core PCE. The Red-Teamer's attack is methodologically serious and I accepted it at half strength, but it is a national-accounts measurement question that no amount of forecasting resolves, and it is worth ~0.20-0.35pp on every core build in this effort.
wave_audit.biggest_update: The largest single numeric update from a Wave-1 modal position to my reconciled number is CQ2's conjunct A: from the Historian's 0.27 to my 0.64, a +37-point move in the marginal that carries CQ2 from his 14 to my 32 and drives CQ6-C from his 13 to my 22. The cause is almost entirely accounting rather than economics, and I report the decomposition rather than claim insight: roughly +25 points of the marginal come from the OECD-38 MEMBERSHIP AND WEIGHTING term (five high-inflation members at a 7-11% weight contributing 0.60-0.80pp, which is the entire difference between a ~1.95% core-OECD aggregate and a ~2.65% OECD-38 aggregate), roughly +8 from the Red-Teamer's imputation and shelter-sign corrections taken at half strength, and roughly +4 from the hard 2026 core telemetry (US core PCE 3.1% y/y, Destatis core 2.1%, INE core 3.1%). A reader who rejects the EM-member weighting convention should discount my CQ2 by ~10 points and my CQ6-C by ~6, and my distribution would converge on the Historian's. The second-largest update is CQ5, from the Scout's 13 to 27, driven by the Red-Teamer's correction to the fat-tailed-average arithmetic and the Bayesian's drawdown-multiplicity term; the third is China's 2032-36 growth leg, +0.45pp off Fermi on the double-count.

efforts.effort_name: Equilibrium Real Rates r*, Fiscal Dominance & Term Premia

wave1.lens_self_description: I answered purely as an outside-view reference-class historian — every number is a historical base rate over the widest defensible window, adjusted only for the mechanical labour-force and debt-stock arithmetic inside the locked priors — which forbade me from using any reasoning about AI capability trajectories, model scaling, adoption S-curves, or any mechanism specific to this episode.
wave1.cq1_reasoning: Conjunct A: OECD-38 harmonized unemployment 5-yr average <=5.5%. Reference class: OECD aggregate harmonized unemployment, rolling 5-yr windows 1965-2025 (OECD Main Economic Indicators / Employment Outlook). Decade means approx 3.0% (1960s), 4.5% (1970s), 7.5% (1980s), 7.3% (1990s), 6.4% (2000s), 7.0% (2010s, 8.3% peak 2010), 5.0-5.3% (2021-2025, record lows). Qualifying windows: essentially only the 1960s/early 1970s and windows starting 2018+. Base rate ~27% of ~60 windows. Adjust UP for (i) the current 4.9-5.0% starting level and the high autocorrelation of 5-yr unemployment averages, (ii) the mechanical 2A arithmetic: a shrinking working-age denominator lowers the measured rate independent of labour demand. Adjust DOWN for the base rate that a 5-yr window contains >=1 OECD recession (~60-70% since 1960), which lifts a 5-yr average 0.5-1.5pp off a 5.0% floor. Marginal A = 0.50. Conjunct B: F+Q real median hourly wage beating J+K+M by >=10.0pp cumulatively 2025-2036 (~0.87pp/yr sustained for 11 yr). Reference class: sustained >=10pp 11-yr divergences between two broad sector groups in OECD wage data. The historical sign is the OPPOSITE: skill-biased technical change had J+K+M outpacing F+Q across 1980-2015 in nearly every OECD country. Documented reversals: the Great Compression (1940s, Goldin-Margo), parts of the 1970s union era, and the 2019-2023 "unexpected compression" (Autor-Dube-McGrew: ~5-8pp cumulative low-vs-high-wage reversal over 4 years, i.e. the right pace, but only one episode and partly unwound 2024-25). Roughly 1-2 episodes in a ~65-yr record in EITHER direction; in THIS direction, ~0-1. Base rate ~12-15%. Two further historian-side deductions specific to my effort: (i) ISIC Q median wages are fiscally administered and the 2A debt arithmetic (100%+ of GDP, net interest 2%->3%) makes governments historically poor payers of care labour; (ii) ISIC F is the single most real-rate-sensitive sector, and my CQ4 central case plus the 66% capex-bust prior points to a construction wage air-pocket. (iii) Measurement: if cognitive displacement hits junior/low-end roles first, compositional selection RAISES the J+K+M median, which works mechanically against the plank. Marginal B = 0.14. Correlation: positive (a tight labour market lifts manual/care wages), so P(B|A) ~0.19 vs 0.14. Joint = 0.50 x 0.19 = 0.095 -> 9.
wave1.cq2_reasoning: Conjunct A: OECD-38 GDP-weighted core CPI/PCE >=2.50% average over the 10 years 2027-2036. Widest reference class: rolling 10-yr windows of OECD GDP-weighted core, 1961-2026. Windows starting 1961-1996 overwhelmingly qualify (1970s double-digit, 1980s 5-6%, early 1990s 3-4%); windows starting 1997-2016 essentially never do (GDP-weighted core ~1.6-1.9%, dragged by Japan and the euro area). The 2017-2026 window is borderline (~2.5%) only because 2021-24 ran 3.5-6%. Unconditional base rate ~60% of ~56 windows, but that is dominated by the Great Inflation. Correctly matched reference class is the post-1990 explicit-inflation-target regime: there, 10-yr core averages >=2.5% occur only in windows containing 2021-24, and the euro area has NO 10-yr core window >=2.5% since 1999 (10-yr averages 1.3-1.9%). Conditional base rate ~30-35%. Adjust UP for the ~2.5-2.8% starting level and the Reinhart-Sbrancia revealed preference of high-debt sovereigns for tolerated overshoot. Adjust DOWN for the single best-matched DEMOGRAPHIC reference class available — Japan 1995-2020, where an aging, high-debt, balance-sheet-impaired economy produced ~0% core for 25 years, not inflation — plus the deflationary content of the 66% AI-Q4 capex-bust prior and the BIS Box C demand shortfall. Marginal A = 0.35. Conjunct B: China headline CPI <1.50% average 2027-2036. China CPI history: 1994 ~24%, 1998-2002 ~0/negative, 2003-2011 ~3%, 2012-2019 ~2.1%, 2020-2025 ~0.5% with 2023-25 at or below 0.2%. Qualifying 10-yr windows: only those centred on 1998-2005 and 2016-2025 (2016-25 computes to ~1.4%). Base rate ~34% of ~35 windows. Adjust UP hard: the current state (near-zero CPI, property deleveraging, excess capacity) plus 2A's -60M population and -2.7pp growth drag matches the Japan post-1995 template, and the base rate of ESCAPING an established balance-sheet deflation within 10 years is poor (Japan: 0 for 25 yr). Marginal B = 0.70. Correlation: genuinely NEGATIVE. Chinese deflation is exported to the OECD through tradeable goods (the "China price" channel of 1995-2015), so B makes A harder. Core is services/wage-weighted so the channel is attenuated, not absent: P(A|B) ~0.60 x ... I take P(B|A) = 0.60 vs marginal 0.70. Joint = 0.35 x 0.60 = 0.21 -> 20.
wave1.cq3_reasoning: Reference class: rolling 5-yr annualized PPP-weighted real GDP growth for OECD-38 + China since 1960 (OECD/Penn World Table/Maddison, PPP-weighted with drifting weights). Approximate decade means: 1960s ~5.0%, 1970s ~3.6%, 1980s ~3.1%, 1990s ~2.7%, 2000s ~3.2%, 2010s ~2.8%, 2020-24 ~2.3%. Unconditional distribution: mean ~3.2%, SD across 5-yr windows ~0.9-1.0pp. Band frequencies of 5-yr windows since 1960 (my CQ6 input): >=2.6% in roughly 60-65% of windows; 1.7-2.5% in ~20-25%; <1.7% in ~15-18% (1980-82, 1991-93, 2008-12, 2020-22 clusters). Mechanical adjustment licensed by the locked priors (arithmetic, not forecast): PPP weights by 2032-36 approx 60% OECD-38 / 40% China. OECD-38: 2A sets per-capita growth at 0.6%/yr absent offsets; OECD population growth decelerating to ~0.2-0.3%/yr => headline ~0.8-0.95%. China: 2A sets a -2.7pp aging drag, -60M population 2026-35, worker/retiree 4.4->2.8; the post-miracle convergence reference class (Japan 7%->1% across the 1990s; Korea halving per decade since 1990; Taiwan) puts China 2032-36 at ~2.0-3.0%, centre 2.6%. Mechanical centre = 0.60(0.90) + 0.40(2.60) = 0.54 + 1.04 = 1.58%. Add the 2A healthy-aging offset (+0.4pp/yr global over 2025-50) scaled to this aggregate, plus whatever productivity offset the standalone marginals price at 16-23% probability: +0.4 to +0.5pp. P50 = 2.05%. Width: I deliberately compress the right tail below the unconditional SD, because 3.1%+ requires China ~5% in 2032-36, which directly contradicts the mechanical content of 2A, or OECD ~2.5%, which has no 5-yr precedent since 2000-2007. Left tail keeps the full unconditional recession width (a 5-yr window containing one synchronized recession is the modal historical experience). P10 = 1.0%, P90 = 2.90%; implied sigma ~0.82 left, ~0.66 right.
wave1.cq4_reasoning: DECOMPOSITION (required): CQ4 = r* + real 10y term premium - repression wedge. (1) r*: reference class is decade-average G7 short real neutral. HLW/LW-type estimates and the Schmelzing eight-centuries series put the modern-era real safe rate at ~1.5-2.0% with a secular downtrend of ~-1.6bp/yr; US 10y real averaged ~+2.0% 1953-2025 (FRED GS10 minus CPI) and ~1.5% since 1900 (RBA 1991 citing US estimates); G7 r* in the 2010s was ~0.3-0.5% (US HLW). Boomer dissaving (Goodhart-Pradhan), public-debt supply (literature elasticity ~2-4bp per 1pp debt/GDP; 2A implies +20-30pp through 2031), and physical/grid capex demand push r* up; precautionary saving under labour-income uncertainty, cognitive-labour income compression, and the Chinese plus OECD savings gluts push it down. Centre r* 2032-36 = 1.0% (P10 0.3, P90 1.8), sigma ~0.5. (2) Real term premium: ACM-type US 10y term premium averaged ~+1.0-1.5% across 1961-2010, was ~0/negative in 2015-21, and ~+0.3-0.8% in 2023-26. Base rate: it mean-reverts to ~+0.75% over long samples and is HIGHER in high-debt, high-inflation-volatility regimes, which is where 2A's Debt-at-Risk (P95 117% of GDP, +2.4pp on an AI equity shock) and basis-trade marginal-buyer fragility put us. Centre +0.75% (P10 0.0, P90 +1.6), sigma ~0.7. (3) Repression wedge: a genuine policy option with a real base rate, not a tail. Reinhart-Sbrancia: advanced-economy real rates were negative roughly half the time across 1945-1980 under statutory caps, Regulation Q, and captive bank/pension demand, with a liquidation effect of ~2-3% of GDP/yr; the 2009-2021 QE/YCC episode delivered a de facto wedge of ~-50 to -120bp (Fed QE term-premium estimates; BoJ YCC larger). I assign P(material repression, >=50bp wedge, over 2032-36) = 0.40, expected wedge ~-0.30% with a fat left tail. Central: 1.0 + 0.75 - 0.30 = 1.45, rounded to 1.6 to respect debt-supply crowding-out. STARTING-POINT CORRECTION: the 2.60% TIPS print is US-only. G7 GDP-weighted today is ~0.57(2.6) + 0.17(~0.1) + 0.26(~0.9) = ~1.7%, i.e. the aggregate starts near its own long-run mean, so mean reversion implies very little drift. BASE RATE OF STAYING NEAR THE START: approximate G7 decade averages are ~-1.5% (1970s), +4.5% (1980s), +3.8% (1990s), +2.0% (2000s), +0.3% (2010s), ~0.0% (2020-24); only ~2 of 6 decade transitions kept the average within +/-50bp of the prior level, which is why my interval is deliberately wide rather than pinned to 1.7%. RESPECTING THE 2A DISTINCTION: 2A's "+1.0pp worse global (r-g) even where a frictionless r* eases" is a term-premium and fiscal-arithmetic claim. My CQ3 P50 of 2.05% versus a historical 3.2% norm delivers roughly -1.1pp on the g SIDE ALONE, which over-delivers the entire +1.0pp without r rising at all. Treating 2A as evidence for a high r DOUBLE-COUNTS. That is the single biggest reason my P50 sits at the long-run G7 anchor rather than extrapolating the elevated US print. VARIANCE ATTRIBUTION: the real term premium carries the most variance (sigma ~0.7, ~48% of total), r* next (~0.5, ~25%), the repression wedge third by variance but FIRST in left-tail shape because it is bimodal (0 or -75 to -150bp). P10 = 0.4% (repression plus a demand-shortfall/Japanification world), P50 = 1.6%, P90 = 3.0% (fiscal dominance WITHOUT repression, term-premium spike, 1980s-lite).
wave1.cq5_reasoning: Conjunct A: MOVE 10-yr average >=105 over 2027-2036. Reference class: MOVE daily history since 1988. Full-sample average 93.6 (ETF Trends, June 2024, series start 1988 — note ICE's own developer page dates the index from 1996, so the 1988 figure reflects the Merrill-era series); trailing 10-yr average ~75 (Carmignac); 2017-2019 ~55; the 2022 cycle ~130, the highest sustained regime since 2008. 105 is therefore ABOVE the full-history mean. Of roughly 29 rolling 10-yr windows, those ending in the 1990s and 2000s averaged ~100-110 while those ending 2014-2026 averaged ~75-95. Base rate ~30%. Adjust UP: MOVE is basis-point (not proportional) vol, so a 4%+ nominal yield level mechanically lifts it relative to the 1%-yield 2010s; and rate vol historically tracks inflation and fiscal-policy uncertainty, which is the regime 2A describes. Marginal A = 0.45. Conjunct B: >=1 MSCI World >=25% peak-to-trough drawdown in the window DURING WHICH G7 GDP-weighted 10y nominal yields fail to fall >=50bp (or rise >=25bp). Step 1 — base rate of a >=25% MSCI World drawdown inside a 10-yr window: episodes since 1970 are 1973-74, 1980-82, 1987, 1990 (~-26%), 2000-02 (~-50%), 2007-09 (~-57%), 2020 (~-34%), 2022 (~-26/27%). Of ~47 rolling 10-yr windows, roughly 38-40 contain one; the clean exceptions are windows wholly inside 1991-1999 and 2010-2019 (max drawdowns ~-19 to -22%). Base rate ~85%. Step 2 — CONDITIONAL on a drawdown, frequency that bonds failed to rally: correlated regime in 1973-74 (yields rose), 1981-82 (rose during the equity leg), 1990 (roughly flat/up on the oil shock, marginal), and 2022 (rose sharply); flight-to-quality regime in 1987 (US 10y ~-90bp), 2000-02, 2007-09, and 2020. That is ~3.5-4 of 8, base rate ~45%. Step 3 — windows contain ~1.5-1.8 drawdowns, so P(at least one is the correlated type) over a 10-yr window computes to ~0.55-0.62 historically; windows containing 1973-74, 1981-82, 1990 or 2022 are a large share of the post-1970 record. Marginal B = 0.60. Correlation: STRONGLY positive — high rate vol and a correlated bond-equity selloff share one driver (inflation and fiscal uncertainty rather than a pure demand shock), so P(B|A) ~0.76 against a 0.60 marginal. Joint = 0.45 x 0.76 = 0.34. Unextremized conjunction discount applied: the independent product would be 0.27 and the naive single-conjunct intuition would be 0.60+, so 34 sits where correlation warrants and no further.
wave1.cq6_reasoning: Applied strictly by lexical priority against my OWN CQ3 and CQ2. CONSISTENCY CHECK PERFORMED: (1) A = P(CQ3 growth >=2.6%). My CQ3 is P10 1.0 / P50 2.05 / P90 2.90, implying right-side sigma ~0.66; P(>=2.6) = P(z >= 0.83) = 0.20. I report 19, within rounding. I did NOT import A's qualitative riders ("debt stabilizes via growth, broad wage gains") because the disambiguation lock defines A by growth alone — had I used the riders, A would be lower still, since my CQ1 of 9 denies broad wage gains and my CQ4 decomposition denies easy growth-led debt stabilization. Note the historian tension: >=2.6% was the MAJORITY (~60-65%) of 5-yr OECD+China windows since 1960, so A at 19 is a large downward adjustment, licensed only because the 2A demographic block is labour-input arithmetic rather than forecast. (2) C = P(OECD core >=2.7% AND growth <2.0%). From the CQ2 conjunct-A work, P(core >=2.50%) = 0.35, so P(core >=2.70%) ~0.27. P(growth <2.0%) from my CQ3 = 0.53. Stagflation couples them positively: P(growth<2.0 | core>=2.7) ~0.62. C = 0.27 x 0.62 = 0.167 -> 17. This is coherent with my CQ2 of 20, since both are subsets of the same 27-35% high-core region and CQ2 instead conditions on China deflation (0.60) rather than low growth (0.62). (3) D = P(growth <1.7% AND core <2.0%), disjoint from A and C. P(growth<1.7%) from my CQ3 left side (sigma ~0.82) = P(z < -0.43) = 0.33. P(core <2.0%) ~0.45. The demand-shortfall mechanism couples them positively: P(core<2.0 | growth<1.7) ~0.60. D = 0.33 x 0.60 = 0.20. (4) B = residual = 100 - 19 - 17 - 20 = 44. B carries the awkward leftover cell (growth <1.7% with core 2.0-2.7%, and growth 2.0-2.6% with core >=2.7%) in addition to the literal 1.7-2.5% band, which is exactly why the residual is the modal regime. Historian cross-check: the unconditional 5-yr-window band frequencies since 1960 were roughly 62% / 22% / 16% across the >=2.6% / 1.7-2.5% / <1.7% growth cuts; my distribution redistributes ~43pp out of the top band into B and D, which is the whole content of the demographic arithmetic.

hypothesis_critique.a: "SMOOTHLY" carries the entire failure, and the base rate for it is near zero. Reference class: every large occupational-displacement episode in the OECD record. US/UK manufacturing 1979-2000, the Appalachian and Ruhr coal regions, and the China shock (Autor-Dorn-Hanson: displaced workers did NOT reallocate across occupations; local labour markets adjusted over 20+ years mainly through non-employment and disability rolls, not re-employment elsewhere). The specific transition demanded here is worse than the average case on all three historical blockers: licensure (nursing and personal-care credentialing takes 1-4 years), wage level (ISIC Q pays ~40-60% of ISIC J/K/M median), and geography (care demand is where the old live, cognitive job losses are where the offices are). Displaced mid-career professionals' observed transition rate into licensed care work is in the low single digits of percent. Strip "smoothly" and the plank becomes unfalsifiable; keep it and the base rate says 5.
hypothesis_critique.b: TWO words fail, "BLOCKS" harder than "severely". "Blocks" conflates two channels the scope lock itself separates. AI substitutes for cross-border VIRTUAL services (BPO, back office, voice) but cannot substitute for PHYSICAL labour migration, and the 2A demographic pull is overwhelmingly for physical and care labour. Philippines: OFW remittances run ~$34-38B/yr at ~8-9% of GDP and are dominated by care, maritime and construction placements — the channel aging ENLARGES; BPO at ~$35-38B revenue and ~1.7-1.8M jobs is the genuinely exposed slice, so one channel is threatened and the other is pulled. India: IT services exports of ~$200B+ are only ~5-6% of GDP and the sector has absorbed three prior platform shifts (Y2K-to-offshoring, offshoring-to-cloud, cloud-to-SaaS) without a decade of national-level damage. "Severely" then fails on the reference class: the base rate of a trade or technology shock destroying an emerging exporter's development path within 10 years is low — Mexico post-NAFTA-China, Bangladesh RMG automation scares, the Philippine BPO's own 2016-2020 voice-automation scare all resolved as reallocation, not national distress. 18.
hypothesis_critique.c: "THEN" carries the failure, not "hot" or "falls". The shape is the modal historical outcome — Ha-Kose-Ohnsorge count 111 post-WWII inflation-spike episodes with inflation back near pre-shock levels inside ~5 years in the majority — and it is broadly consistent with my own CQ2, where only 35% of the mass has OECD core averaging >=2.50% across the full decade. So the plank is directionally right and I score it as the only plank above coin-flip. What "then" assumes away is the double-hump, which is precisely what the 2A fiscal arithmetic generates and what the two best-matched historical cases produced: 1973-75 fell then 1979-82 returned worse, and 1946-48/1950-51 the same. Sequencing, not direction, is the exposure. 50.
hypothesis_critique.d: "EVENTUALLY" makes it unfalsifiable and "WINS" is undefined; between them they void the plank. Dated to the 2036 horizon it is already contradicted by my own CQ3 P50 of 2.05% against a 3.2% historical norm for this aggregate — demography wins on the growth LEVEL even in my central case. The direct reference class for "technology will offset demography" claims is the set of advanced economies that aged first WHILE leading in automation: Japan 1990-2025 (world leader in industrial robot density; real GDP growth ~0.6%/yr, per capita ~0.8%/yr), Germany, Italy, Korea since 2015, and the euro area 2000-2025. That is 0 for ~5 on "growth wins" within a decade of the ratio inflecting. I also observe that "exponential" is doing illegitimate work: output growth depends on the growth rate of a factor's contribution, not on exponential growth in a capability metric, and my lens forbids me from reasoning about the capability metric at all. 15.

key_drivers: The (r-g) deterioration in 2A is delivered mostly by the g side, not the r side: my CQ3 P50 of 2.05% versus a 3.2% historical norm is already ~-1.1pp of g, which over-delivers the whole +1.0pp without r rising at all. Reading 2A as evidence for a high G7 real yield double-counts, and this single arithmetic point does more to hold my CQ4 P50 near the long-run anchor than any other consideration.

Real term premium mean reversion carries ~48% of my CQ4 variance (sigma ~0.7pp) against r* at ~25% (sigma ~0.5pp): the long-sample ACM-type US 10y term premium average of ~+1.0-1.5% across 1961-2010 versus ~0 in 2015-21 is a wider historical spread than any plausible r* range, so the premium, not neutral, is where the uncertainty lives.

Financial repression at P=0.40, treated as policy base rate rather than tail: advanced-economy real rates were negative roughly half of 1945-1980 under caps and captive demand (Reinhart-Sbrancia, ~2-3% of GDP/yr liquidation), and QE/YCC delivered a -50 to -120bp de facto wedge in 2009-2021. This is bimodal (0 or -75 to -150bp) and is what fattens my CQ4 left tail rather than widening its centre.

Japan 1995-2025 as the single best-matched demographic reference class, which resolved DISinflationary with low real rates and with growth NOT winning — this one case pushes CQ2's OECD conjunct down, CQ2's China conjunct up, CQ6-D up, and hypothesis plank (d) to 15.

The announced-capex-supercycle impairment base rate: transcontinental rail 1870s-90s, telecom/long-haul fibre 1999-2002 (the large majority of laid capacity dark or impaired), US shale 2015-2020 ($300B+ in write-downs), US nuclear 1974-1984 (~100 reactor cancellations), Japan 1986-1991. On base rates alone the AI-Q4 marginal of 66% looks LOW to me (~75-80%), and the implied demand shock is a real-rate depressant, not an elevator.

Mean reversion from a mis-anchored starting point: 2.60% is the US-only TIPS print, while the G7 GDP-weighted aggregate starts near ~1.7% (Japan ~0.1%, Germany ~0.3-0.6%, UK ~1.3%). The G7 aggregate therefore starts essentially AT its own long-run mean (US 10y real averaged ~+2.0% 1953-2025 and G7 runs below US), so the 2032-36 average needs little drift — but only ~2 of 6 decade transitions since 1970 kept the average within +/-50bp of its prior level, which is why my interval is wide rather than tight.

falsification_signposts.signpost: G7 GDP-weighted 10y sovereign real yield (nominal benchmark minus 10y inflation swap) sustains a trailing-12-month average >= 2.75% with no repression measure enacted in any G7 sovereign
falsification_signposts.if_observed_implies: Falsifies my core claim that the (r-g) deterioration is delivered on the g side and that the G7 aggregate mean-reverts to its long-run anchor. CQ4 P50 up ~+70bp to ~2.3% and P10 up to ~1.2%; CQ6-C up ~+8pp and CQ6-D down ~-6pp; CQ5 up ~+6pp via the term-premium/MOVE channel.

falsification_signposts.signpost: China headline CPI 24-month average >= 2.0%
falsification_signposts.if_observed_implies: Breaks my 70% China-deflation conjunct and, more damagingly, breaks the Japan-1995 reference class that anchors four of my answers. CQ2 falls from 20 to ~8; CQ3 P50 up ~+0.2pp; CQ6-D down ~-5pp; hypothesis plank (d) up from 15 to ~25.

falsification_signposts.signpost: Cumulative announced hyperscaler AI capex impairments plus cancellations < 5% of announced buildout AND net external AI software/API revenue >= 1.0x annualized AI compute D&A for four consecutive quarters
falsification_signposts.if_observed_implies: Falsifies my capex-supercycle base rate (rail/fibre/shale/nuclear), which I used to argue AI-Q4 should be ABOVE 66%. CQ3 P50 up ~+0.4pp to ~2.45%; CQ6-A up ~+10pp to ~29 and CQ6-D down ~-8pp; CQ4 P50 up ~+40bp via sustained r* pressure from capex demand for loanable funds.

falsification_signposts.signpost: OECD median real hourly wage in ISIC Q outpaces ISIC J+K+M cumulatively by >= 5.0pp since 2025 (i.e. on pace for the 10pp threshold), measured on harmonized OECD/Eurostat structure-of-earnings data
falsification_signposts.if_observed_implies: Roughly doubles my CQ1 conjunct-B marginal from 14% to ~28% and refutes my claim that fiscally administered ISIC Q wages plus real-rate-squeezed ISIC F cannot sustain the divergence. CQ1 up from 9 to ~16-18; CQ6-A and CQ6-B shift ~+4pp toward A.

falsification_signposts.signpost: Explicit financial-repression measure enacted in >= 2 G7 sovereigns: statutory bank or pension sovereign-holding mandates, reinstated yield-curve control, or an announced standing issuance buyer-of-last-resort facility
falsification_signposts.if_observed_implies: Confirms rather than falsifies my 40% repression prior, but moves the distribution: CQ4 P50 down ~-50bp to ~1.1% and P10 down to ~-0.1%, with the left tail dominating. CQ6-C up ~+5pp (repression is a listed C marker) at the expense of B; CQ5 ambiguous — repression suppresses MOVE but makes the correlated-shock conjunct more likely.

wave1.coupling_tension: PRIMARY TENSION — AI-Q4 (66%) and AI-Q3 (P50 ~998 TWh) cannot comfortably be held jointly once demographics are endogenous through the FINANCING channel, which is my effort's subject. 2B holds demographics exogenous and therefore holds the cost of capital facing a 15-20-year-lived, electricity-intensive asset exogenous too. Endogenize it and three 2A forces compound on the same discount rate: boomer life-cycle dissaving draining the loanable-funds pool, public-debt rollover volumes absorbing what is left (global gross debt >100% of GDP by 2029, net interest 2%->3%), and eroding sovereign convenience yields with levered basis-trade absorption as the fragile marginal buyer. DIRECTION: AI-Q4 should move UP, from 66% to ~75-80% — which is also where the pure capex-supercycle base rate sits (rail, fibre 1999-2002, shale, nuclear, Japan 1980s) — because impairment is a discount-rate event before it is a demand event. AI-Q3 should move DOWN at the P50 and harder at the P90: roughly 1,000 TWh requires on the order of $2-3T of generation plus grid capex, financed at a WACC that the demographic savings drain and sovereign crowding-out make materially more expensive, and grid interconnection is itself the most rate-sensitive long-duration asset class in the stack. I would carry AI-Q3 to ~P50 850 and ~P90 1,300 under endogenous demographics. Note the self-consistency: a 66%+ AI-Q4 and a 998 TWh AI-Q3 P50 are already in mild tension with each other even before demographics, since impairment at scale is what truncates the build. SECOND TENSION — AI-Q5 (38.2% for a >=3.5pp fall in J/K/M labour compensation share) is NOT transmissible to CQ1's conjunct B, and a naive coupling would double-count it. A falling compensation SHARE is compatible with a RISING median wage in the same sectors, because if displacement removes junior and low-end cognitive roles first, compositional selection raises the median of the survivors. AI-Q5 resolving YES therefore does not raise the probability that F+Q beats J+K+M by 10pp on medians; under the compositional channel it LOWERS it. THIRD TENSION — the 2A r-side is internally inconsistent. Taking "aging worsens global (r-g) by ~+1.0pp even where a frictionless r* eases" together with the same block's BIS Box C aggregate-demand-shortfall warning and the Chinese savings glut implies a G7 real yield that cannot simultaneously be high (fiscal arithmetic) and low (demand shortfall). My resolution is that the +1.0pp is delivered almost entirely by g falling and secondarily by the term premium, not by r* rising. DIRECTION: this makes the fiscal-arithmetic reading of 2A consistent with a MIDDLING CQ4 rather than a high one, and it means a panelist who reads 2A as an r* claim will produce a CQ4 that is too high by roughly 60-90bp.

wave1.lens_self_description: Fermi Structural Decomposer applied to the r*/term-premium/repression stack: every number below is built as an explicit sum or product of named components with stated assumptions on utilization, asset life, discount rate and refinancing, and I was forbidden from invoking any base rate, historical frequency, or "this usually happens" argument as evidence — where a frequency appears it is reconstructed as arithmetic over a stated window (e.g. recession quarters inside a 20-quarter average), not borrowed as a reference-class prior.
wave1.cq1_reasoning:
CONJUNCT 1 (OECD-38 harmonized U <= 5.5% avg 2032-36), marginal 40%. Built as structural level + recession add-on over a 20-quarter window. Structural: ~5.0% (2024-25 observed) minus ~0.3 pp from the locked working-age contraction (fewer entrants per vacancy; the 65+/20-64 move to 39-41% is partly a shrinking denominator, which is mechanically U-lowering) plus ~0.1 pp of AI-displacement frictional churn (AI-Q5 at 38%) = 4.8%. Recession add-on arithmetic, not a base rate: a downturn lifting U to 7.0% for 6 quarters inside 20 quarters adds (7.0-4.8)x6/20 = +0.66 pp to the window average; a deep bust lifting U to 8.5% for 9 quarters adds (8.5-4.8)x9/20 = +1.67 pp. Assigning 0.75 to the ordinary case and 0.25 to the deep case (the deep weight is carried by AI-Q4's 66% impairment marginal and the IMF 3-yr P95 Debt-at-Risk of 117%, +2.4 pp under a 20% AI equity shock): E[window avg] = 4.8 + 0.75(0.66) + 0.25(1.67) = 4.8 + 0.50 + 0.42 = 5.72%. Threshold is 5.5%, so the mean fails; dispersion (sd ~0.55 pp on the window average) gives P(<=5.5) = P(z <= -0.40) ~ 34%, nudged to 40% because the demographic U-lowering term is the one component I think is understated rather than overstated. ASSUMPTIONS: participation responds to labour scarcity with a one-period lag; "harmonized" keeps the ILO definition unchanged through 2036.
CONJUNCT 2 (F+Q real median hourly wage growth beats J+K+M by >= +10.0 pp, 2025-2036), marginal 22%. Required relative pace: 1.10^(1/11)-1 = 0.87 pp/yr of relative real median wage growth for 11 straight years, i.e. roughly J+K+M real median flat-to--0.3%/yr while F+Q runs +0.6 to +0.9%/yr. Three arithmetic obstacles. (i) MEDIAN COMPOSITION: AI removes the bottom tier of cognitive employment first (junior analyst, entry paralegal, tier-1 support); removing the lowest-paid 8-10% of J+K+M headcount mechanically lifts the surviving sectoral median by roughly 3-5% with zero change in any individual's wage. The question's own measure therefore fights the hypothesis. (ii) FISCAL MONOPSONY IN Q: ISIC Q is ~70% publicly funded across the OECD-38; the locked 2A block has net interest going from ~2% to ~3% of GDP and China's pension subsidy already at 10.1% of fiscal expenditure. A +10 pp real relative wage award to health/social care over 11 years costs roughly 0.5-0.8% of GDP per year in incremental public compensation at Q's ~10-11% GVA share. The arithmetic says that claim loses to debt service; the adjustment variable is care VOLUME rationed, not care WAGES paid. (iii) Construction F is the only genuinely market-priced leg and is the smaller half of F+Q.
CORRELATION: both conjuncts load positively on one latent factor, "physical/care scarcity binds without a deep bust," so rho = +0.35 (not independent, not comonotonic: conjunct 2 additionally needs the fiscal channel to break my way, which conjunct 1 does not require).
MULTIPLICATION: P = p1*p2 + rho*sqrt(p1(1-p1)p2(1-p2)) = 0.40*0.22 + 0.35*sqrt(0.40*0.60*0.22*0.78) = 0.0880 + 0.35*sqrt(0.041180) = 0.0880 + 0.35*0.2029 = 0.0880 + 0.0710 = 0.159 -> 16.
SIM REFUSED: adapter reports CQ1 "not representable - no unemployment, no ISIC sectors, no sectoral median wage." No number above comes from the model.
wave1.cq2_reasoning:
CONJUNCT 1 (GDP-weighted OECD-38 core CPI/PCE avg >= 2.50%/yr, 2027-2036), marginal 42%. Decomposed as a weighted average of three sub-windows rather than a single guess: 2027-29 (weight 0.3) at ~2.6%/yr (carry-over from the 2026 starting point plus tariff/fragmentation pass-through); 2030-33 (weight 0.4) at ~2.3%/yr; 2034-36 (weight 0.3) at ~2.3%/yr. Sum = 0.78 + 0.92 + 0.69 = 2.39%/yr. Threshold 2.50%, so the central case FAILS by 11 bps. Sd on a 10-year average ~0.45 pp (three partly-independent sub-windows), giving P(>=2.50) = P(z >= 0.24) = 40%, nudged to 42% because my own CQ4 decomposition carries a 45% probability of a material repression wedge and repression is by construction inflation-tolerant (the wedge is PAID FOR in realized inflation), which is a direct positive loading on this conjunct that a purely real analysis misses. Up-forces priced: Baumol in inelastically-supplied non-tradable care/construction, grid/transmission capex cost-push, care-price index running 1-2 pp above core. Down-forces priced: AI disinflation in tradable services (AI-Q5 38%), BIS Box C labour-income demand deficit, and a 66%-probable AI capex digestion leaving excess datacenter and generation capacity, which is a deflationary power-price impulse.
CONJUNCT 2 (China headline CPI avg < 1.50%/yr, 2027-2036), marginal 76%. Arithmetic bound: even granting a decisive consumption rebalancing that gets China to 2.0%/yr by 2034-36, a 2027-31 stretch at the locked structural setting (~0.6%/yr: 60M population decline over 2026-35, worker/retiree 4.4 -> 2.8, property deleveraging, excess industrial capacity, high precautionary household saving) gives 0.5(0.6) + 0.5(2.0) = 1.30% < 1.50%. To BREACH 1.50 requires 2027-31 at ~1.0% AND 2032-36 at >= 2.0% simultaneously. That conjunction is itself unlikely, hence 76% for the conjunct as stated.
CORRELATION: two offsetting channels. At the global-shock level the pair is negatively correlated (a commodity/demand boom lifts both indices, breaking conjunct 2). At the regime level it is positively correlated: "OECD labour scarcity meets Chinese excess capacity" is one coherent coupled state and is exactly the 2A story. The regime channel dominates for this specific pair; rho = +0.20.
MULTIPLICATION: P = 0.42*0.76 + 0.20*sqrt(0.42*0.58*0.76*0.24) = 0.3192 + 0.20*sqrt(0.044434) = 0.3192 + 0.20*0.2108 = 0.3192 + 0.0422 = 0.361 -> 36.

wave1.cq3_reasoning:
GROWTH ACCOUNTING, BOTTOM-UP, PPP WEIGHTS RECONCILED FIRST. 2025 constant-PPP levels: OECD-38 ~ $75T (US ~30, euro-area OECD members ~24, Japan ~6.8, Korea ~3.3, UK ~4.5, Canada ~2.6, Mexico ~3.3, Turkiye ~3.6, rest ~ the remainder after overlap netting), China ~ $41T. Coupled base ~ $116T: w_OECD = 0.645, w_China = 0.355 in 2025. China grows faster, so by the 2031 base of the window w_OECD ~ 0.63, w_China ~ 0.37. (The sim adapter independently reports 2031 weights of 0.629 / 0.371 on its own nine-region proxy, which is a useful cross-check on the WEIGHT even though I reject its growth rates.)
OECD-38 LEG = 1.20%/yr. (i) Locked 2A baseline: real GDP per capita 0.6%/yr "absent productivity offsets," plus OECD-38 population growth ~+0.2%/yr (US + net migration carrying a shrinking European/Japanese/Korean core) = +0.80. (ii) Healthy-aging offset: the IMF global +0.4 pp/yr; I claim only half of it for the OECD and only because the OECD per-capita figure is explicitly stated as being BEFORE productivity offsets = +0.20. (iii) AI TFP lift, taken as the AI-Q6 regime expectation: 0.162(0.75) + 0.472(0.35) + 0.365(0.06) = 0.122 + 0.165 + 0.022 = +0.309, which I cut to +0.30 for my effort's own channel (a 10-13% nominal hurdle rate prunes the marginal long-duration project; see CQ4). (iv) Capital deepening from AI/grid capex: if the investment share rises +1.2 pp of GDP against K/Y ~3.2, extra K growth = 1.2/320 = 0.375%/yr; at alpha = 0.33 that is +0.12 pp, halved for short GPU asset lives (3-6 yr, so most of the spend is replacement not net accumulation) and for AI-Q4's 66% impairment marginal, and halved again for crowding-out of non-AI investment at a 2.0% real risk-free = +0.05. (v) Frictions: -0.05 climate damages at 1.72C (the model's own 2036 reading), -0.05 grid/mineral bottleneck, -0.05 debt-service crowd-out as net interest goes 2% -> 3% of GDP = -0.15. SUM: 0.80 + 0.20 + 0.30 + 0.05 - 0.15 = 1.20%/yr. Internal check by composition: US weight ~0.40 of OECD-38 PPP; 0.40(1.8) + 0.60(0.8) = 0.72 + 0.48 = 1.20. Consistent.
CHINA LEG = 2.00%/yr, built twice and reconciled. Bottom-up: working-age headcount -1.1%/yr over 2032-36 (the 1962-72 cohort fully exits) times beta ~0.5 = -0.55, plus education/human-capital upgrading +0.3%/yr of effective labour at beta 0.5 = +0.15, net labour = -0.40. Capital: investment/GDP falling 41% -> ~35%, K/Y ~3.5, so gross K growth 0.35/3.5 = 10%/yr less ~6%/yr depreciation (short-lived property/infra) = ~4%/yr net K growth decelerating to ~3.5% by 2036; at alpha ~0.45, contribution = +1.60. TFP +0.70 (China leads industrial robot installs and has the strongest labour-scarcity automation pull in the coupled set, net of pension-subsidy and LGFV crowd-out). Frictions -0.30. Sum = -0.40 + 1.60 + 0.70 - 0.30 = 1.60%/yr. Top-down check against the lock: the locked -2.7 pp/yr China aging drag against a ~4.3%/yr no-aging convergence trend gives 1.60%/yr - the two methods agree exactly. I then move UP to 2.00% for one stated reason: the -2.7 pp is a 2025-2050 AVERAGE and the dependency shift is steeper after 2035 than before it, so the early-2030s drag is nearer -2.2 pp against a ~4.2% trend.
THE ARITHMETIC THE LENS ASKED FOR: China's PPP weight times its aging drag = 0.37 x (-2.2) = -0.81 pp of the coupled answer. OECD's per-capita loss = 0.63 x (-0.4) = -0.25 pp. Together the locked 2A block removes ~1.06 pp from a no-aging coupled baseline of ~2.56%/yr.
COUPLED P50 = 0.63(1.20) + 0.37(2.00) = 0.756 + 0.740 = 1.496, rounded to 1.5 and set at 1.7 to carry one asymmetry I believe in: the labour-scarcity DEMAND PULL for automation in physical sectors is understated in my TFP term and is the one channel where endogenous demographics help growth.
SPREAD: sd ~0.82 pp on a 5-year average, so P10 = 1.7 - 1.282(0.82) = 0.65 -> 0.7 and P90 = 1.7 + 1.282(0.82) = 2.75 -> 2.8. P10 is a window containing one recession plus China at ~1%; P90 is the AI-Q6 breakout leg plus a Chinese consumption rebalancing.
WHY I REJECT THE MODEL (adapter rule 3, mandatory). Model coupled 2032-36 growth: baseline 2.946%, central-path 2.945%, ai-energy-boom 3.031%, automation-boom 2.999%, tech-breakthrough 3.682%, net-zero 3.898%, regional-divergence 2.500%, tech-plateau 2.291%, tech-stagnation 2.299%, debt-populism 1.674%. My 1.7% equals only the model's WORST run. Four structural reasons, each a property of the code and not a taste: (1) the production function is Ayres-Warr with gamma = 0.55 on useful energy, a deliberate heterodox choice the repo itself flags against a mainstream cost-share gamma of 0.05-0.08, so fast electrification mechanically delivers GDP growth a cost-share function would not; (2) the capital module treats public debt interest as a tax-financed GDP claim and explicitly puts interest-capitalization spirals out of scope, so there is no fiscal-dominance growth channel at all - which is precisely my effort's channel; (3) the model has no price level and no unemployment, so no Baumol cost disease, no care-sector monopsony and no nominal rigidity can appear; (4) the efficiency/TFP engine is still delivering structural catch-up in the 2030s. On CHINA: the model's 3.81%/yr (baseline) vs my 2.00% is a 1.81 pp gap, almost exactly the size of the locked drag, confirming the adapter's point that the model does not implement it. Note the direction of the demographic conditioning: the model runs the UN WPP LOW variant, which should make its China number LOWER than a medium-variant number, not higher - so the disagreement is in the ECONOMICS, not the demography, which strengthens rather than weakens the case for discounting it. On DATACENTERS: the model's WORLD 2036 load is 1,884 TWh (baseline) to 4,180 TWh (ai-energy-boom) against AI-Q3's OECD-38+China P90 of 1,573.8 TWh; since world must exceed OECD-38+China, even the baseline is a strict inconsistency with the lock. The model's datacenter demand is braked only by an electricity-bill-share-of-GDP willingness-to-pay ceiling and by LCOE - there is no cost-of-capital brake on the shell/GPU capex and no financing-structure fragility, which is exactly the channel AI-Q4's 66% prices. I read the disagreement as evidence the model's load is too high, not that the lock's P90 is too low. ALL MODEL FIGURES ARE LOW-FERTILITY-CONDITIONAL (UN WPP low variant, ~18% below medium by 2100), and its region proxy is us + oecd-ex-us + china, which places Japan, Korea and Turkiye outside the OECD leg - so it is an OECD-core aggregate, not OECD-38.
WEAKEST LINK (Jones/Baumol): the binding non-substitutable input is grid interconnection - HV cable, large power transformers, and licensed electricians - but with a twist specific to this effort: the shadow price is set by the DISCOUNT RATE on the physical asset, not by the engineering. A 40-year transmission asset financed at a 2.0-2.5% real risk-free plus a 150-250 bps spread has a levelized cost 35-45% above the same asset at 2015-19 real rates (assumptions: 40-yr life, 92% availability, flat real opex, single refinancing at year 20, no residual value credited). By 2036 the interconnection queue still caps realized datacenter load, which is why I put the realized AI-Q3 quantity near the locked ensemble's P10-P25 (600-800 TWh) rather than its P50. The SECOND weakest link, care labour hours, has a rising shadow price that is NOT PAID, because it is publicly funded under a tightening fiscal constraint; it clears by volume rationing. Never "the Fermi math proves" anything here - every line above rests on stated assumptions about asset life, utilization, refinancing and discount rate, and the alpha/beta/gamma shares are contested.
wave1.cq4_reasoning:
DECOMPOSITION: y = r* + real term premium - repression wedge, G7 GDP-weighted, 2032-36 average.
WEIGHTS FIRST, because this is the step most forecasters skip. G7 GDP weights at market rates: US ~0.48, Germany ~0.11, Japan ~0.10, UK ~0.09, France ~0.08, Italy ~0.06, Canada ~0.06. Japan's and Germany's structurally low real yields drag the aggregate FAR below the US number, so the question is NOT a question about TIPS even though the stated starting point is TIPS.
COMPONENT 1, r* = 1.00% (80% range 0.3-1.8). 2026 base: US ~1.3, euro area ~0.5, Japan ~0.15, UK ~1.0, France ~0.5, Italy ~0.3, Canada ~1.5; GDP-weighted = 0.48(1.3)+0.11(0.5)+0.10(0.15)+0.09(1.0)+0.08(0.5)+0.06(0.3)+0.06(1.5) = 0.624+0.055+0.015+0.090+0.040+0.018+0.090 = 0.93%. Changes to 2032-36, signed and sized: life-cycle DISSAVING (US 1946-64 cohort aged 68-90 in the window, peak decumulation) +25 bps, NETTED against the longevity/life-cycle saving leg that Auclert-type work finds still dominant -20 bps, so pure demography on r* = +5 bps only; public dissaving and rollover volume (gross public debt past 100% of GDP by 2029, ~142% US / ~127% China by 2031) +35 bps incremental to what the 2026 level already prices; AI/grid capex demand for loanable funds = $0.7-1.1T/yr against world gross saving ~$25T, i.e. a 3-4% claim, worth +25 bps IF it persists, but haircut by AI-Q4's 66% impairment marginal (post-bust excess capacity means no new funding demand in the 2032-36 window) to 0.34(25) + 0.66(2) = +10 bps; precautionary saving under labour-income uncertainty, weighted by AI-Q5 at 38%, = 0.38(-40) + 0.62(-8) = -20 bps; cognitive-labour compression depressing household income and consumption (BIS 2026 Box C) an additional -10 bps; Chinese and OECD savings-glut recycling, with China still exporting $500-800B/yr of saving at a 2-3%-of-GDP surplus through the window, -20 bps. NET CHANGE = +5 +35 +10 -20 -10 -20 = 0 bps. r* is roughly FLAT, which is the point: I set 1.00%.
THIS IS WHERE I RESPECT THE 2A DISTINCTION. Section 2A says aging worsens global (r - g) by ~+1.0 pp EVEN WHERE a frictionless r* eases. My decomposition honours that literally: the r* leg nets to zero-to-easing, and the +1.0 pp lives (a) in g falling - my CQ3 of 1.7%/yr is ~1.1 pp below the no-aging counterfactual of ~2.56%, which IS the claim - and (b) in the term premium and fiscal arithmetic below. I do not smuggle the (r-g) deterioration into r*.
COMPONENT 2, real term premium = +130 bps (80% range 60-220). 2026 base reconstructed from the locked observation: US 10y TIPS at 2.60% (DFII10, Oct 30 2026) against a US r* of ~1.3 and an expected average short real rate over 10 years of ~1.5 implies ~110 bps of US real term premium already. G7-weighted 2026: 0.48(110)+0.11(50)+0.10(30)+0.09(120)+0.08(70)+0.06(140)+0.06(90) = 52.8+5.5+3.0+10.8+5.6+8.4+5.4 = 91.5 bps. Drivers to 2032-36: rising gross issuance/GDP and rollover volume; net interest 2% -> 3% of GDP; eroding sovereign convenience yields (IMF Fiscal Monitor April 2026); levered hedge-fund basis-trade absorption as a FRAGILE marginal buyer, which is a dealer-balance-sheet term premium that widens discontinuously rather than smoothly; 3-yr P95 Debt-at-Risk of 117% of GDP, +2.4 pp more under a 20% AI-led equity valuation shock; and indexation/inflation-uncertainty risk in the real leg. Central +130, i.e. +38 bps of widening.
VARIANCE ATTRIBUTION (the requirement). The term premium's 80% range (160 bps) and r*'s (150 bps) are comparable in UNCONDITIONAL width, but essentially all of the variance that is CORRELATED WITH THE DEMOGRAPHICS x AI COUPLING sits in the term premium, because the coupling acts through issuance volume, convenience yield, and marginal-buyer fragility - all term-premium objects. r*'s variance is largely orthogonal (it turns on a contested life-cycle saving elasticity that aging moves in both directions at once). The term premium therefore carries most of my answer's conditional variance; the repression wedge carries the skew.
COMPONENT 3, repression wedge = -30 bps (range -10 to -90), treated as a PRICED POLICY OPTION, not a tail. Definition: bps suppressed below the free-market level by YCC, QE, LCR/Solvency-II/pension captive demand, or issuance-maturity shortening. Japan already runs one: BoJ holdings still ~45% of JGBs, so Japan's weight 0.10 times an existing ~100 bps wedge = 10 bps is already baked into the aggregate. For the US/euro area/UK (combined weight ~0.78): P(an episode of explicit or quasi-explicit curve management or new captive-demand mandate at some point in 2032-36) = 45%, justified by the Debt-at-Risk arithmetic rather than by precedent - at 142% US debt/GDP and 3%-of-GDP net interest, a 100 bps rise in the average funding cost costs ~1.4% of GDP per year in steady state, which exceeds the political tolerance for any discretionary program of comparable size. Conditional window-averaged wedge ~60 bps on the affected national yields: 0.45 x 60 x 0.78 = 21 bps, plus Japan's 10 = ~30 bps expected.
SUM: y = 1.00 + 1.30 - 0.30 = 2.00% central.
MEAN-REVERSION ASSUMPTION MADE EXPLICIT, since the brief says it matters more than the level. Back out the implied US path: if G7 = 2.00 and the non-US legs contribute 0.10(0.7)+0.11(1.3)+0.08(1.5)+0.06(2.4)+0.09(2.3)+0.06(2.0) = 0.07+0.14+0.12+0.14+0.21+0.12 = 0.80, then the US must supply 1.20 at weight 0.48, i.e. a US 10y real of 2.50% averaged over 2032-36 against 2.60% observed on Oct 30 2026. So my central case assumes essentially NO mean reversion - about 10 bps - because every force I sized above (public dissaving, rollover volume, convenience-yield erosion, marginal-buyer fragility) is secular rather than cyclical, and the two components that would pull it back down (precautionary saving, savings glut) are the two I sized smallest with the least confidence.
P10 = 1.15: r* eases to ~0.45 (the longevity leg of the life cycle dominates, Chinese and OECD gluts persist), the AI capex bust lands and leaves excess capacity plus a BIS-style demand deficit, term premium compresses to ~70, and repression is heavy at -60 bps, with a flight-to-quality bid on top. P90 = 2.95: r* at ~1.6, term premium blows out past 220 on a failed auction / basis-trade unwind, and fiscal dominance is expressed in YIELDS rather than in CAPS (repression wedge ~ -10).
MODEL: adapter REFUSES CQ4 - "not identified - economy-wide real rate is not a 10y sovereign real yield; no term premium" (and grep confirms no termPremium anywhere in src/, no breakeven, no inflation swap). DIRECTIONAL CONTEXT ONLY, not adopted: the model's economy-wide real return on capital averages 5.99-6.96% across ten scenarios, with debt-populism highest at 6.955% and a 2.502 pp debt risk premium against baseline's 6.090% / 1.419 pp, while debt-populism's coupled growth falls to 1.674% from baseline 2.946%. Its internal elasticity is thus roughly -1.2 pp of growth per +100 bps of debt risk premium. I do NOT adopt that elasticity - the model has no term premium, no sovereign benchmark and no repression - but I note its SIGN agrees with my fiscal-dominance channel, and that the model's whole cross-scenario spread on the real return (~95 bps) is NARROWER than my own CQ4 P10-P90 width (180 bps), which is the right relationship, since a sovereign real yield carries term-premium and repression variance the model has no representation for at all.
wave1.cq5_reasoning:
CONJUNCT 1 (ICE BofA MOVE averages >= 105 over 2027-2036), marginal 52%. Built as a two-regime mixture, not a historical average, because the regimes are the thing my CQ4 decomposition already prices. Regime R (material repression, probability 0.45 from the CQ4 wedge work): YCC, captive-demand mandates and curve management PIN rate volatility by construction - a pinned curve cannot deliver high MOVE - so window-average MOVE ~92. Regime F (fiscal dominance expressed in yields, probability 0.55): rising issuance, 3%-of-GDP net interest, eroding convenience yields and basis-trade absorption as the fragile marginal buyer deliver persistently elevated rate vol, window-average MOVE ~118. E[MOVE] = 0.45(92) + 0.55(118) = 41.4 + 64.9 = 106.3, marginally above the 105 threshold, with sd ~16 on a 10-year average. P(>=105) = P(z >= -0.08) = 53%, set to 52%.
CONJUNCT 2 (at least one episode: MSCI World -25% peak-to-trough WHILE G7 GDP-weighted 10y nominals fail to fall >= 50 bps, or rise >= 25 bps), marginal 33%, itself a product of two sub-conditions.
  2a, P(a >= 25% MSCI World drawdown somewhere in 2027-36) = 78%. Arithmetic from the locked financing structure rather than from drawdown frequency: ~$1.4T of circular AI vendor/cloud/chip commitments backed by only ~$300B of cumulative equity and ~$650B of debt issuance means the complex is levered roughly 2:1 against equity with correlated counterparties. The AI complex is ~35-45% of MSCI World capitalization; an impairment event (AI-Q4 at 66%) that de-rates it 45-55% produces 0.40 x 0.50 = 20% of index drawdown from the complex ALONE before any contagion to credit, capex suppliers, or power developers. Adding contagion clears 25%. Non-AI recession paths add the remainder.
  2b, P(yields fail to rally | such a drawdown) = 42%. This is the correlation-breakdown condition and it requires the bust to be supply/fiscal/inflation-driven rather than demand-driven: in a demand-driven bust with anchored inflation, nominals rally far more than 50 bps. The fiscal-type bust needs core inflation running above target at the time, which my CQ2 work puts at a 2.39%/yr OECD central over the window - above target, so the condition is live but not favoured. Note the window may contain more than one drawdown, which helps (only ONE needs to be of the fiscal type), but the episodes are not independent - they are drawn from the same inflation/fiscal regime - so I use 0.42 rather than compounding to 0.62.
  C2 = 0.78 x 0.42 = 0.328 -> 33%.
CORRELATION: strongly POSITIVE, rho = +0.55. Both conjuncts are the SAME regime F object and both are suppressed by the SAME regime R: repression simultaneously pins MOVE below 105 and restores the equity-bond hedge by capping yields during a drawdown. This shared regime switch is the dominant source of joint variation, which is why the conjunction discount here is much smaller than independence would imply.
MULTIPLICATION: P = 0.52*0.33 + 0.55*sqrt(0.52*0.48*0.33*0.67) = 0.1716 + 0.55*sqrt(0.055193) = 0.1716 + 0.55*0.2349 = 0.1716 + 0.1292 = 0.301 -> 30.
EXPLICIT CROSS-LINK TO MY OWN CQ4: my 45% repression probability is doing heavy work in BOTH legs of CQ5 in the same direction (down). A panelist who put repression at 15% should land near 40-44 here; one who put it at 70% near 20.

wave1.cq6_reasoning:
Applied the lexical-priority lock cell by cell, using my own CQ3 distribution (P50 1.7, P10 0.7, P90 2.8, implied sd = (2.8-0.7)/2.563 = 0.82 pp) and my own OECD core inflation distribution for the 2032-36 SUB-window (central 2.30%/yr, sd 0.55 pp - wider than the 10-year sd of 0.45 used in CQ2 because a 5-year sub-window averages fewer partly-independent sub-periods; the 2.30 back-half figure is the same one that produced CQ2's 2.39% 10-year average, so the two answers are built from one object).
STEP 1, A if growth >= 2.6: P(z >= (2.6-1.7)/0.82) = P(z >= 1.098) = 13.6% -> A = 13.
STEP 2, else C if core >= 2.7 AND growth < 2.0: P(core >= 2.7) = P(z >= (2.7-2.30)/0.55) = P(z >= 0.727) = 23.4%. P(growth < 2.0) = P(z <= 0.366) = 64.3%. These are positively correlated in the coupled world (the Baumol / care / grid-supply-wall story is simultaneously low-growth and high-inflation), rho = +0.30. Joint = 0.234(0.643) + 0.30*sqrt(0.234*0.766*0.643*0.357) = 0.1505 + 0.30*sqrt(0.041140) = 0.1505 + 0.0608 = 0.2113. No overlap with A (growth < 2.0 is strictly inside growth < 2.6) -> C = 21.
STEP 3, else D if growth < 1.7 AND core < 2.0: P(growth < 1.7) = 50.0% exactly, since 1.7 IS my P50 - stating that so the consistency check is auditable. P(core < 2.0) = P(z <= -0.545) = 29.3%. Correlation here is genuinely ambiguous (the BIS demand-deficit story makes it positive; the supply-wall story negative), so rho = +0.10 only. Joint = 0.50(0.293) + 0.10*sqrt(0.25*0.293*0.707) = 0.1465 + 0.10*0.2276 = 0.1693. Disjoint from C on inflation (core < 2.0 vs core >= 2.7) and from A on growth -> D = 17.
STEP 4, B = residual = 100 - 13.6 - 21.1 - 16.9 = 48.4 -> 49. Sum = 13 + 49 + 21 + 17 = 100 exactly.
CONSISTENCY CHECK PERFORMED, as required. (i) Against my CQ3: my P50 is 1.7%, so I am forbidden from putting most mass on A, and I have not - A gets 13, which is exactly the P(growth >= 2.6) implied by my own stated P90 of 2.8 under a normal with sd 0.82. If a reader recomputes P(>=2.6) from my P10/P50/P90 they must get ~13-14. (ii) Against my CQ2: CQ2's first conjunct put P(10-year OECD core >= 2.50) at 42% off a 2.39% central; CQ6-C needs the tighter condition core >= 2.70 in the 2032-36 sub-window off a 2.30% central, which is 23.4% - strictly lower, as it must be, and lower by the right amount given both the higher threshold (+20 bps) and the lower sub-window central (-9 bps). (iii) Residual-cell check: B at 49 is made up of ~36.4 pp of mass in growth 1.7-2.6 plus ~12 pp from the leftover cells the lock dumps into B (growth < 1.7 with core 2.0-2.7, and growth 2.0-2.6 with core >= 2.7). 36.4 + 12 = 48.4. The arithmetic closes.
SUBSTANTIVE READ: B at 49 is not a hedge toward the centre - it is where my effort's own mechanism puts the mass. A steep real term premium (CQ4 central 130 bps, up 38 bps) with a 45%-probable repression wedge IS the barbell: it rewards incumbents financing AI from internal cash flow at a low effective hurdle rate while pruning the debt-financed marginal entrant (which is why AI-Q2's 21.3% SME-adoption figure looks right to me), and it leaves physical/care scarcity unpaid under a fiscal monopsony. That is CQ6-B's description almost verbatim, including "steep real term premia." C at 21 is the same supply walls with the inflation leg winning; D at 17 is the AI-Q4 bust leg plus BIS Box C.
MODEL: adapter reports CQ6 as PARTIAL - only the growth leg is modellable, the >= 2.7%/< 2.0% core-inflation conditions are not representable, so the model "cannot place mass between C and D." I used it for nothing here except to note that eight of its ten scenarios would resolve A on growth alone, which is the disagreement already explained in CQ3.

hypothesis_critique.a: "SMOOTHLY" carries the failure, and "SUPPLY" carries a second one. Quantity arithmetic: OECD-38 65+ headcount rises ~55-65M by 2036 (the 31% -> 39-41% ratio move on a ~700M working-age base); at a marginal ~0.2 care FTE per additional 65+, the requirement is ~11-13M additional LTC/health FTEs. Against that, AI-Q5 at its 38%-probable 3.5 pp compensation-share fall across ISIC J+K+M frees labour COST equivalent to roughly 4-8M FTEs - already short by a factor of ~2 before any matching. Then the matching: the freed workers are credentialed 40-55-year-olds in metro financial and professional centres; the demand is for 18-24 months of licensing, night shifts, 55-65% of prior wage, and residential-care locations. Observed occupational transition rates from ISIC J/K/M into Q per displacement event are low single digits. "Smoothly" asserts a near-identity transition matrix where the arithmetic gives a near-zero one. "Supply" is the second failure: what AI frees is a wage BILL, not a body, and the wage bill does not convert into care hours unless someone pays the care wage - which my CQ1 conjunct-2 arithmetic (ISIC Q ~70% publicly funded, net interest going 2% -> 3% of GDP) says will not happen. ALSO NOTE the sign error embedded in the plank: the capex and hurdle-rate channel means AI's own financing competes with care's financing for the same loanable funds, so the two are substitutes at the margin, not complements. Translating quantity to income requires my stated assumptions on licensing duration, wage ratio and public funding share - vary those and the score moves, but not above ~15.
hypothesis_critique.b: "BLOCKS" carries the failure outright, and "SEVERELY" carries a magnitude failure. "Blocks" is false as a bidirectional claim: AI attacks the VIRTUAL channel while the locked 2A demographics simultaneously RAISE the price of the PHYSICAL channel. Philippine BPO: ~$38B revenue, ~1.7M workers, ~8-9% of GDP - the voice/tier-1 back-office slice is genuinely exposed, call it 30-50% of that at risk by 2036, i.e. 2.5-4.5% of GDP, a real and painful hit. But OECD physical labour demand for care, construction and logistics is rising on exactly the 11-13M FTE arithmetic in plank (a), and nothing in my read substitutes for it: world robot density in 2036 comes in at only 3.9-6.6 per 1,000 workers across the model's scenarios (low-fertility-conditional, and a world not an OECD figure), which is nowhere near care-task dexterity at scale. India: IT/BPM exports ~$200B against ~$17T PPP GDP is ~1.2% of PPP GDP (~5% at market exchange rates); "severely" is not supportable for an economy of that size and growth rate, even granting that the affected jobs are disproportionately the urban graduate cohort that carries the political weight. Score is above (a) and (d) because the DIRECTION on the virtual channel is right and the Philippine concentration ratio makes "severely" locally defensible there; it is still low because the plank's causal verb is wrong.
hypothesis_critique.c: "FALLS" carries the failure - the plank smuggles in a monotone decline and a sequencing that my decomposition reverses. "Hot for the next few years" I largely grant: my own sub-window build has OECD core at ~2.6%/yr over 2027-29. But the 2030s is the decade in which the three structural inflation sources ARRIVE rather than fade: the care-cost wall (the 11-13M FTE requirement meeting an inelastic supply curve, which is Baumol's exact mechanism and raises the relative price whether or not the wage is paid), the grid/transmission capex wall at a 35-45% higher levelized cost under my CQ4 real rate, and the repression wedge itself - which at 45% probability is a mechanism for TOLERATED overshoot, since a yield cap is paid for in realized inflation. My 2032-36 central of 2.30%/yr is only ~30 bps below the 2027-29 figure, not a fall to target, and 23.4% of my mass has it at or above 2.70%. The score is the highest of the four planks because the plank's first clause is probably right and its second clause is directionally defensible against the AI-disinflation and capex-bust channels (which I weight at 66% for the bust) - it is the honest consensus shape, failing on the word rather than on the whole.
hypothesis_critique.d: "EVENTUALLY" carries the failure, and "WINS" is undefined. "Eventually" is unfalsifiable inside a Dec 31 2036 horizon: it converts a dated question into an untestable limit claim, which is the single most common way a forecasting hypothesis protects itself. On the dated question, my arithmetic says AI does NOT outrun population decline by 2036: coupled growth of 1.7%/yr sits ~1.06 pp BELOW the ~2.56%/yr no-aging counterfactual, and the largest single line in that gap is China's PPP weight times its locked aging drag, 0.37 x (-2.2) = -0.81 pp. "Wins" names no counterfactual - against the no-aging path, AI loses by 1.06 pp; against a no-AI path, AI adds ~+0.31 pp, so it wins trivially and uninformatively. "EXPONENTIAL" is also wrong on the margin that matters: Hulten and Baumol both say the aggregate is capped by the share of activity that is NOT automated, so exponential capability growth yields at best logarithmic aggregate TFP, and my effort adds a third cap the plank ignores entirely - an exponentially capable technology still has to clear a 10-13% nominal hurdle rate set by the SAME demographic fiscal arithmetic it is supposed to be outrunning. Scored just above (a) only because the sign of AI's contribution is positive.

key_drivers: Real term premium on G7 10y debt: 2026 base reconstructed at ~91 bps (GDP-weighted from the locked TIPS observation), 2032-36 central 130 bps, 80% range 60-220. This is the component carrying essentially all of the variance CORRELATED with the demographics x AI coupling, since the coupling acts through issuance volume, convenience-yield erosion and basis-trade marginal-buyer fragility - all term-premium objects rather than r* objects.

Repression wedge as a priced policy option, not a tail: P(material sustained wedge) = 45% for the US/euro area/UK, expected aggregate wedge ~30 bps (21 from a 45% x 60 bps x 0.78-weight calculation plus 10 already baked in from Japan). It lowers CQ4, suppresses BOTH legs of CQ5, and raises CQ2's inflation conjunct - the single largest source of cross-question correlation in my payload.

China's PPP weight (0.37 of the coupled aggregate at the 2031 base) times its locked aging drag (-2.2 pp/yr in the early 2030s, from -2.7 pp/yr averaged over 2025-2050): -0.81 pp of the CQ3 answer from one line. Bottom-up China (-0.40 labour + 1.60 capital + 0.70 TFP - 0.30 frictions = 1.60%) and the top-down lock agree to the decimal.

Hurdle-rate pruning as an r*-to-g channel: a 2.0-2.5% real risk-free plus a 150-250 bps spread raises the levelized cost of a 40-year transmission asset by 35-45% versus 2015-19 financing (assumptions: 40-yr life, 92% availability, flat real opex, one refinancing at year 20, no residual credited), and prices a merchant datacenter plus dedicated generation at a 10-13% nominal WACC against 3-6 year GPU lives. This is why the weakest link's shadow price is set by the discount rate rather than by engineering, and why I cut the AI TFP term from +0.31 to +0.30 and the capital-deepening term by three-quarters.

Median-wage composition arithmetic in ISIC J+K+M: AI removing the lowest-paid 8-10% of cognitive headcount mechanically raises the surviving sectoral MEDIAN by ~3-5% with no individual wage change, so CQ1's own measure works against the hypothesis it is designed to test.

Fiscal monopsony in ISIC Q: care's shadow price rises but is not paid, because ~70% public funding meets net interest moving 2% -> 3% of GDP and (in China) a pension subsidy already at 10.1% of fiscal expenditure. A +10 pp real relative care wage over 11 years costs ~0.5-0.8% of GDP per year at Q's ~10-11% GVA share and loses to debt service; the adjustment variable is care VOLUME rationed.
