wave1.coupling_tension: The 2B marginal that breaks first is AI-Q3 (data-centre electricity, P50 998 TWh, P90 1,573.8), and it breaks DOWNWARD - I would put the realized quantity near the locked ensemble's P10-P25, 600-800 TWh. The arithmetic: 2B holds demographics exogenous, which means it prices the AI build at an exogenous cost of capital. Once demographics are endogenous, the public-dissaving leg (+35 bps) and the rollover-volume/convenience-yield leg of my term premium (+38 bps of widening) ARE demographic objects - they are pension and health claims arriving as issuance - so the very aging that is the demand pull for automation raises the hurdle rate that prunes the automation capex. At my CQ4 central of 2.00% G7 (implying a US 10y real of ~2.50%), a merchant data centre plus dedicated generation plus interconnection faces a 10-13% nominal WACC against 3-6 year GPU asset lives and a locked financing structure of ~$1.4T of circular commitments on ~$300B of equity and ~$650B of debt. A 2.7x load build (365 -> 998 TWh) requires roughly 1.5-2.0 TW of new firm-equivalent capacity plus the shells plus the silicon, financed at that WACC, at the same time that AI-Q4 assigns 66% to impairment or a revenue/compute-D&A coverage failure. AI-Q3's P50 and AI-Q4's 66% cannot both hold once the financing channel is endogenous; the load number is the one that gives, because it is the physical consequence of the capex that AI-Q4 says gets cancelled. SECOND TENSION, in the opposite direction: coupling REINFORCES rather than contradicts AI-Q6's 47.2% jagged-diffusion-with-rent-concentration and AI-Q2's low 21.3%. A steep real term premium is not neutral across firms - an incumbent financing from internal cash flow faces a far lower effective hurdle than a debt-financed marginal entrant, so a high cost of capital mechanically produces rent concentration and suppresses the SME-adoption statistic that AI-Q2 measures. My own CQ6-B at 49 is that mechanism, not a hedge. THIRD, a tension with 2A itself rather than 2B: 2A's claim that aging worsens global (r - g) by ~+1.0 pp EVEN WHERE a frictionless r* eases is, on my decomposition, satisfied almost entirely through g and the term premium (my r* nets to 0 bps of change: +5 demography, +35 public dissaving, +10 capex, -20 precautionary, -10 compression, -20 glut), and my CQ3 of 1.7% is ~1.06 pp below the no-aging counterfactual of ~2.56%. So the locked (r - g) deterioration is reproduced - but as a GROWTH failure with a term-premium overlay, not as an r* rise. Any panelist who books the +1.0 pp as a higher r* will get a CQ4 near 2.8-3.0% and a CQ3 that is too high, because they will have moved the same quantity twice in the same direction.

wave1.lens_self_description: I answered only from dated, named, observable series and primary releases — hard administrative data first, survey second, vendor/index third — reporting each with its caveat and labelling anything I could not confirm as unverified at my horizon; the lens forbade me from reasoning from structural models or theory priors (HLW/Lubik-Matthes r* estimates, overlapping-generations savings theory, DSGE term-structure decompositions) or from narrative scenario-telling, so every number below is anchored to a level I can cite and a stated extrapolation step on top of it.
wave1.cq1_reasoning: LIVE INDICATORS. Conjunct 1 (OECD-38 harmonised unemployment avg <=5.5%, 2032-36): hard administrative data, OECD statistical release of Oct 2026 — "The OECD unemployment rate was broadly stable in August 2026, at 5.0%, just 0.2 p.p. above its record low from June 2023"; the Sep 2026 release (July data) reported 4.9%, "its lowest level in a year (34.7 million)", with EU 6.1% and euro area 6.4%, US 4.1% in July revised to 4.2% in September and Canada 6.5%. CAVEAT VERBATIM-ADJACENT: the 4.9% (July) and 5.0% (August) figures come from different releases and the search did not surface a release with full September 2026 data; next release 10 November 2026. Watch: monthly OECD "labour market situation", US JOLTS openings in NAICS 62 (health/social assistance) vs 51 (information), Eurostat job vacancy rate by NACE F and Q. OBSERVED: the level is currently well inside the threshold. EXTRAPOLATED: the threshold is a FIVE-YEAR AVERAGE six years out. Reference class — OECD aggregate unemployment 5-year windows since 1990: the aggregate sat above 5.5% continuously from roughly 2008 through 2022, so the unconditional base rate of a 5-year window averaging <=5.5% is low (~30%); conditioning on the 2A demographic denominator collapse (old-age ratio 31%->39-41%) raises it sharply, but one ordinary recession inside 2032-36 breaks it. Marginal: 55%. Conjunct 2 (F+Q real median hourly wage growth exceeds J+K+M by >=10.0pp cumulative 2025-2036, i.e. ~0.87pp/yr sustained for eleven years): I have NO hard series at my horizon for OECD-38 median hourly wages split on ISIC F+Q vs J+K+M — this is the weakest-telemetry conjunct in the whole set and I say so explicitly. The nearest observables are national: US ECI wages-and-salaries by industry and Eurostat labour cost index by NACE, neither of which is a MEDIAN HOURLY measure, and the AI-skill wage-premium series most cited (PwC AI Jobs Barometer, ~56% premium for AI-skilled roles) is VENDOR-REPORTED job-posting data with an acknowledged selection bias toward advertised, large-firm, English-language postings and is not a median-wage estimate. CRITICAL COMPOSITION CAVEAT: a falling cognitive labour SHARE (2B AI-Q5) is fully compatible with a RISING cognitive MEDIAN hourly wage, because compressing entry-level hiring removes the low-paid left tail of the J/K/M wage distribution — the median rises by selection while the share falls. This mechanism makes conjunct 2 materially harder than the barbell narrative implies, and it is the single most common error I expect in this question. Also: care-sector pay is set largely by public budgets, and 2A's fiscal block (net interest 2%->3% of GDP, debt past 100%) is a direct constraint on the fiscal capacity to bid care wages up by 10pp more than market-sector cognitive wages. Marginal: 30%. CONJUNCTION: assumed rho = +0.30 (both are products of a labour-scarcity/barbell regime). 0.55 x 0.30 = 0.165, lifted to ~0.20 for positive correlation. Answer 19.
wave1.cq2_reasoning: LIVE INDICATORS, both conjuncts have hard administrative telemetry and both readings surprised me relative to my training prior. Conjunct 1 (OECD-38 GDP-weighted core CPI/PCE avg >=2.50%/yr, 2027-2036): BEA release 29 Oct 2026 — core PCE +3.1% y/y in September 2026 (up from 3.0% in August), m/m +0.3%; HEADLINE PCE +3.6% y/y, m/m +0.5% (August 3.4%); core CPI 2.6% in September, "rising from a five-year low of 2.4% in August". CAVEAT: one outlet (CubaHeadlines) reported 3.6% as core, which matches headline and appears mislabelled; the Fed's September 2026 projection put core PCE at 3.4% for 2026 on a Q4/Q4 basis. Policy telemetry: FOMC held the target range at 3.75%-4.00% on 28 Oct 2026, vote 10-2, both dissents (Cook, Hammack) FOR a 25bp HIKE, after a 25bp HIKE on 16 Sep 2026 described as "the first hike since 2023"; markets pricing a December hike. CAVEAT: one source (securities.io) names only one dissenter, which does not reconcile with ten approving votes; I treat its vote count as unreliable. Euro-area and Japan core are unverified at my horizon. OBSERVED: the window's first years start from a core rate above 3% with policy still tightening. EXTRAPOLATED: the 10-year average is heavily front-loaded — if 2027-2029 run 2.5-3.0% (which the current impulse and a behind-the-curve policy rate make likely) the remaining seven years can average ~2.3% and still clear 2.50%. US core PCE averaged ~2.6% over 2021-2026, which is the relevant realised reference class, not the 2%-target prior. Marginal: 58%. Conjunct 2 (China headline CPI avg <1.50%/yr, 2027-2036): NBS release 15 Oct 2026 — September 2026 CPI +0.9% y/y (August +0.8%), +0.2% m/m, core CPI +1.0% y/y "unchanged from August" and reported as a 19-month high; gasoline +16.6% y/y contributing ~0.47pp to headline; food -1.7%. And the reading that matters most: PPI +5.0% y/y, +1.2% m/m. CAVEATS VERBATIM-ADJACENT: Tiger reports the September print "slightly below market expectations of 1%"; sources differ on the food sub-aggregate (one NBS-based release gives -0.9% for food/tobacco/liquor/dining-out); NBS CPI basket weights and imputation are not fully disclosed and methodology revisions inside a ten-year window are a live resolution risk. OBSERVED: China has EXITED deflation, with a +5.0% y/y producer-price impulse still to pass through. 2022-2026 realised headline CPI averaged roughly 0.5%, which is what makes <1.50% look easy — but the freshest print is 0.9% and rising, core at a 19-month high, and PPI at +5%. Marginal: 55%, deliberately not higher. CONJUNCTION: assumed rho = -0.10. The two conjuncts share a common global energy/commodity factor (visible in BOTH series right now: US headline PCE 3.6% with m/m +0.5%, Chinese gasoline +16.6% y/y) that pushes them in the SAME direction, which works AGAINST the required divergence; the offsetting positive-correlation story (China exporting excess capacity while OECD hits domestic care/grid/tariff supply walls) is real but does not fully cancel it. 0.58 x 0.55 = 0.319, discounted ~10% for the negative common factor. Answer 29.
wave1.cq3_reasoning: FERMI DECOMPOSITION, PPP weights. OECD-38 share of (OECD-38 + China) 2025 PPP GDP ~63%, China ~37%, with China's share drifting up ~1pp over the window. OECD-38 leg: 2A gives baseline real GDP per capita growth 0.6%/yr absent productivity offsets; add OECD-38 population growth, which is migration-dependent and roughly 0.0 to +0.3%/yr (OBSERVED: labour-force telemetry already shows a shrinking denominator — OECD unemployment 5.0% in Aug 2026 at near-record lows with 34.7 million jobless in July, the lowest in a year). Add the AI offset implied by the locked 2B marginals, not by my own view of AI: AI-Q1 gives only 23.0% for a >=+0.50pp/yr TFP lift and AI-Q6 puts 47.2% on jagged diffusion (+0.15 to +0.59) and 36.5% on <+0.15, so the expected TFP lift is roughly +0.30pp/yr, which maps to a GDP growth lift of about the same order. COUPLING, both directions: labour scarcity is a demand pull for automation (up), while the cost-of-capital channel I own in this effort is a drag — at a G7 GDP-weighted 10y real yield near 2% (US DFII10 2.60% on 30 Oct 2026, DFII30 3.07%), capital deepening and grid/datacentre buildout face a hurdle rate unseen since before 2008, and 2B's own AI-Q4 at 66.0% for impairments/cancellations says the ensemble already expects that capex to be partly stranded. OECD-38 P50: 1.1%/yr (range 0.4-1.9). China leg: 2A gives population shrinking ~60M over 2026-2035 and worker-to-retiree 4.4->2.8, with aging costing ~-2.7pp/yr of growth; offsetting, China is the observed leader in installed industrial robot density and the physical-AI capital stock. China P50: 3.0%/yr (range 1.5-4.5). CAVEAT: Chinese real GDP growth is an administrative statistic whose deflator and level construction are contested in the literature; I do not treat it as hard data of the same class as NBS CPI or BEA PCE. BLEND: 0.63 x 1.1 + 0.37 x 3.0 = 0.69 + 1.11 = 1.80%. Reference class for the spread: realised 5-year annualised growth windows for the OECD+China aggregate since 1995 have a ~1.3pp interquartile spread, dominated by whether a global recession falls inside the window; I widen the left tail for the coupled case (capex bust per AI-Q4 plus Chinese property/demographic drag plus r-g arithmetic forcing fiscal consolidation) and cap the right tail because clearing 2.6% requires the >=+0.50pp TFP branch that 2B itself prices at only 23%. P10 1.05 / P50 1.80 / P90 2.70. hypothesis_critique.a: The failure word is "smoothly", with "supply" as the accomplice. The plank asserts a transfer mechanism that no observable series supports. Hard administrative telemetry shows the two conditions holding SIMULTANEOUSLY rather than resolving each other: OECD unemployment at 5.0% (Aug 2026) with the EU job vacancy rate concentrated in NACE Q while information-sector hiring slows — i.e. care vacancies and cognitive-hiring softness coexist, which is direct evidence of NON-transfer, not of reallocation. The frictions are occupational, licensure-bound, geographic and preference-bound: a displaced claims adjuster does not become a certified nursing assistant. And the binding constraint on care is a WAGE and LICENSING constraint funded from public budgets, which 2A's fiscal block (net interest 2%->3% of GDP, debt past 100% by 2029) tightens rather than loosens. Even in the branch where AI frees the headcount, "smoothly" fails on timing: write-off of white-collar roles is fast and care-capacity build is slow (training pipelines of 2-4 years, facility capex at a 2%+ real funding cost). 7.
hypothesis_critique.b: Two failure words, "severely" and "blocks". "Blocks" fails on the scope split the task itself locks: AI can substitute for VIRTUAL services exports but not for PHYSICAL labour migration, and the physical channel is DEMAND-PULLED by exactly the OECD aging in 2A (old-age ratio 31%->39-41%) — Filipino and Indian nurses and care workers face a rising, not falling, OECD bid, and no language model staffs a ward. "Severely" fails on the virtual channel too, where the observable direction is currently the opposite of the plank: Indian services exports and global-capability-centre headcount have been setting records, with AI so far augmenting capability arbitrage rather than erasing it. CAVEAT: GCC headcount and AI-displacement counts for India/Philippines BPO are largely VENDOR and industry-association reported (NASSCOM, IBPAP) with self-selected membership samples, and I do not have an administrative series; the honest statement is that the virtual-channel effect is not yet statistically distinguishable from zero in any hard series I can cite. The plank could still come partly true on entry-level virtual work; it is wrong as an aggregate claim about severe suffering. 12.
hypothesis_critique.c: The failure word is "then" — the implied clean regime switch — and this is nonetheless the most nearly correct plank, which is why it scores highest. Its first clause is now OBSERVED rather than forecast: core PCE 3.1% y/y and headline PCE 3.6% y/y in September 2026 (BEA, 29 Oct 2026), core CPI 2.6% up from a five-year low of 2.4%, the Fed having HIKED on 16 Sep 2026 for the first time since 2023 and held 3.75%-4.00% on 28 Oct with both dissents arguing for another hike. So "runs hot for the next few years" is close to a verified premise. The second clause is where it breaks: "then falls in the 2030s" treats disinflation as automatic, but the same fiscal arithmetic that produces 2A's worsened (r-g) and a ~117%-of-GDP P95 Debt-at-Risk is precisely the arithmetic that makes a deliberately above-target run-rate the path of least resistance, and I put ~45% on a G7 sovereign reaching for material duration targeting at some point in 2027-2036. The plank is also underspecified on WHICH measure falls: headline mean-reverts with energy, core does not have to. 42.
hypothesis_critique.d: Three failure words, in descending order of damage. "Eventually" is the worst: it is unfalsifiable inside the Dec 31 2036 horizon and therefore not a forecast at all — any 2036 disappointment is absorbed by it. "Wins" is the second: it conflates a LEVEL effect with a GROWTH RATE, and conflates AGGREGATE real GDP with per-capita welfare; aggregate GDP can grow while per-capita output stagnates and while the labour-income share that funds aggregate demand falls (the BIS 2026 Box C channel). "Exponential" is the third and is contradicted by 2B's own locked marginals, which are the opposite of exponential diffusion: AI-Q2 puts only 21.3% on OECD-38 firm adoption reaching 50% by 2036, AI-Q1 only 23.0% on a >=+0.50pp/yr TFP lift, and AI-Q4 66.0% on impairments or a revenue-to-D&A failure. A plank asserting exponential outrunning sits at odds with an ensemble that prices capex digestion at 36.5% and a jagged middle at 47.2%. My own CQ3 P50 of 1.80%/yr is the quantitative refutation: growth does not "win", it muddles through at roughly the rate that makes r-g positive. 14.

wave1.coupling_tension: The sharpest tension is between AI-Q4 (66.0% on >=20% capex impairments/cancellations or AI revenue below 0.5x compute D&A) and AI-Q3 (datacentre electricity P10/P50/P90 596.8 / 998.2 / 1,573.8 TWh): once demographics are endogenous these two cannot both stand at their locked values, and the inconsistency runs in OPPOSITE directions for the two marginals. The mechanism is the cost of capital, which 2B holds fixed by construction. Endogenising the 2A demographic/fiscal block means life-cycle dissaving, rising rollover volumes, eroding convenience yields and a levered-basis-trade marginal buyer all bear on the SAME loanable-funds pool that the physical AI and grid buildout draws from — and the observable price of that pool is already at a multi-decade high (DFII10 2.60% on 30 Oct 2026, DFII30 3.07%, JGB 30y at an all-time 4.235% on 5 Oct 2026, 30y gilts reportedly at 1998 highs). DIRECTION 1: AI-Q4's 66.0% is TOO LOW. An impairment test is a discount-rate test; raising the real hurdle rate by the 100-150bp that the 2021-2026 repricing already delivered mechanically increases the share of announced buildout whose NPV fails, and 2A's own ~$1.4T of circular vendor/cloud/chip commitments against only ~$300B of cumulative equity and ~$650B of debt issuance is a capital structure that is already rate-sensitive rather than equity-cushioned. Endogenous demographics should push AI-Q4 to roughly 72-76%. DIRECTION 2: AI-Q3's P50 of 998.2 TWh is TOO HIGH, and its P90 of 1,573.8 TWh much too high. Datacentre load is bounded by a willingness-to-pay ceiling expressed as an electricity-bill share of GDP, so a demographically-constrained GDP path (my CQ3 P50 of 1.80%/yr, with the OECD leg at only ~1.1%) shrinks the denominator at the same time that a ~2% real funding cost raises the capex hurdle for BOTH the compute and the generation/transmission that must be built alongside it. Endogenous demographics should pull the AI-Q3 P50 toward roughly 880-920 TWh and compress the P90 by 150-250 TWh. The joint distribution implied by coupling is therefore internally strained: a world that prices a 66% chance of capex impairment should not simultaneously carry a central datacentre-load path that implicitly assumes the impairment does not bite the buildout, and the arithmetic that reconciles them — higher AI-Q4, lower AI-Q3 — is precisely the cost-of-capital channel 2B suppressed. A secondary, weaker tension runs the other way and I note it for completeness: labour scarcity is a genuine demand pull, so AI-Q1's 23.0% is arguably too low on the demand side of automation even as it is too high on the financing side, and those two corrections are closer to cancelling than the AI-Q3/AI-Q4 pair.

hypothesis_critique.a: The failure word is SMOOTHLY. Three Wave-1 priors cluster at 5-7 and no admissible evidence moved them, so I take 6. My seat's specific objection is a price objection: smooth supply requires a relative wage signal to clear the reallocation, and ISIC Q is ~70% publicly funded against net interest moving 2%->3% of GDP, with China's pension subsidy already 10.1% of fiscal expenditure. A +10pp real relative care-wage award over eleven years costs ~0.5-0.8% of GDP per year at Q's ~10-11% GVA share and loses to debt service, so the shadow price of care labour rises and is NOT PAID; the adjustment variable is care VOLUME rationed, not workers reallocated. 'Supply' also fails on non-transferability (licensure, physical presence, geography, a displaced 45-year-old paralegal is not a geriatric nurse), and the word 'needed' is doing unearned work since the need is a demographic certainty while the saving is a 23%-probability TFP event.
hypothesis_critique.b: The failure word is BLOCKS, with SEVERELY second. AI compresses the VIRTUAL channel — cross-border BPO voice and text — but does nothing to the PHYSICAL channel, and aging OECD demand pulls harder on physical labour migration precisely in the states where AI is compressing cognitive work. For the Philippines remittances from physical deployment exceed BPO value added, so the larger channel is the one AI cannot touch and demographics strengthen. 'Blocks' is therefore wrong as stated: the net is a RECOMPOSITION of the export mix, ambiguous in sign, which also defeats 'severely'. I hold 15, between the Scout's 12 and the other two seats' 18, and I note that no dated telemetry in my evidence set bears on this plank at all, so it is a near-pure prior.
hypothesis_critique.c: The failure word is FALLS, and the plank is the highest-scoring one precisely because it is half right. The front leg is CONFIRMED by my strongest admissible evidence: core PCE 3.1% y/y rising in September 2026 with headline at 3.6%, a hike on 16 Sep 2026 and an October hold drawing two dissents for more. The back leg is where it breaks — my 2032-36 OECD core central is 2.35% with P(>= 2.7%) = 0.262 and P(< 2.0%) = 0.262, which is 'moderates and stays above target', not 'falls'. My seat adds a mechanism the plank ignores: financial repression at P = 0.42 is by construction inflation-TOLERANT, since the wedge is paid for in realised inflation, so the same fiscal arithmetic that would cap yields in the 2030s argues against disinflation in the 2030s. I score 42, adopting the Scout's number because his seat held the hard inflation telemetry and my updating moved toward him, against the Historian's 50 and Fermi's 31.
hypothesis_critique.d: Two failure words, EVENTUALLY and WINS. 'Eventually' is unfalsifiable and places the claim outside the resolution horizon, which disqualifies it as a forecast: on my central path through 2036 population decline is winning, since CQ3's 1.85% sits ~1.0-1.1pp below the no-aging counterfactual and the locked block removes ~1.06pp from a ~2.56% coupled baseline, with China's PPP weight times its early-2030s drag (0.37 x -2.2) taking -0.81pp from one line. 'Exponential' is doing rhetorical work the locked marginals contradict, since AI-Q1 is 23.0% and AI-Q6's Hulten branch is 36.5%. wave2.coupling_tension: PRIMARY TENSION, and my updating makes it SHARPER than the Wave-1 seats had it: AI-Q3 (data-centre electricity, P50 998.2, P90 1,573.8 TWh) and AI-Q4 (66.0% impairment) cannot both hold at their locked values once demographics are endogenous, because 2B holds demographics exogenous and therefore holds the COST OF CAPITAL facing a long-lived, electricity-intensive asset exogenous too. DIRECTION: AI-Q4 UP, AI-Q3 DOWN. The Bayesian content my seat adds is that this channel is not a theory prior — it has a 2.5:1 likelihood ratio behind it. The observable price of the loanable-funds pool is at a multi-decade high in THREE independent sovereigns at once (DFII10 2.60% and DFII30 3.06-3.08% with a POSITIVE +45bp real 10s30s slope, JGB 30y at an all-time 4.235% on 5 Oct 2026), and that shape is 2.5x more probable in the world where the real term premium stays above 100bp than in the mean-reverting world. An impairment test is a discount-rate test before it is a demand test, and a capital structure of ~$1.4T of circular vendor/cloud/chip commitments on ~$300B of cumulative equity and ~$650B of debt issuance is rate-sensitive rather than equity-cushioned. So I carry AI-Q4 to 74-78% and AI-Q3 to a P50 near 820-880 TWh with the P90 cut to ~1,250-1,350. Two reinforcing arithmetic points: a 2.7x load build (365 -> 998 TWh) needs on the order of 1.5-2.0 TW of new firm-equivalent capacity plus shells plus silicon at a 10-13% nominal WACC against 3-6 year GPU lives, with grid interconnection the most rate-sensitive long-duration asset in the stack (a 40-year transmission asset at 2.0-2.5% real plus a 150-250bp spread levelizes 35-45% above 2015-19 financing, on stated assumptions of 40-year life, 92% availability, flat real opex, one refinancing at year 20 and no residual credited); and the load is braked by a willingness-to-pay ceiling expressed as an electricity-bill share of GDP, so a demographically-constrained GDP path shrinks the denominator at the same moment the hurdle rate rises. Note the self-consistency: 66% and 998 TWh are already in mild tension BEFORE demographics, since impairment at scale is what truncates the build, and the load number is the one that gives because it is the physical consequence of the capex AI-Q4 says gets cancelled. SECOND TENSION, OPPOSITE SIGN, and it is a REINFORCEMENT rather than a contradiction: a steep real term premium is not neutral across firms. An incumbent financing from internal cash flow faces a far lower effective hurdle than a debt-financed marginal entrant, so a high cost of capital mechanically PRODUCES rent concentration and suppresses the SME-adoption statistic AI-Q2 measures. Coupling therefore supports AI-Q6's 47.2% jagged-diffusion-with-rent-concentration and AI-Q2's low 21.3% rather than straining them, and my CQ6-B at 50 is that mechanism rather than a hedge. THIRD TENSION, the one I resolve differently from a naive coupling and the one where my lens does the most work: AI-Q5 (38.2% for a >= 3.5pp fall in the J/K/M labour compensation share) is NOT transmissible to CQ1's conjunct B, and the transmission has the WRONG SIGN. A falling compensation SHARE is fully compatible with a RISING median wage in the same sectors, because if displacement removes junior and entry-level roles first then compositional selection raises the median of the survivors — removing the lowest-paid 8-10% of J/K/M headcount lifts the surviving sectoral median 3-5% with no individual wage changing. So AI-Q5 resolving YES LOWERS rather than raises the probability that F+Q beats J+K+M by 10pp on MEDIANS. In likelihood-ratio terms, a forecaster who couples AI-Q5 into CQ1 positively is applying an LR above 1 to a signal whose true LR is below 1, and the question's own measure fights the hypothesis it was built to test. FOURTH TENSION, with 2A rather than 2B: the r-side of 2A is internally strained, since '(r-g) worse by +1.0pp even where a frictionless r* eases' sits in the same block as the BIS Box C demand-shortfall warning and the Chinese savings glut, implying a G7 real yield that is simultaneously high on fiscal arithmetic and low on demand. My resolution, forced by my own CQ3, is that the +1.0pp is delivered almost entirely by g falling (my 1.85% is ~1.0-1.1pp below the no-aging counterfactual) with a term-premium overlay, and NOT by r* rising — which is why my CQ4 sits at a middling 1.8% rather than near 3%, and why my r* component is flat at 0.95% while my term-premium component does all the updating.

wave2.lens_self_description: I applied a premortem / devil's-advocate red-team lens against my effort's three Wave-1 panelists — attacking their single shared assumption, their shared internal inconsistency, and their shared right-tail truncation — which forbade me from averaging them, from treating the locked Section 2B marginals as evidence (they are an ensemble's own output, not data), and from building any number by splitting the Wave-1 range.
wave2.cq1_reasoning: RED-TEAM NOTE FIRST: the strongest single argument in the whole Wave-1 set is the median-composition point on conjunct 2 (removing the lowest-paid 8-10% of J/K/M headcount raises the surviving sectoral median 3-5% with no individual wage change), and all three found it independently. A red team that manufactures disagreement with the panel's best argument is noise, so I keep it. I attack conjunct 1 instead. CONJUNCT A (OECD-38 harmonized U <= 5.5% avg 2032-36): Wave 1 put 0.40/0.50/0.55 by adding a recession term to a ~4.8-5.0% structural level. All three committed drag/pull asymmetry on the denominator: they treated working-age contraction as a modest -0.3pp mechanical shaver. OECD-38 working-age population over 2026-36 falls outright in Japan (~-0.8%/yr), Korea (~-1.3%/yr), Italy, Spain, Germany and the EU aggregate, with the OECD-38 aggregate roughly flat to -0.2%/yr. Japan runs 2.4-2.6% and Korea 2.7-3.5% measured unemployment at a far worse dependency ratio than the OECD mean - the demographic end-state is a LOW-unemployment regime, not a high one, and the care/construction scarcity the question's second conjunct posits is by construction a tight-labour regime. The binding risk is one deep bust inside the 20-quarter window; I weight that at 0.30 (the AI capex complex is ~40% of MSCI World cap on ~$300B of equity against ~$650B of debt) but note a capex bust concentrates job loss in cognitive/tech employment, which is a small share of OECD-38 headcount, not in the mass-employment sectors that move the aggregate rate. Marginal A = 0.52. CONJUNCT B (F+Q real median hourly beats J+K+M by >=10.0pp, 2025-36, i.e. 0.87pp/yr for 11 years): I go above Wave 1's 0.14-0.30 but not far. For: the 2019-2023 episode already delivered ~5-8pp of cumulative reversal in four years in exactly this direction (Autor-Dube-McGrew) off a tight-labour mechanism that aging makes structural rather than cyclical; US and EU construction and health/social-care vacancy rates sit at or near record highs; and the measure is a MEDIAN, which in F is market-priced and in Q is pulled up by the statutory minimum-staffing and licensure floors several OECD states have legislated since 2022. Against, and decisive: (i) the J/K/M composition-selection effect runs the wrong way; (ii) ISIC Q is ~70% publicly funded and the locked 2A fiscal block (net interest 2%->3% of GDP) makes care the rationed-by-volume adjustment variable, not the paid one; (iii) ISIC F is the most rate-sensitive sector in the economy and my own 0.70 weight on a capex bust implies a construction real-wage air-pocket somewhere in the window. Marginal B = 0.22. CORRELATION: both load on one "physical/care scarcity binds without a deep bust" factor; rho = +0.35. JOINT = 0.52(0.22) + 0.35*sqrt(0.52*0.48*0.22*0.78) = 0.1144 + 0.35(0.2070) = 0.1868 -> 19, reported 20. I sit above all three Wave-1 panelists but only by ~5pp, because the honest red-team finding here is that the panel got conjunct 2 right and conjunct 1 slightly wrong, not that the conjunction is live.
wave2.cq2_reasoning: I go BELOW all three Wave-1 panelists (20/36/29) and the move is entirely in the China conjunct. CONJUNCT A (OECD-38 GDP-weighted core >= 2.50% avg 2027-2036): sub-window build, 2027-29 at 2.80 (weight 0.3; observed US core PCE 3.1% y/y in Sep 2026, a Fed that hiked 25bp on 16 Sep 2026 and held 10-2 on 28 Oct with both dissents for a further hike - the carry-over is real), 2030-32 at 2.20 (0.4), 2033-36 at 2.05 (0.3). Average = 0.84 + 0.88 + 0.615 = 2.335%. Note the GDP weighting: the euro area and Japan are ~30% of OECD-38 and the euro area has NO 10-year core window >=2.5% since 1999. With sigma 0.45 on a 10-year average, P(>=2.50) = P(z >= 0.37) = 0.356, call it 0.37. This is BELOW Panelist 3's 0.58 because he front-loaded off US prints without GDP-weighting in Japan and the euro area, and below Panelist 2's 0.42 because my 2032-36 leg is lower (my CQ3 is higher and my CQ4 is lower - a high-productivity, cheap-capital back half is disinflationary). CONJUNCT B (China headline CPI < 1.50% avg 2027-2036): THIS IS WHERE WAVE 1 IS WRONG. Panelists 1 and 2 put 0.70 and 0.76 by running the Japan-1995 template as a reference class; Panelist 3 put 0.55 on live data and was right to. The observable: NBS 15 Oct 2026 has September CPI +0.9% y/y (August +0.8%), core +1.0% y/y at a 19-month high, gasoline +16.6% y/y contributing ~0.47pp, and PPI +5.0% y/y with +1.2% m/m. China has EXITED deflation with a large unpassed producer-price impulse. The Japan analogy is the anchoring error of this effort: Japan's deflation ran alongside a 25-year appreciating real effective exchange rate and a FALLING services share, while China is deliberately depreciating pressure out of the system, has pension indexation running against a subsidy already at 10.1% of fiscal expenditure, and has a rising services share in a shrinking labour force - a shrinking population is an UPWARD force on non-tradable prices once the property overhang clears, which is the drag/pull asymmetry the panel applied to growth but never to prices. A 10-year average below 1.50% now requires ten consecutive years at or below ~1.4% starting from a 0.9% print that is rising. Marginal B = 0.48. CORRELATION: a shared global energy/commodity factor is visible in BOTH series right now (US headline PCE 3.6% with m/m +0.5%; Chinese gasoline +16.6%) and it pushes them the SAME way, against the required divergence; the offsetting "Chinese excess capacity meets OECD supply walls" regime channel is real but weaker now that the PPI impulse is positive. rho = -0.10. JOINT = 0.37(0.48) - 0.10*sqrt(0.37*0.63*0.48*0.52) = 0.1776 - 0.10(0.2384) = 0.1538 -> 16.
wave2.cq3_reasoning: THE SINGLE STRONGEST SHARED ASSUMPTION ACROSS ALL THREE WAVE-1 PANELISTS, AND MY ATTACK ON IT. None of the three questioned that the locked 2A drag coefficients are COUNTERFACTUAL-NET and can therefore be subtracted from a historical or current growth base. Panelist 1: mechanical centre 0.60(0.90)+0.40(2.60) = 1.58, then adds back 0.4-0.5. Panelist 2: 0.63(1.20)+0.37(2.00) = 1.50, nudged to 1.70, and states explicitly that "the locked 2A block removes ~1.06 pp from a no-aging coupled baseline of ~2.56%". Panelist 3: 0.63(1.1)+0.37(3.0) = 1.80. All three subtract an aging drag from a base that ALREADY CONTAINS four decades of aging. The OECD old-age ratio rose from ~14% (1960) to ~31% (2023/24); Japan's went 6% -> 30%; China's working-age share peaked in 2010-2015 and has fallen since. Realized OECD+China PPP-weighted growth over 2015-2024 was ~2.5-2.8%/yr WITH that deterioration in progress. The locked "-2.7pp China" and "0.6%/yr OECD per capita absent productivity offsets" are PARTIAL DERIVATIVES from models (IMF WEO Apr 2025 Ch.2; OECD EO 2025), and the OECD figure says "absent productivity offsets" on its face - it is not a forecast. Subtracting the full partial from a realized base that embeds the historical response double-counts. The incremental 2026-36 demographic deterioration relative to the 2015-24 realized base is roughly -0.5pp, not -1.1pp. MY BUILD. Base: 2015-2024 realized OECD-38 + China PPP-weighted ~2.55%/yr (COVID-neutralized). Incremental demographic deterioration 2026-36 vs that base: -0.50. Expected AI TFP lift from the locked AI-Q6 regime weights: 0.162(0.70) + 0.472(0.35) + 0.365(0.07) = 0.113 + 0.165 + 0.026 = +0.30. Automation demand-pull that all three under-weighted (this is the drag/pull asymmetry the brief names): China already installs more than half of world industrial robots at >470 units per 10,000 manufacturing workers, above Germany and Japan, and faces the steepest labour contraction in the set - the economy with the largest labour scarcity shock is the one with the deepest installed automation capability and the lowest effective hurdle rate (state-directed credit); OECD care-sector capital substitution is the same mechanism with worse measurement. +0.15. Healthy-aging offset, half of the locked global +0.4 scaled to this aggregate: +0.20. Capex-bust and fiscal-consolidation drag inside or just before the window: -0.25. SUM = 2.55 - 0.50 + 0.30 + 0.15 + 0.20 - 0.25 = 2.45; I cut to 2.25 to respect the Chinese-deflator measurement problem (Chinese real GDP is an administrative statistic) and the possibility that the 2015-24 base itself flatters. CROSS-CHECK BY LEG: US has grown ~2.4%/yr 2015-2025 with an aging population and is ~0.40 of OECD-38 PPP; 0.40(2.0) + 0.60(1.0) = 1.40 for the OECD leg, vs Wave 1's 1.10-1.20 - their OECD leg requires the US to decelerate to ~1.6% AND Europe/Japan to 0.7%, which is a double pessimism. China at 3.2% (between Panelist 3's 3.0 and the model's 3.8, far above Panelist 2's 2.0): China PPP GDP per capita is ~30-35% of the US, and Korea grew 4.5%/yr through 2000-2010 from a higher relative income with a working-age share already turning. Blend at 0.62/0.38: 0.62(1.40) + 0.38(3.20) = 0.868 + 1.216 = 2.08; with the automation-pull asymmetry I carry 2.25. SPREAD - THE OTHER SHARED WAVE-1 ERROR: all three TRUNCATED THE RIGHT TAIL BY CONSTRUCTION and said so ("I deliberately compress the right tail", "cap the right tail because clearing 2.6% requires the >=+0.50pp TFP branch that 2B itself prices at only 23%"). That is using the ensemble's own prior as evidence about the world - circular, and it is scope insensitivity on the upside: 2.6% coupled growth does NOT require a TFP breakout, it requires China at 3.5% and the OECD at 1.8%, both of which have five-year precedent inside the last decade. P10 = 0.90 (one synchronized recession plus China at ~1.5%), P50 = 2.25, P90 = 3.40. Implied left sigma 1.05, right sigma 0.90 - wider on both sides than any Wave-1 panelist, which is the correct red-team shape when the centre was built by stacking point adjustments.
wave2.cq4_reasoning: I am 70bp BELOW the Wave-1 centre (1.60/2.00/1.95) with a strong right skew. THE SHARED WAVE-1 INCONSISTENCY I AM ATTACKING: all three assign 66-80% to an AI capex impairment event (two of them argue the locked 66% is TOO LOW, at 72-80%), and all three then build a 2032-36 central case out of fiscal dominance and a WIDENING term premium - a world conditional on the bust NOT having happened. They each put the post-bust world only in their P10. That is narrative coherence mistaken for likelihood: the fiscal-dominance story is internally elegant, and it is the minority branch of their own stated probabilities. If P(bust resolved before or early in the window) = 0.70 and the post-bust path averages ~0.95%, while the no-bust fiscal-dominance path averages ~1.70% [reflecting the historical sign evidence below, not the Wave-1 2.0-2.6%], E = 0.70(0.95) + 0.30(1.70) = 0.665 + 0.510 = 1.18. THE EVIDENCE THAT BREAKS THEIR DEBT-SUPPLY ELASTICITY: Panelists 1 and 2 lean on a 2-4bp-per-1pp-of-debt/GDP elasticity. US federal debt/GDP went from ~62% (2007) to ~100% (2012) - roughly +38pp, i.e. +76 to +152bp on that elasticity - while the US 10y TIPS yield went from ~+2.4% to ~-0.7%, a 310bp FALL. Japan reached ~250% debt/GDP with a 10y real yield around zero for two decades. Over 1981-2000 US debt/GDP rose and real yields fell by ~500bp. For a reserve-currency sovereign with its own central bank, the time-series sign of the debt-supply channel is the OPPOSITE of the one the panel priced, because the fiscal deterioration and the real-yield collapse have a common cause: the bust. The panel has mistaken a cross-sectional spread story (which applies to Italy, not the G7 aggregate) for an aggregate-level one. MANDATED DECOMPOSITION, G7 GDP-weighted 2032-36 average = r* + real term premium - repression wedge. (1) r* = +0.80%. Current G7 GDP-weighted level ~0.93% on the panel's own reconstruction. I take the locked 2A language literally - "even where a frictionless r* eases" - and size the easing legs bigger than Wave 1 did: precautionary saving under labour-income uncertainty was sized at only -20bp by Panelist 2, when the three economies that actually ran a cognitive-employment-security shock plus aging (Japan post-1995, Korea post-2015, Germany post-2003) each show saving-rate responses consistent with -80 to -150bp on the domestic neutral rate; post-bust excess capacity suppresses investment demand (the 2002-2004 and 2009-2015 precedents) for the whole first half of the window; the Chinese surplus still recycles $500-800B/yr. Against: boomer dissaving (+25 net of the longevity leg: +5), public dissaving (+35), physical/grid capex demand (+25 raw, haircut by the bust to +10). Net change -13bp, so r* = 0.80. (2) Real term premium = +0.55%, against Wave 1's +0.75 to +1.30. Two reasons they are too high. First, SCOPE INSENSITIVITY ON THE ISSUANCE MIX: the first-line fiscal response to a rollover-cost problem is not to pay the term premium, it is to stop issuing duration. The US Treasury is already bill-heavy with a falling weighted-average maturity, and the UK DMO has been shortening since 2023. A term premium is the price of DURATION SUPPLY; shortening the mix truncates the 10-year point mechanically, and it requires no announcement, no legislation, and no "repression" label - which is why the panel's framing (a 40-45% probability of an announced wedge) under-counts it. Second, the largest structural duration BUYER in history arrives inside this window: OECD pension and insurance balance sheets at peak retiree-liability matching, under LDI, Solvency II matching-adjustment and IORP rules that force long bonds, which is a demographic force the panel counted only on the supply side. Offsetting upward: convenience-yield erosion, basis-trade absorption as the fragile marginal buyer (a discontinuous, not a level, risk - it belongs in the tail, not the mean), the observed synchronized long-end repricing (JGB 30y 4.235% intraday 5 Oct 2026; 30y gilts near 1998 highs). Central +0.55, 80% range 0.00 to +1.70. (3) Repression wedge = -0.40%, bigger and likelier than Wave 1's -0.25 to -0.30. All three assumed the US is "the least likely adopter" and GDP-weighted the wedge away. The US has the deepest precedent of any G7 sovereign: an explicit 2.5% long-bond ceiling from 1942 to 1951, Regulation Q, and a 2020 QE-plus-forward-guidance package that functioned as a cap without being called one. Repression does not require an announced cap - it is bank and money-fund liquidity rules that create captive Treasury demand, SLR calibration, Basel endgame softening, buyback and WAM management, and statutory reserve-asset requirements on new instrument classes. Several of those are already live policy in 2025-26. P(material wedge, >=50bp, somewhere in 2032-36 on >=0.80 of G7 GDP weight) = 0.60; conditional wedge ~-75bp; expected -0.40, bimodal. SUM: 0.80 + 0.55 - 0.40 = 0.95; I shade UP to 1.15 out of respect for the one hard observation that cuts against me - DFII10 at 2.60% on 30 Oct 2026 with policy TIGHTENING, and the historical fact that only ~2 of 6 G7 decade transitions since 1970 kept the average within +/-50bp of the prior level. VARIANCE ATTRIBUTION: the repression wedge carries the most variance in MY answer (bimodal, 0 vs -75 to -150bp) and therefore the left tail; the real term premium carries the second most (sigma ~0.60) and the entire right tail; r* carries the least (sigma ~0.40) and is largely orthogonal to the demographics x AI coupling, exactly as Panelist 2 argued and for his reason. I RESPECT THE 2A DISTINCTION differently from Wave 1: they satisfied the +1.0pp (r-g) deterioration through g falling to 1.7-2.05%. My CQ3 is 2.25%, so I cannot buy that route as fully as they did - I deliver the (r-g) claim through the term premium and fiscal arithmetic in the no-repression branch and concede that in my modal branch the locked +1.0pp is NOT fully reproduced, which is an explicit tension with 2A and not a smuggled reconciliation. P10 = 0.10 (bust plus heavy repression plus flight-to-quality; a 5-year average near zero real has 2011-2013 and 2020-2021 precedent), P50 = 1.15, P90 = 2.80 (fiscal dominance expressed in yields, basis-trade unwind, no repression response - the Wave-1 central case as my upper decile).
wave2.cq5_reasoning: Below all three (34/30/18). CONJUNCT A (ICE BofA MOVE averages >= 105 over 2027-2036) = 0.30. Live telemetry is against it: the index appears to have traded roughly 65-103 through 2026 (70.9 on 17 Jul 2026; ~103 at the March 2026 spike; ~66 on an undated calm reading), i.e. below the threshold even at its own 2026 high. Trailing 10-year average ~75; 2010-2019 ~70-80; 2022 ~120 and 2023 ~125. Clearing 105 as a TEN-YEAR MEAN requires sustaining 2022-23 conditions for a decade, which has no precedent in the index's history. Two further points: the series was reconstructed after the ICE acquisition, so a 10-year mean threshold is partly a methodology bet; and my 0.60 repression probability PINS rate vol by construction - a managed curve cannot deliver high MOVE, so my own CQ4 decomposition suppresses this conjunct harder than Panelist 2's 0.45 suppressed his. Basis-point-vol mechanics at a 4-5% yield level are the one force pushing up, worth ~10-15 points of index level, and that is already in my 0.30. CONJUNCT B = 0.24, and THIS IS MY SHARPEST DIVERGENCE FROM WAVE 1. Sub-condition 2a, P(>=25% MSCI World peak-to-trough drawdown somewhere in 2027-36) = 0.85, built from the locked financing structure: ~$1.4T of circular AI vendor/cloud/chip commitments on ~$300B of cumulative equity and ~$650B of debt, in a complex that is ~40% of MSCI World capitalization; a 45-55% de-rating of the complex alone delivers ~20% of index drawdown before any contagion. Sub-condition 2b, P(G7 nominals FAIL to rally >=50bp, or rise >=25bp, during that drawdown) = 0.28, against Wave 1's 0.42-0.45. Their number is availability bias on 2022. The mechanism they themselves assign 66-80% probability to is a BURSTING INVESTMENT BUBBLE - a credit and capex shock with disinflationary content (stranded datacenter capacity, collapsing power prices, capex going to zero, employment loss concentrated in high-income cognitive labour). Every bursting-investment-bubble drawdown in the record produced a large bond rally: 2000-02 US 10y -250bp, 2007-09 -200bp, 1989-92 Japan, 1929-32. The 2022 counterexample was a commodity and supply-side inflation shock with NO equity-valuation bubble bursting in capital goods - it is the wrong template for the shock they are forecasting. Add that a sovereign at 142% debt/GDP with 3%-of-GDP net interest has the strongest possible incentive AND the 2020 playbook to force the rally, which is the same 0.60 repression option appearing a third time. So 0.85 x 0.28 = 0.238. CORRELATION: strongly positive, both conjuncts are the same regime object and both are suppressed by the same repression switch; rho = +0.45. JOINT = 0.30(0.238) + 0.45*sqrt(0.30*0.70*0.238*0.762) = 0.0714 + 0.45(0.1952) = 0.0714 + 0.0878 = 0.159 -> 15 after a small further haircut for the MOVE methodology risk cutting the same way. CROSS-LINK: my 0.60 repression probability and my disinflationary-bust mechanism both push this down; a panelist at 0.15 repression and a supply-shock bust mechanism lands near 40.
wave2.cq6_reasoning: Applied the lexical-priority lock mechanically against MY OWN CQ3 and my own OECD core distribution. My CQ3: P10 0.90 / P50 2.25 / P90 3.40, so right sigma = (3.40-2.25)/1.282 = 0.897 and left sigma = (2.25-0.90)/1.282 = 1.053. My OECD-38 GDP-weighted core for the 2032-36 SUB-window: central 2.15%, sigma 0.55 (the same object that produced CQ2's 2.335% ten-year average - the 2030-32 leg at 2.20 and the 2033-36 leg at 2.05 blend to ~2.11, carried at 2.15). STEP 1, A if growth >= 2.6%: P(z >= (2.6-2.25)/0.897) = P(z >= 0.390) = 0.348. I report 33, haircutting ~1.5pp for resolution risk on the growth measure itself (PPP weighting convention; the Chinese deflator). STEP 2, else C if core >= 2.7 AND growth < 2.0: P(core >= 2.7) = P(z >= (2.7-2.15)/0.55) = P(z >= 1.000) = 0.159. P(growth < 2.0) = P(z <= (2.0-2.25)/1.053) = P(z <= -0.237) = 0.406. P(core < 2.0) = P(z <= (2.0-2.15)/0.55) = P(z <= -0.273) = 0.393. rho = +0.25 (the BIS Box C demand-deficit mechanism couples them; the supply-wall story would decouple them): joint = 0.301(0.393) + 0.25*sqrt(0.301*0.699*0.393*0.607) = 0.1183 + 0.25(0.2238) = 0.1743 -> 17. Disjoint from C on inflation and from A on growth. STEP 4, B = residual = 100 - 33 - 12 - 17 = 38. Sum exactly 100. CONSISTENCY CHECK PERFORMED, as required. (i) Against my own CQ3: A at 33 is exactly P(g >= 2.6) recomputed from my stated P50 and P90 under a normal with sigma 0.897, less a 1.5pp measurement haircut - a reader who recomputes from my P10/P50/P90 must get 34-35. My P50 of 2.25 sits in B's literal band and B is still modal, so I have not violated the lock's prohibition. (ii) Against my own CQ2: CQ2's conjunct A put P(2027-36 core >= 2.50) at 0.37 off a 2.335 central; C needs the tighter 2032-36 core >= 2.70 off a 2.15 central, which is 0.159 - strictly and substantially lower, as the higher threshold (+35bp) and lower sub-window central (-18bp) require. My low CQ2 of 16 is driven by the CHINA conjunct, not the OECD one, so it does not force C down further than this. (iii) Residual-cell audit: B at 38 comprises ~36.6pp of mass in growth 1.7-2.6 that is not captured by A or C, minus the ~11pp of that band that C and the growth-2.0-2.6-with-core>=2.7 cell claim, plus the ~12pp leftover cells the lock dumps into B (growth < 1.7 with core 2.0-2.7). SUBSTANTIVE SHAPE, AND IT IS THE POINT: my distribution is BIMODAL - A at 33 and D at 17 both above the Wave-1 panel (13-19 and 17-20), with B thinned from their 44-49 to 38. That is the direct consequence of taking their own 66-80% bust probability seriously instead of leaving it in a P10: the coupled world either gets the productivity and the cheap post-bust capital (A) or gets the demand shortfall and the stranded capacity (D), and the elegant barbell with steep real term premia and coexisting scarcity rents is the state that requires the bust to be permanently deferred. Wave 1's modal B is narrative coherence, not probability mass. C at 12 is well below all three because my inflation central for 2032-36 is lower than theirs - a high-productivity, low-real-rate back half with China's goods disinflation only partly spent is not a 2.7% core world.

hypothesis_critique.a: "SMOOTHLY" carries the whole failure, and the three Wave-1 scores of 5/7/7 are nonetheless slightly overconfident. The transfer is blocked by three separate frictions, not one: occupational (a displaced paralegal is not a licensed nurse; care work is credentialed in every OECD-38 state and the credential takes 1-3 years), geographic (cognitive employment is metropolitan, care demand is where the old people are, which is increasingly not metropolitan), and - the binding one for my effort - FISCAL. Care demand is a publicly funded claim; the locked 2A block has net interest going 2% -> 3% of GDP, so the sector that must absorb the labour cannot bid for it. The plank also has the sign of the wage signal backwards: a smooth supply response requires a relative wage rise in care, which is exactly what CQ1's conjunct 2 asks for and what I put at 0.22. I score 8 rather than 5 because partial reallocation is real at the margin - care-adjacent coordination, scheduling, remote monitoring and case-management roles are genuinely fed by displaced administrative labour, and OECD immigration policy is already loosening for care visas, which is the plank's mechanism arriving by a different route.
hypothesis_critique.b: "BLOCKS" is false and "SEVERELY" is half-true, and Wave 1 (12/18/18) scored the plank as one claim when the scope lock explicitly splits it in two. On the PHYSICAL channel the plank is simply wrong in direction: the locked 2A demographics are the largest care-labour demand pull in history, and the Philippines is the world's largest exporter of nurses and care workers - physical migration demand RISES, and the binding constraint is OECD visa policy, not AI. On the VIRTUAL channel "severely" is defensible for the Philippines specifically and much weaker for India: Philippine BPO is ~7-8% of GDP with ~1.3-1.7M direct seats concentrated in voice and chat, the single most directly automatable export activity on earth, and that concentration has no Indian equivalent - India's ~$200B+ of IT services exports are weighted toward integration, maintenance and managed services, where AI raises output per engineer before it removes the engineer, and India also captures the global capability centre reshoring that the same technology enables. So the plank fails on "blocks" (AI displaces a channel, it does not block labour export), fails on India, and survives only as a Philippines-specific virtual-services claim. I score 30 against the panel's 12-18 because they scored the weaker half of a compound claim and discarded the half that is live.
hypothesis_critique.c: "THEN" carries it - the plank is a claim about SEQUENCING, and it is the one plank where the Wave-1 panel contradicted itself. All three built sub-window inflation paths that are literally this plank (Panelist 2: 2.6 -> 2.3 -> 2.3; Panelist 3: "heavily front-loaded... 2027-2029 run 2.5-3.0%" with the back half lower; Panelist 1's reference-class work has the same shape) and then scored the plank 31/42/50. My own numbers say 2027-29 at ~2.8% and 2032-36 at ~2.15%, which is hot-then-falling. The residual failure risk is in "falls": it may fall to 2.1-2.3% rather than to target, so a reader who requires "falls" to mean "returns to 2%" gets a lower score, and the alternative paths are a 2022-style second impulse (grid, care, tariffs) or a China PPI pass-through that keeps the 2030s at 2.5%+. I score 58 - materially above all three - because scoring the plank below 50 while publishing a monotonically declining sub-window path is incoherent.
hypothesis_critique.d: "EVENTUALLY" and "WINS" both fail, but for opposite reasons and the panel scored only one of them. "Eventually" is a horizon dodge: the resolution date is Dec 31 2036, and nothing in the plank's mechanism is testable on that horizon - a claim that cannot be falsified by the question's own resolution date is not substantially correct as stated. "Wins" is undefined: against what counterfactual, and wins on what metric? My CQ3 P50 of 2.25%/yr is above the Wave-1 panel and above a naive demographic-arithmetic baseline, but it is still below the 1960-2024 historical norm of ~3.2% - so even on my relatively optimistic numbers, AI narrows the demographic gap without closing it. "Exponential" is the third failure: the locked AI-Q6 regimes put 83.7% of mass on sub-breakout diffusion, and the growth channel I actually model is capital deepening plus a +0.30pp TFP lift plus a labour-scarcity substitution pull - a level shift, not an exponent. I score 22 against the panel's 11-15 because they derived their score from a CQ3 that double-subtracts the demographic drag; on my CQ3 the plank is closer to half-right on direction while still failing on every operative word.

key_drivers: THE DOUBLE-SUBTRACTION. All three Wave-1 panelists subtract the locked 2A aging drags (-2.7pp China, OECD per-capita 0.6%/yr) from a base that already embeds four decades of aging - the OECD old-age ratio went 14% (1960) -> 31% (2023/24), Japan 6% -> 30%, China's working-age share peaked 2010-2015 - while realized OECD+China PPP-weighted growth over 2015-2024 ran ~2.55%/yr through that deterioration. The locked coefficients are partial derivatives (the OECD figure says 'absent productivity offsets' on its face), not counterfactual-net forecasts. Correcting the double count moves my CQ3 P50 from their 1.70-2.05 to 2.25 and is the single largest driver in my payload.

THE DEBT-SUPPLY ELASTICITY HAS THE WRONG SIGN AT THE AGGREGATE LEVEL. Panelists 1 and 2 price 2-4bp of real yield per 1pp of debt/GDP. US federal debt/GDP went 62% -> 100% over 2007-2012 (+38pp, i.e. +76 to +152bp on that elasticity) while the US 10y TIPS yield fell ~310bp, from +2.4% to -0.7%; Japan reached ~250% debt/GDP at a ~0% real 10y; 1981-2000 US debt rose and real yields fell ~500bp. For a reserve-currency sovereign with its own central bank the fiscal deterioration and the real-yield collapse share a cause - the bust. This is why my CQ4 P50 is 1.15% against their 1.60-2.00%.

THE PANEL LEFT ITS OWN MODAL WORLD IN ITS P10. All three assign 66-80% to an AI capex impairment event and then build a 2032-36 fiscal-dominance / widening-term-premium central case that is conditional on the bust not having happened, parking the post-bust world in the tenth percentile. Mixing properly - 0.70 on a post-bust ~0.95% real yield path, 0.30 on a no-bust ~1.70% path - gives 1.18%. The same correction thins CQ6-B from their 44-49 to 38 and fattens both A (33) and D (17): my distribution is bimodal, theirs is unimodal around an elegant narrative.

REPRESSION IS BIGGER, LIKELIER, AND MOSTLY UNANNOUNCED. Wave 1 put 0.40-0.45 on a material wedge and only -25 to -30bp expected, GDP-weighting the US away as 'the least likely adopter'. The US ran an explicit 2.5% long-bond ceiling 1942-1951 plus Regulation Q, and in 2020 ran a de facto cap without the label. More important, the first-line response to a rollover-cost problem is not paying the term premium, it is not issuing duration: bill-heavy issuance and WAM management, SLR calibration, bank and money-fund liquidity rules creating captive Treasury demand, and statutory reserve-asset requirements on new instrument classes are all repression without an announcement, and several are live policy now. I carry P = 0.60 and an expected -0.40pp, which lowers CQ4, truncates its upper tail, pins MOVE in CQ5's first conjunct, and forces the bond rally that kills CQ5's second conjunct.

THE 2022 TEMPLATE IS THE WRONG SHOCK FOR THE BUST THEY FORECAST. Wave 1 put P(no bond rally | >=25% equity drawdown) at 0.42-0.45 off 2022 - a commodity and supply-side inflation shock with no bursting capital-goods bubble. The shock they assign 66-80% to is a bursting investment bubble, which is disinflationary (stranded datacenter capacity, collapsing power prices, capex to zero, job loss concentrated in high-income cognitive labour) and produced a large bond rally every time in the record: 2000-02 US 10y -250bp, 2007-09 -200bp, Japan 1989-92, 1929-32. This single substitution takes my CQ5 to 15 against their 18-34.

DRAG/PULL ASYMMETRY ON PRICES AS WELL AS GROWTH. The panel applied the aging-as-demand-pull correction (partially) to growth and never to inflation. A shrinking labour force in a rising-services-share economy is an UPWARD force on non-tradable prices once the property overhang clears - which is why Panelists 1 and 2 are wrong to put 0.70-0.76 on China averaging under 1.50% CPI for ten years when the observed September 2026 NBS print is +0.9% and RISING, core at a 19-month high of 1.0%, and PPI at +5.0% y/y with +1.2% m/m. China has exited deflation. My 0.48 on that conjunct is what takes CQ2 to 16, below all three.

wave2.coupling_tension: PRIMARY FINDING, AND IT REVERSES THE WAVE-1 UNANIMITY. All three Wave-1 panelists concluded that endogenizing demographics moves AI-Q4 UP (66% -> 72-80%) and AI-Q3 DOWN (P50 998 -> 600-920 TWh), through a single cost-of-capital channel. The direction on AI-Q3 is wrong, and the direction on AI-Q4 is not established, for two reasons they all missed. (1) AI-Q4's first limb is measured as a share OF ANNOUNCED buildout. They treated the denominator as fixed. If the demographic savings drain and sovereign crowding-out raise the hurdle rate, FEWER projects get announced in the first place - the announcement book is the most rate-sensitive object in the whole stack, since announcing is free and cheap only while the equity market pays for it. A higher cost of capital shrinks the denominator faster than it grows the numerator, which makes the >=20% threshold HARDER, not easier. The second limb (net external AI revenue < 0.5x annualized compute D&A for >=2 consecutive years) is a REVENUE test and is essentially untouched by demographics except through the labour-scarcity demand pull, which raises willingness to pay for cognitive substitution and therefore cuts AGAINST resolution. Net: AI-Q4 under endogenous demographics is roughly unchanged at 62-68%, possibly slightly LOWER, not 72-80%. (2) AI-Q3 MOVES UP, to roughly P50 1,060 / P90 1,650 TWh. The panel conflated financial impairment with physical non-utilization. The closest reference event is long-haul fibre 1999-2002: the overwhelming majority of laid capacity was written down or went dark on the owners' balance sheets, and it was close to fully lit by the early 2010s, because impairment destroys the CLAIM on the asset, not the asset. Stranded datacenter shells, interconnection rights and depreciated GPUs clear at distressed prices to buyers with a low cost of capital, and cheap stranded capacity plus collapsed merchant power prices RAISES utilization, which is what AI-Q3 actually measures (strict operational electricity, not announced capacity). Layer on the demographic demand pull the brief names explicitly - elder care, logistics, 24/7 inference substituting for scarce cognitive labour, and China's labour contraction meeting the world's deepest installed automation base at >470 robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers - and the coupled load is above the exogenous-demographics load, not below it. SECOND FINDING: AI-Q1 (23.0% for a >=+0.50pp/yr TFP lift) is the marginal most clearly too LOW once demographics are endogenous, and it is too low in the demand direction the panel systematically neglected. My CQ3 P50 of 2.25% and CQ6-A of 33 imply something nearer 32-38% on AI-Q1. This is the quantitative form of the drag/pull asymmetry: 2B holds demographics exogenous and therefore holds the WAGE SIGNAL and the care/physical demand schedule exogenous too, which removes the single strongest adoption incentive in the coupled world. THIRD, A TENSION WITH 2A ITSELF, AND I CONCEDE IT RATHER THAN RECONCILE IT. Wave 1 satisfied 2A's '+1.0pp worse global (r-g) even where a frictionless r* eases' by letting g fall to 1.70-2.05%, which over-delivers the claim on the growth side alone and lets them hold a middling-to-high r. My CQ3 is 2.25% and my CQ4 P50 is 1.15%, so on my numbers the locked (r-g) deterioration is NOT fully reproduced - I deliver perhaps +0.4 to +0.6pp of it, through the term premium and the fiscal arithmetic in my minority no-repression branch. That is a genuine inconsistency between my joint distribution and a locked 2A marginal, in the direction of 2A being too pessimistic on both legs at once, and I report it as a finding rather than bending either answer to meet it. FOURTH, THE MODEL (Panelist 2's Fermi seat used the adapter, so the brief requires this attack, and I verified the code rather than taking his summary). src/modules/production.ts line 84 sets gamma = 0.55 on useful energy with alpha + beta + gamma validated to sum, against a mainstream cost-share gamma of 0.05-0.08 - so the model's 2.9-3.9% coupled growth is substantially an electrification artifact, and cutting gamma by the factor of 7-11 that cost-share logic implies would remove most of the energy channel. Direction: every growth number read off the model is biased UP, so it cannot serve as a ceiling (which is how Panelist 2 used it - he read its 1,884-4,180 TWh world datacenter load as evidence the LOCK's P90 is right and the model is too high, when the inference is unidentified in both directions and the lock is itself an ensemble output, not data). The adapter's own disclosures confirm the region problem is worse than a proxy caveat: 'us + oecd-ex-us + china' places Korea, Japan and Turkiye in seasia/mena and Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Costa Rica in latam, so the model's OECD leg EXCLUDES the two best-matched aging economies on earth (Japan and Korea, together ~12-14% of OECD-38 PPP GDP) while including some non-OECD states - which biases its OECD leg UP, compounding the gamma bias in the same direction. The UN WPP low-variant demographic path biases its labour input DOWN, which means its high growth is achieved DESPITE low fertility and the capital/energy channel is carrying even more weight than the headline suggests - that strengthens the gamma criticism rather than excusing the model. And the model has no price level, no unemployment, no sectoral wage, no sovereign benchmark, no term premium and no repression, with interest-capitalization spirals explicitly out of scope, so it is silent on CQ1, CQ2, CQ4 and CQ5 and speaks to CQ3 only through the one parameter the repository itself flags as heterodox. No number in my payload is model-derived; I used the code only to verify that Panelist 2's rejection was correctly signed, which it was, and under-sized, which it also was.

wave3.coupling_tension: THREE FINDINGS, and on the first one I partially REVERSE my own effort's Wave-1 unanimity. (1) AI-Q3 x AI-Q4: all three Wave-1 seats and the Bayesian concluded that endogenizing demographics moves AI-Q4 UP (66% -> 74-80%) and AI-Q3 DOWN (P50 998 -> 600-920 TWh) through one cost-of-capital channel. The red-team landed a real hit on BOTH legs and I move on both. On AI-Q4: its first limb is a share OF ANNOUNCED buildout, and the announcement book is the single most rate-sensitive object in the stack because announcing is free only while equity pays for it — a higher hurdle rate shrinks the denominator at least as fast as the numerator, and the second limb is a revenue-coverage test essentially untouched by demographics except through the labour-scarcity demand pull, which cuts AGAINST resolution. Direction: AI-Q4 under endogenous demographics is 64-70%, i.e. roughly the locked 66%, NOT 74-80%. I withdraw my effort's Wave-1 upward revision. On AI-Q3: the fibre-1999-2002 precedent is decisive on mechanism — impairment destroys the CLAIM on the asset, not the asset; shells, interconnection rights and depreciated accelerators clear at distressed prices to low-cost-of-capital buyers and stranded capacity plus collapsed merchant power RAISES utilization, which is what a strict-operational-electricity question measures. But the red-team over-read the timing: the fibre re-lighting took the better part of a decade, and the window closes Dec 31 2036, so the re-utilization leg is only partly in-sample. Direction: AI-Q3 P50 roughly UNCHANGED at 930-1,000 TWh (not the 600-880 the Wave-1 seats carried, not the 1,060 the red-team carried), with the P90 compressed to ~1,350-1,450 because the top decile requires an uninterrupted financed build at a 10-13% nominal WACC. (2) AI-Q5 is NOT transmissible to CQ1 conjunct B and the naive coupling has the WRONG SIGN. A falling J/K/M compensation SHARE is fully compatible with a RISING sectoral MEDIAN wage: removing the lowest-paid 8-10% of cognitive headcount lifts the surviving median 3-5% with no individual wage changing. SUM = 100 exactly. CONSISTENCY CHECK AGAINST MY OWN CQ3, as required: my P50 is 1.95%, which sits inside B's literal 1.7-2.5% band, and B is my modal regime — the lock's prohibition on putting most mass on A with a low P50 is respected, and A at 20 is exactly P(growth >= 2.6) recomputable from my stated P50 and P90 under a normal with sigma 0.80, less the measurement haircut. A reader who redoes that arithmetic must get 20-21. CONSISTENCY CHECK AGAINST MY OWN CQ2, as required: CQ2's conjunct A puts P(2027-36 core >= 2.50%) at 0.46 off a 2.42% ten-year central; CQ6-C needs the strictly tighter condition of 2032-36 core >= 2.70% off a 2.25% sub-window central, which is 0.207 — lower, as it must be, and lower by about the right amount given the +20bp higher threshold and the -17bp lower sub-window central. C at 17 then sits below 20.7 because of the added growth condition, and my CQ2 joint of 24 sits below 46 because it additionally conditions on China at 0.55. All three numbers are siblings of one inflation object and none contradicts another. COHERENCE WITH MY CQ4, as required: CQ6-B's text names 'steep real term premia', and my decomposition gives a premium of 0.95% against a reconstructed 2026 base of ~0.92% — steep by 2015-21 standards and flat by its own 2026 standard, which is why B is modal at 46 rather than the 49-50 the Wave-1 seats and the Bayesian carried, and why C is 17 rather than 21-22: a 0.95% premium with a 52%-probable wedge is the barbell, not the stagflationary spike. COHERENCE WITH MY CQ5, as required: CQ5 at 19 is driven by a modest premium plus a sizable repression wedge plus a disinflationary bust template, and C+D at 34 (versus the Wave-1 seats' 37-40 and the red-team's 29) is the consistent mass for that configuration. SUBSTANTIVE READ: the red-team's bimodality argument — that the panel left its own 64-80% bust probability in a P10 and so produced a unimodal distribution around an elegant narrative — is PARTIALLY upheld. A rises from the Wave-1/Bayesian 12-19 to 20 and B thins from 44-50 to 46, but I do not reach his 33/38/12/17, because his A rests on a CQ3 P50 of 2.25 built on a China leg of 3.2% that imports a Korea-2000-2010 convergence analogy with less support than the locked block he is attacking. (r-g) cross-check: at CQ3 1.95% and CQ4 1.50%, r-g = -0.45, so debt/GDP stabilizes only with a primary balance near zero — which is why I did NOT import A's qualitative rider ('debt/GDP stabilizes via growth'); the lock defines A by growth alone, and had I used the rider, A would be nearer 14.
