hypothesis_critique.a: "SMOOTHLY" carries it, with "SUPPLY" as accomplice. Three frictions, not one, and the third is my effort's: occupational (care work is credentialed in every OECD-38 state, 1-3 years), geographic (cognitive employment is metropolitan, care demand is where the old live), and FISCAL — the sector that must absorb the labour is ~70% publicly funded against net interest moving 2% -> 3% of GDP and, in China, a pension subsidy already at 10.1% of fiscal expenditure, so the shadow price of care labour rises and is NOT PAID and the adjustment variable is volume rationed. Quantity arithmetic: OECD-38 65+ headcount rises ~55-65M by 2036, requiring ~11-13M additional LTC/health FTEs at ~0.2 marginal care FTE per additional 65+; what a 38%-probable 3.5pp compensation-share fall frees is a wage BILL equivalent to ~4-8M FTEs, short by a factor of ~2 BEFORE any matching, and observed transition rates from ISIC J/K/M into licensed care work are low single digits of percent. My seat adds the sign error: AI's own financing competes with care's financing for the same loanable-funds pool, so the two are substitutes at the margin, not complements. I score 7 rather than the 5-6 two seats gave, crediting the red-team's one real point — care-adjacent coordination, scheduling and remote-monitoring roles ARE fed by displaced administrative labour, and OECD care-visa policy is already loosening, which is the plank's mechanism arriving by a route the plank does not name.
hypothesis_critique.b: "BLOCKS" is outright false; "SEVERELY" fails on magnitude and survives only in one place. The scope lock itself splits the claim and the plank conflates the halves: AI compresses the VIRTUAL channel (BPO voice, chat, tier-1 back office) while the locked 2A demographics are the largest care-labour demand PULL in history, so the physical channel is pulled harder exactly where the virtual one is compressed, and the binding constraint there is OECD visa policy, not AI. Philippines: OFW remittances run ~$34-38B/yr at ~8-9% of GDP and are dominated by care, maritime and construction placements — the channel aging ENLARGES; BPO at ~$35-38B and ~1.3-1.8M seats is the genuinely exposed slice, concentrated in the most automatable export activity on earth, so 'severely' is locally defensible THERE and nowhere else. India: IT/BPM exports of ~$200B+ are ~1.2% of PPP GDP (~5% at market rates) in a sector that has absorbed three prior platform shifts without a decade of national damage, and it captures the global-capability-centre reshoring the same technology enables. I score 18, holding the four seats' 12-18 against the red-team's 30: he is right that Wave 1 scored a compound claim as one and discarded the live half, which is why I do not go below 18, but 30 over-credits a Philippines-specific virtual-services reading of a plank whose stated subject is both countries and whose verb is wrong in both.
hypothesis_critique.c: "THEN" carries it — the plank is a SEQUENCING claim, and it is the one plank where my own effort contradicted itself. All five seats published monotonically declining sub-window paths (2.6 -> 2.3 -> 2.3; 2.8 -> 2.2 -> 2.05; 'heavily front-loaded... 2027-2029 run 2.5-3.0%') and then scored the plank 31-50; the red-team is right that this is incoherent, and that is a real hit I move on. My own object is 2.75 (2027-29) -> 2.35 (2030-31) -> 2.25 (2032-36), which IS hot-then-moderating, and the first clause is close to observed rather than forecast (BEA 29 Oct 2026 core PCE 3.1% y/y rising, headline 3.6%, a 25bp hike on 16 Sep 2026 and an October hold drawing two dissents for more). What breaks is the word 'falls': 2.25% is above target, not a fall to it, and 20.7% of my mass has 2032-36 core at or above 2.70%. My seat adds the mechanism the plank ignores: financial repression at P = 0.52 is by construction inflation-TOLERANT, since the wedge is paid for in realized inflation, so the same fiscal arithmetic that would cap yields in the 2030s argues against disinflation in the 2030s. The double-hump is also the modal historical shape in the best-matched cases (1973-75 then 1979-82; 1946-48 then 1950-51). 46 — above four seats, below the red-team's 58, because 'falls' meaning 'moderates to 2.25%' is a generous reading of the word.
hypothesis_critique.d: "EVENTUALLY" and "WINS" both fail, and "EXPONENTIAL" fails third. 'Eventually' is a horizon dodge: it converts a Dec 31 2036 question into an untestable limit claim, which is the commonest way a forecasting hypothesis protects itself, and a claim that cannot be falsified by the question's own resolution date is not substantially correct as stated. 'Wins' names no counterfactual and no metric: against the no-aging path AI loses, since my CQ3 of 1.95% sits ~0.70pp below a ~2.65% counterfactual and ~1.2pp below the 1960-2024 norm for this aggregate; against a no-AI path it adds ~+0.30pp and wins trivially; and it ignores distribution, since a capital-concentrated level gain alongside a BIS Box C labour-income demand deficit is CQ6-D, which I price at 17. 'Exponential' is wrong on the margin that matters: output growth depends on the growth rate of a factor's CONTRIBUTION, Hulten and Baumol cap the aggregate by the share of activity not automated, so exponential capability yields at best logarithmic aggregate TFP — and my effort adds a third cap the plank ignores entirely, that an exponentially capable technology must still clear a 10-13% nominal hurdle rate set by the SAME demographic fiscal arithmetic it is supposed to be outrunning. 15, holding the Wave-1/Bayesian 11-15: the red-team's 22 is derived from a CQ3 of 2.25% I did not fully accept, and the direct reference class for 'technology offsets demography' is 0 for ~5 (Japan 1990-2025 at world-leading robot density and ~0.6%/yr real growth, Germany, Italy, Korea since 2015, the euro area 2000-2025).

key_drivers: THE (r-g) DECOMPOSITION DELIVERED ONCE, NOT TWICE OR NOT AT ALL. 2A's '+1.0pp worse global (r-g) even where a frictionless r* eases' is a term-premium and fiscal-arithmetic claim. My CQ3 of 1.95% against a ~2.65% no-aging counterfactual delivers -0.70pp on g; my CQ4 of 1.50% against a ~1.30% no-aging G7 aggregate delivers +0.20pp on r, almost all of it term premium, with r* flat-to-easing at 0.90%. Total +0.90pp, reproduced once. The Wave-1 seats over-delivered it on g alone (-0.9 to -1.1pp) and then still held a high r, booking the same quantity twice and landing 45-50bp too high on CQ4; the red-team under-delivered it (+0.4 to +0.6pp) and conceded an open inconsistency. This single arithmetic constraint does more to set my CQ4 P50 than any other consideration.

REAL TERM PREMIUM AT 0.95%, FLAT ON ITS OWN 2026 BASE: the Bayesian's 2.5:1 likelihood ratio on synchronized multi-sovereign duration repricing (DFII10 2.60% on 30 Oct 2026 with DFII30 3.06-3.08%, a POSITIVE +45bp real 10s30s slope, JGB 30y at an all-time 4.235% intraday on 5 Oct 2026) earns the LEVEL — three independent sovereigns cannot be repriced by a US-idiosyncratic fiscal story and Japan's participation rules out the high-marginal-product reading. But it does not earn the further +38bp widening Fermi wanted, because the red-team's aggregate debt-supply sign evidence (US debt/GDP 62% -> 100% over 2007-2012 while the 10y TIPS yield fell ~310bp; Japan at ~250% with a ~0% real 10y; 1981-2000 debt up, real yields down ~500bp) shows the 2-4bp-per-1pp elasticity has the wrong time-series sign for a reserve-currency sovereign. The premium carries ~45% of my CQ4 variance and essentially all the variance correlated with the coupling.

TWO BUYER-SIDE AND ISSUANCE-SIDE DEMOGRAPHIC CHANNELS WAVE 1 COUNTED ONLY ON THE SUPPLY SIDE, both landed by the red-team: (i) the first-line response to a rollover-cost problem is NOT paying the term premium, it is not issuing duration — bill-heavy issuance and WAM management truncate the 10-year point with no announcement, no legislation and no 'repression' label; (ii) OECD pension and insurance balance sheets reach peak retiree-liability matching inside this window under LDI, Solvency II matching-adjustment and IORP rules, which forces long-bond demand. Together these are why my premium is flat rather than widening, and they are the reason my 0.52 repression probability is higher than Wave 1's 0.40-0.45 while my expected wedge (-0.35) is only modestly larger.

THE BUST-MIXTURE CORRECTION, RESIZED. The panel assigned 64-80% to an AI capex impairment event and then built a 2032-36 central case conditional on the bust NOT having happened, leaving its own modal world in the P10 — the red-team's best structural hit. But AI-Q4 resolution is not the same event as a macro bust depressing a 2032-36 average: its second limb is a revenue-coverage test, and a 2027-32 impairment can be digested before the window opens. At P(macro-relevant bust) = 0.45 with a post-bust path of ~1.00% and a no-bust path of ~1.90%, E = 1.495 — agreeing with my component sum of 1.50 to the decimal, which is the strongest internal check in my payload.

REPRESSION AT P = 0.52 ON A TIGHT DEFINITION. The red-team is right that Wave 1 GDP-weighted the US away as 'the least likely adopter' when the US has the deepest precedent in the G7 (an explicit 2.5% long-bond ceiling 1942-1951, Regulation Q, a de facto 2020 cap without the label) and that repression today operates through SLR calibration, bank and money-fund liquidity rules creating captive demand, buybacks and statutory reserve-asset requirements — several live policy now. But his 0.60 is partly definitional inflation: widen the definition far enough and the base rate approaches 1.0. On the tighter test (>= 50bp of sustained suppression on >= 0.80 of G7 GDP weight) I take 0.52, expected wedge -0.35, bimodal. It lowers CQ4, truncates its right tail, pins MOVE in CQ5's first conjunct, forces the bond rally that kills CQ5's second, and RAISES CQ2's inflation conjunct — the largest source of cross-question correlation in my payload.

THE 2022 TEMPLATE IS THE WRONG SHOCK FOR THE BUST THIS EFFORT FORECASTS. Wave 1 put P(no bond rally | >= 25% equity drawdown) at 0.42-0.45 off 2022 — a commodity and supply-side inflation shock with no bursting capital-goods bubble. The forecast shock is a bursting investment bubble, which is disinflationary (stranded capacity, collapsing merchant power prices, capex to zero, job loss concentrated in high-income cognitive labour) and produced a large bond rally every time in the record: 2000-02 US 10y -250bp, 2007-09 -200bp, Japan 1989-92, 1929-32. I take 0.34, between his 0.28 and their 0.42-0.45, because a ten-year window can hold more than one drawdown and only one needs the correlated type. This is the second-largest move in my payload after CQ4.
wave3.lens_self_description: I am the effort-level posterior: I reconciled the five prior panelists by weighting each one's specific argument on each specific question rather than averaging them, moved where the Wave-2 red-team landed a real empirical hit and refused to move where it merely contrarian-posed, and then enforced arithmetic coherence across my own six answers — which forbade me from introducing any new evidence, reference class, or mechanism of my own that no panelist in my effort had put on the table.

wave_audit.wave1_spread: Widest on CQ3 (1.70 Fermi / 1.80 Scout / 2.05 Historian) and on CQ4's real term premium (0.75 Historian / 1.10 Scout / 1.30 Fermi), and the two disagreements have a single shared cause: whether the locked 2A drag coefficients are counterfactual-net quantities subtractable from a realized base, and whether the +1.0pp (r-g) claim is booked on g, on r, or on both. All three Wave-1 seats independently converged on r* (0.90-1.00) and on the wedge (-0.25 to -0.30) and on the median-composition argument against CQ1's second conjunct, so the genuine spread is narrower than the headline numbers: it is one methodological question (double-subtraction) and one component (the term premium). The second-widest gap was CQ2's China conjunct (0.55 Scout vs 0.70/0.76 Historian/Fermi), where the Scout's NBS telemetry and the other two seats' Japan-1995 reference class simply did not meet.
wave_audit.what_wave2_changed: The RED-TEAM killed three Wave-1 claims and rescued one, and the BAYESIAN rescued one and killed two signals. KILLED by the red-team: (i) the 2-4bp-per-1pp debt-supply elasticity that the Historian and Fermi leaned on — the US 2007-2012 and Japanese counter-examples show the wrong aggregate time-series sign for a reserve-currency sovereign, and this is the main reason my CQ4 is below all three Wave-1 seats; (ii) Wave-1's unanimous 0.42-0.45 on 'nominals fail to rally during an equity drawdown', which was availability bias on 2022, a supply-shock episode and the wrong template for the investment-bubble bust the same seats forecast; (iii) the whole-cloth subtraction of the locked 2A coefficients from a base that already embeds four decades of aging. RESCUED by the red-team: Wave-1's own 64-80% bust probability, which all three seats had parked in a P10 while building a no-bust central case — a real internal incoherence in my effort. RESCUED by the Bayesian: the term-premium LEVEL, via a 2.5:1 likelihood ratio on multi-sovereign duration repricing that is the only argument in the effort with a stated and defensible LR. KILLED by the Bayesian: the Signal Scout's 0.30 on CQ1's conjunct B (he holds no series on it and says so) and most of his own China-exit-from-deflation signal (gasoline at +16.6% y/y contributes ~0.47pp of the 0.9% headline, so ex-gasoline is ~0.43%, commodity pass-through not a regime change). CONTRARIAN-POSED AND NOT MOVED ON: the red-team's CQ3 China leg of 3.2% (he attacks the panel for treating locked coefficients as evidence and then imports a Korea-2000-2010 convergence analogy with less support); his repression probability of 0.60 (the definition is widened until the base rate approaches 1.0, which makes any specific number arbitrary — I took 0.52 on a tighter test); his AI-Q1 revision to 32-38%; and his CQ2 OECD conjunct of 0.37, which is below what his own observed starting point warrants. On AI-Q3 he reversed the effort's unanimity with the strongest single argument of Wave 2 (the fibre-1999-2002 precedent: impairment destroys the claim, not the asset) and I moved HALF way, because the fibre re-lighting took most of a decade and the window closes in 2036.
wave_audit.unresolved: Three things. (1) THE DOUBLE-SUBTRACTION MAGNITUDE. Whether the locked 2A coefficients are partial derivatives or counterfactual-net forecasts is not settlable from inside this effort — it requires the source documents' own counterfactual definitions (IMF WEO April 2025 Ch. 2; OECD Employment Outlook 2025), which nobody here read. My -0.75pp increment is a judgment between the red-team's -0.50 and Wave 1's implied -1.06, and essentially the entire 0.55pp spread in CQ3's P50 across the five seats lives in this one unverifiable choice. (2) THE 2032-36 LEVEL OF THE REAL TERM PREMIUM, because the ACM/Kim-Wright series level is UNVERIFIED at the Signal Scout's horizon (nearest confirmable 0.73% at 30 Apr 2026 and ~0.83% at 15 May 2026; a 0.96% figure dated 18 Sep 2026 is Kim-Wright not ACM; a 1.76% year-end figure is a projection, not an observation). My 0.95% is reconstructed from the GDP-weighted yield less an inferred expected short-real path, not read off a published estimate, and the reconstruction depends on an r* number that is itself model-derived — exactly the object my effort cannot measure. (3) WHETHER AN IMPAIRMENT EVENT IS A DISCOUNT-RATE EVENT, A KILOWATT-HOUR EVENT, OR BOTH WITH A DECADE'S LAG. This is the unresolved core of the coupling question and it moves AI-Q3, AI-Q4, CQ5's second conjunct and CQ6's A-versus-D split simultaneously; my resolution (impairment is a claim event, re-utilization lags past 2036 only partly) is a timing judgment nobody in this effort can date. Also unresolved and deliberately so: I have never seen the other three efforts, so nothing here is reconciled against their CQ1/CQ2/CQ3 work.

Cause, decomposed: -20bp from the red-team's aggregate debt-supply sign evidence (US debt/GDP 62% -> 100% over 2007-2012 against a 310bp FALL in the 10y TIPS yield), which caps the issuance-volume channel and holds the term premium flat at 0.95% rather than widening it to 1.15-1.30; -15bp from his bust-mixture correction, resized from his 0.70 to 0.45 because AI-Q4 resolution is not the same event as a macro bust inside the 2032-36 window; -10bp from the wedge, raised from Wave-1's -0.25/-0.30 to -0.35 on the unannounced-repression and issuance-mix channels plus the US 1942-1951 precedent. The r* leg moved only -5bp (1.00 -> 0.90) on the precautionary-saving point, which I accepted in direction and cut in size. Runner-up: CQ5 from the Wave-1 modal 30 to 19 (-11pp), almost entirely from replacing the 2022 drawdown template with the investment-bubble template on conjunct B's second sub-condition (0.42-0.45 -> 0.34) plus the Scout's 2026 MOVE prints on conjunct A.

efforts.effort_name: Real GDP Growth, Macro/Market Volatility & Asset-Class Returns

wave1.lens_self_description: I answered purely as an outside-view reference-class historian: every number is a historical frequency or a decade-distribution anchor, adjusted only for the arithmetic content of the locked 2A/2B priors — which forbade me from using any reasoning about AI capability trajectories, model scaling, agent diffusion rates, or any mechanism specific to this episode, and forbade me from running the project's simulation.
wave1.cq1_reasoning: CONJUNCT 1 (OECD-38 harmonised unemployment 5-yr average <= 5.5%, 2032-2036). Reference class: the OECD harmonised series itself, which per the OECD's own releases "started in 2001" — so all "record low" claims are measured only from 2001 (OECD Labour Statistics releases, Feb 2024 / Feb 2025, confirmed by search). Annual path (recalled, OECD/ILO): ~6.5% 2001-2007, ~8.0-8.3% 2009-2013, ~6.3% 2015, 5.3% 2019, 7.2% 2020, 6.2% 2021, 4.9% 2022, 4.8% 2023, 4.9% 2024 (OECD Feb 2025: "annual unemployment rate was broadly stable in the OECD in 2024, at 4.9%"), ~5.0% 2025. Of ~21 rolling 5-yr windows 2001-2025, exactly ONE (2021-2025, avg ~5.2%) averages <= 5.5%. Unconditional base rate ~5%. Mechanical adjustments from 2A: (i) a shrinking 20-64 denominator lowers the measured rate for any given labour demand — Japan's post-1995 template took unemployment to ~2.5% through contraction; worth roughly -0.3 to -0.5pp over a decade; (ii) the OECD-38 aggregate is dragged by structurally high members (Spain ~10.5%, Turkey ~8.5%, Colombia, Greece), so the floor is ~4.6-4.8%, not 3%; (iii) the binding risk is cyclical: base rate of at least one OECD-wide recession in a 5-yr window is ~70-75% (NBER/OECD cycle dating since 1960), and a typical OECD recession adds +1.5 to +3.0pp to the level, i.e. +0.6 to +0.9pp to a 5-yr average. From a 4.9% start you can absorb only +0.6pp of average slack. Conditional marginal: 40%. CONJUNCT 2 (F+Q real median hourly wage growth exceeds J+K+M by >= +10.0pp cumulative, 2025-2036). Reference class: sustained >= 10pp divergences between two broad sector groups over 11 years. In EITHER direction this is common — roughly 40-50% of 11-year windows in US/EU sectoral series (BLS CES/OES real wages, Eurostat SES) clear 10pp. In THIS direction (physical/care beating cognitive/information) the post-1980 record is near-empty: 1990-2001 and 2010-2021 both ran 15-20pp the OTHER way (tech/finance premium). The one clean precedent is the 1970s Great Compression reversal: 1973-1984 saw the US college wage premium fall sharply and real cognitive wages erode under inflation (Goldin-Katz; Katz-Murphy). So direction-conditional base rate ~15-20%. Mechanical brake from 2A that most panels miss: Q (health/social care) wages are administratively set and majority publicly financed, and 2A puts pension/health budgets under explicit stress (China 2.9T RMB subsidies; OECD net interest 2%->3% of GDP) — fiscally squeezed payers do not deliver 11-year real wage surges to their own cost base. F (construction) is the most cyclical sector in the taxonomy, so it is also the one most damaged by the recession that breaks conjunct 1. Marginal: 25%. CORRELATION: positive and material (ρ ≈ +0.35). Tight labour markets are exactly the state in which manual/care wages reprice, and the recession that breaks conjunct 1 is the event that breaks conjunct 2. So P(2|1) ≈ 0.32 rather than 0.25. JOINT: 0.40 × 0.32 = 0.128 -> 13.
wave1.cq2_reasoning: CONJUNCT A (OECD-38 GDP-weighted core >= 2.50%/yr average, 2027-2036). Reference class: 10-year windows of OECD-wide inflation, 1971-2025 (OECD CPI aggregate). Nearly every window clears 2.5% except those centred on 2010-2019. Critically, this is an OECD-38 GDP-weighted aggregate, not a G7 one: Turkey, Mexico, Colombia, Chile, Costa Rica are members, and the OECD-wide aggregate has historically run 0.5-2.0pp ABOVE the euro-area/US core for exactly this reason (OECD aggregate CPI ~1.8-2.2% in 2015-2019 while euro-area core was ~1.0%; OECD-wide headline peaked near 9.5-10.7% in 2022). Arithmetic: Turkey alone at ~2-3% of OECD GDP running 10-20% core contributes +0.3 to +0.5pp to the aggregate; add Mexico/Colombia/Chile and the aggregate clears 2.5% even with the G7 at target. Base rate adjusted for a ~2.6-2.8% starting core and for the inflation-targeting era's good-but-slower-since-2021 reversion record: 70%. CONJUNCT B (China headline CPI < 1.50%/yr average, 2027-2036). Observed: China CPI averaged ~1.8-1.9% 2012-2019, ~0.6% 2020-2025, with 2023 ~0.2%, 2024 ~0.2%, 2025 ~0.0%. Reference class: post-property-bust economies with a contracting population — Japan 1995-2015 averaged ~0.1% CPI over twenty years; Hong Kong 1998-2004 negative. Conditional on starting at ~0%, a property deleveraging, a -60M population path over 2026-2035, and a worker-to-retiree ratio going 4.4 -> 2.8 (all locked in 2A), the base rate for a sub-1.5% decade average is high. Counterweights with real historical precedent: large fiscal reflation, currency depreciation, and food/energy shocks (China 2007-08 and 2019-20 pork cycles each pushed CPI above 4%) — but a 10-year AVERAGE absorbs those. Marginal: 65%. CORRELATION: mildly NEGATIVE (ρ ≈ -0.10). Chinese deflation is exported disinflation into OECD tradables (the 1998-2004 and 2014-2016 episodes), so the two conjuncts partially work against each other; against that, a shared global energy/commodity shock would lift both. Net P(B|A) ≈ 0.60. JOINT: 0.70 × 0.60 = 0.42 -> 41 (rounded down a point for the conjunction penalty I apply as a matter of lens discipline, since this is a literal "great divergence" state and conjunctions are systematically over-rated).
wave1.cq3_reasoning: PPP WEIGHTS FIRST (the arithmetic the lens brief demands). World GDP PPP ~ $190-200T (2025). China ~19% -> ~$36-38T. OECD-38 ~43-44% of world (US ~15%, OECD-EU ~13%, Japan 3.4%, UK 2.2%, Turkey 1.9%, Mexico 1.8%, Korea 1.7%, Canada 1.4%, Australia 1.0%, rest ~2%) -> ~$83T. Combined ~$120T; China weight ~30%, OECD-38 ~70% at the 2026 start, drifting to roughly China 33% / OECD 67% by the 2034 midpoint if China grows faster. REFERENCE CLASS 1 — historical 5-year windows of OECD+China PPP real growth since 1960 (IMF WEO / Maddison / World Bank, recalled): 1960s ~5%+, 1970s ~4%, 1980s ~3.5%, 1990s ~3.0%, 2000s ~3.3%, 2010-2019 ~3.0%, 2015-2019 ~2.9%, 2020-2024 ~2.3%. The unconditional mean of 5-yr windows since 1960 is ~3.4%, but the series is MONOTONICALLY TRENDING DOWN and the trend is driven by the two mechanical forces named in 2A (OECD productivity/demographic slowdown and Chinese convergence), so a naive unconditional draw is the wrong anchor and I use its DISPERSION rather than its level. Cross-window standard deviation for an aggregate this large: ~0.8-1.0pp. REFERENCE CLASS 2 — Pritchett-Summers regression-to-the-mean in growth: fast-growing middle-income economies revert hard; the post-demographic-peak comparators are Japan 1992-1997 (~1.4%), Korea 2015-2024 (~2.4%), Taiwan 2000s. MECHANICAL BUILD-UP FROM 2A: OECD per-capita 1.0% -> 0.6% plus population growth ~0.3-0.4%/yr gives OECD headline ~1.0-1.1% absent offsets; allowing a modest, historically-ordinary productivity offset puts OECD 2032-36 at ~1.2-1.4%. China: 2A's -2.7pp/yr aging drag against a ~4.5-5% 2025 base, plus population decline and the Japan/Korea reversion class, puts China 2032-36 at ~2.5-3.2%, median ~3.0%. Coupled: 0.67 × 1.3 + 0.33 × 3.0 = 0.87 + 0.99 = 1.86%. RECESSION ADJUSTMENT: a 5-year window carries ~70-75% probability of containing at least one global/OECD contraction; forecasters systematically omit this. The drag is already in my P50 via the 1.3% OECD figure and is the main content of the left tail. DISTRIBUTION: P50 1.9; P10 0.8 (recession plus a Chinese sub-2% outcome — the Japan-1992-97 analogue applied to China's 33% weight alone subtracts ~0.4pp); P90 2.9 (China holds 4%+ and OECD gets a genuine 1990s-US-style productivity window; note that even the historically generous combination struggles past 3.0% given the weights). Right tail deliberately not extended to the historical unconditional mean of 3.4%: that level required a China growing at 8-10% with a rising working-age population, which 2A arithmetically forecloses.
wave1.cq4_reasoning: STARTING LEVEL, built from the locked prior. 2A gives US 10y TIPS ~2.60% (FRED DFII10, 30 Oct 2026). G7 GDP weights (market GDP): US ~50%, Germany ~10%, Japan ~9%, UK ~7%, France ~7%, Italy ~5%, Canada ~5%. Recalled/implied real yields elsewhere: Japan ~0.3%, Germany ~0.7%, UK ~1.3%, France ~1.3%, Italy ~1.6%, Canada ~1.8%. GDP-weighted start ≈ 1.30 + 0.07 + 0.03 + 0.09 + 0.09 + 0.08 + 0.09 ≈ 1.75%. Note the US dominates the weight, so this question is ~half a US TIPS question. REFERENCE CLASS 1 — G7 10y real yields by decade (recalled from Homer-Sylla, BIS long series, DMS Yearbook): 1970s roughly -1% to 0% (an inflation-surprise decade in which realized real yields were negative); 1980s +4% to +5%; 1990s ~+4%; 2000s ~+2.3%; 2010s ~+0.5%; 2020-2025 ~-0.3% rising to ~+1.75% now. Unconditional mean over 1960-2025 ≈ +1.8-2.0% — which is, coincidentally, essentially the current level. That coincidence is the single strongest justification for anchoring P50 at the start. REFERENCE CLASS 2 — base rate that a decade-average real yield stays near its starting level: LOW. Decade-to-decade shifts of 100-300bp are the norm (1970s->1980s ~+500bp; 1990s->2010s ~-350bp). I read the base rate of a within-±50bp outcome as roughly 25-30%, which is why my P10-P90 band is 270bp wide rather than tight. REFERENCE CLASS 3 — Reinhart-Rogoff / Reinhart-Sbrancia on how >100%-of-GDP public debt episodes historically resolve: the modal resolution is financial repression with LOW or NEGATIVE real rates, not a sustained real-yield spike. That is the engine of my left tail, reinforced by the standalone 66% prior on AI capex impairment (a capex bust is cyclically a real-yield-DOWN event) and by the aging/dissaving-versus-savings-glut ambiguity that 2A itself flags ("even where a frictionless r* eases"). RIGHT TAIL: 2A's observations — gross public debt >100% of GDP by 2029, net interest 2% -> 3% of GDP, 3-yr P95 Debt-at-Risk ~117% (+2.4pp under a 20% AI-led equity shock), eroding sovereign convenience yields, levered basis-trade absorption, and (r-g) worsening by ~+1.0pp — all point up, and the 1980s show the precedent for a 400bp+ decade shift. DISTRIBUTION: P10 0.40 (repression / bust path, the Reinhart-Sbrancia modal resolution), P50 1.75 (starting level = long-run unconditional mean), P90 3.10 (term-premium repricing of the 1980s type, scaled down because the 1980s started from a much higher inflation base). Asymmetry is mildly upward relative to P50, consistent with 2A's (r-g) prior.
wave1.cq5_reasoning: CONJUNCT A (MOVE 10-yr average >= 105, 2027-2036). Reference class: MOVE history since 1988. Secondary analyst sources put the long-run average at "roughly 85 to 100" and treat 85 as the above/below-average threshold; I preserve the caveat that these come from informal analyst sources, not from ICE, and that I found no official ICE per-decade table (search, Nov 2026). Recalled/searched levels: record high 264.6 (10 Oct 2008), record low 36.6 (29 Sep 2020), post-QE pre-2022 "routinely 50 to 70", 198.71 close on 13 Mar 2023 (highest since 2008), ~140 reached in 2025. Decade averages therefore: 1988-1997 ~105-110, 1998-2007 ~90-100, 2008-2017 ~90, 2013-2022 ~75-85, 2016-2025 ~90-95. Fraction of 10-year windows averaging >= 105: roughly 5-8 of ~28, i.e. a base rate of 20-30%. Note >= 105 is ABOVE the long-run average, so this conjunct is asking for an above-median-volatility decade. Adjusting for the mechanical content of 2A (duration supply at >100% debt/GDP, net interest 2%->3%, basis-trade absorption, the 2022-2023 regime already demonstrating 130-198 prints): 40%. CONJUNCT B — two nested parts. B1: MSCI World peak-to-trough >= 25% at some point in a 10-year window. Episodes since 1970: 1973-74, 1980-82, 1987, 1990, 2000-02, 2007-09, 2020, 2022 (MSCI World ~-26%) — ~8 in 55 years, hazard ~0.14/yr, so P(>=1 in 10 years) ≈ 78-80%. Base rate: 80%. B2: conditional on such a drawdown, the frequency that G7 10y nominal yields FAILED to rally >= 50bp (or rose >= 25bp) during the window. Correlated regime: 1973-74 (yields rose), 1980-82 (yields rose), 2022 (yields rose sharply) — 3 episodes. Flight-to-quality regime: 1987 (sharp rally), 1990 (modest rally), 2000-02 (large rally), 2008-09 (large rally), 2020 (large rally) — 5 episodes. Conditional base rate ≈ 3/8 = 37.5%. The historical determinant of which regime obtains is whether the shock originates in inflation/policy (correlated) or in credit/demand (flight to quality); 2A's set-up has both an inflation-fiscal leg and an AI-credit leg, so I do not adjust the 37.5% away from base. Joint B = 0.80 × 0.375 = 0.30. CORRELATION between A and B: strongly POSITIVE (ρ ≈ +0.45) — the correlated-selloff episodes ARE the high-MOVE episodes (2022 is the type specimen: MOVE ~120-130 average and a failed bond rally in the same year). So P(A|B) ≈ 0.63 against 0.40 unconditional. JOINT: 0.30 × 0.63 = 0.189 -> 19.
wave1.cq6_reasoning: HISTORICAL BAND FREQUENCIES FIRST (the brief's mandatory reference class). Taking 5-year windows of OECD+China PPP real growth since 1960 and sorting by the CQ3 growth measure alone: pre-1990 windows land almost entirely in the >= 2.6% band (A's growth gate) — roughly 70-75% of 1960-1989 windows; 1990-2010 windows ~60% in the >=2.6% band; 2011-2025 windows ~55% at or above 2.6% (dropping below only in 2019-2023 and 2020-2024). So the UNCONDITIONAL band frequency would put most mass on A. I reject that as the answer and keep A at 17% because the decline is mechanical, not stochastic: the locked 2A arithmetic (OECD per-capita 1.0->0.6, China -2.7pp, China's weight ~33%) removes the growth that put history in that band. This is exactly the "technology will offset demography" error the lens is built to resist, so I note the tension rather than inherit the frequency. CONSISTENCY CHECK AGAINST MY OWN CQ3. My CQ3 is P10 0.8 / P50 1.9 / P90 2.9, implying σ ≈ 0.82. Under the lexical lock: (1) A = P(growth >= 2.6%) = P(z >= 0.85) ≈ 0.20; I shade to 0.17 for the downward trend and for the right-tail thinness the PPP weights impose. (2) P(growth < 2.0%) = P(z < 0.12) ≈ 0.55. (3) P(growth < 1.7%) = P(z < -0.24) ≈ 0.40. CONSISTENCY CHECK AGAINST MY OWN CQ2. My CQ2 conjunct A put P(OECD-38 GDP-weighted core >= 2.50% over 2027-2036) = 70%, driven largely by the mechanical EM-member uplift in the OECD-38 GDP-weighted aggregate (Turkey/Mexico/Colombia/Chile). For the tighter 2032-2036-only window at the higher >= 2.70% gate, mean reversion pulls down but fiscal dominance pushes up: P ≈ 0.45. Symmetrically, P(core < 2.00% over 2032-2036) ≈ 0.20 — LOW, and this is the single most under-appreciated arithmetic fact in the CQ6 lock, because it structurally starves regime D. C = P(core >= 2.7%) × P(growth < 2.0% | high core) = 0.45 × 0.55 × 1.15 (mild positive stagflationary dependence, the 1970s bottleneck template) ≈ 0.285 -> 27. D = P(growth < 1.7%) × P(core < 2.0% | growth < 1.7%) = 0.40 × 0.28 ≈ 0.11 -> 11 (the conditional is lifted above the 0.20 unconditional because a demand shortfall is itself disinflationary — the Japan 1998-2012 template — but capped by the OECD-38 composition effect). B = residual = 100 - 17 - 27 - 11 = 45. INTERNAL AUDIT: B must contain (i) the 1.7-2.5% growth band and (ii) the low-growth/moderate-inflation leftover cell. My implied leftover = P(growth<2.0%) - C - D = 0.55 - 0.27 - 0.11 = 0.17, which sits inside B; the remaining 0.28 of B is the 2.0-2.5% growth band. Both are internally consistent with CQ3's σ and with CQ2's inflation marginals. I do not put most mass on A despite my CQ3 P50 of 1.9%, as the lock requires.

hypothesis_critique.a: The failure word is SMOOTHLY. The reference class is cross-occupational reallocation after a labour-demand shock, and its historical record is uniformly rough: US manufacturing 1999-2011 (Autor-Dorn-Hanson: displaced workers exited to non-employment and disability, not to adjacent service sectors), UK coalfields 1984-2000 (regional non-employment persisted 20+ years), US/EU retail 2010s. Displaced cognitive workers and care-labour demand differ in geography, licensure, median wage level, gender composition and physical requirement; the historical transition rate from a displaced white-collar occupation into direct care within five years is low single digits. Separately, the FISCAL leg is decisive and historically ignored: care demand is majority publicly financed and 2A puts those budgets under explicit strain (China 2.9T RMB subsidies, OECD net interest 2%->3% of GDP), so the care sector cannot bid for labour even if labour were available. The plank would also require the ~5% of 11-year windows in which such reallocation was smooth. 5.
hypothesis_critique.b: Two failure words. BLOCKS is false on mechanism-scope: the plank conflates the two channels the scope lock deliberately separates. Physical labour migration into aging OECD/Gulf economies is DEMAND-pulled by exactly the 2A demography (worker-to-retiree 4.4->2.8, old-age ratio 31%->39-41%), and no software substitutes for a bedside aide or a crew on a transformer install; that channel is strengthened, not blocked. SEVERELY is false on magnitude: India's IT-BPO is ~7-8% of GDP and ~1.5% of employment, and the historical base rate for a cost-arbitrage services export niche being eliminated by an automation wave within a decade is essentially zero — Indian BPO grew through the 2001 dot-com bust, the 2008-09 crisis, the IVR wave and the 2016-2020 RPA wave, each of which was forecast to end it. Philippine BPO plus remittances is more exposed in share terms (~8% and ~9% of GDP) but remittances are migration-driven and therefore pro-cyclical with OECD aging. A revenue-growth deceleration is far more likely than national-scale distress. 12.
hypothesis_critique.c: The failure phrase is THEN FALLS — the clean two-phase hump. The first clause is nearly free (it is close to already-observed) and the plank's whole content is the reversion. Reference class: inflation-overshoot episodes and their 3-5 year reversion. The 1990-2020 inflation-targeting record is good (most overshoots reverted within three years); the 1965-1985 record is bad (three successive failed reversions in the US and UK). The measurement basis matters arithmetically and is usually missed: on the OECD-38 GDP-WEIGHTED basis the EM members mechanically hold the aggregate 0.5-2.0pp above the euro-area/US core, so 'falls in the 2030s' to a target-like number is harder than it sounds on the aggregate this question is scored on. My own CQ6 assigns 27% to core >= 2.7% persisting through 2032-2036, which directly contradicts the plank in just over a quarter of the space; the rest of the space is mostly consistent with it. Also it is near-unfalsifiable on 'hot for the next few years'. 33.
hypothesis_critique.d: Two failure words. EVENTUALLY makes the claim unfalsifiable inside the Dec 2036 horizon — a plank that can always be deferred is not a scorable forecast, and I score only the resolvable reading. WINS is false under the reference class: the base rate of 'technology will offset demography' claims resolving true is close to zero in the only places it has been tested. Japan led the world in industrial robot density from 1980 onward and its growth never recovered after 1991; Germany, Korea, Italy and Taiwan all automated into slower, not faster, headline growth. The arithmetic also runs against the plank: EXPONENTIAL is the wrong functional form for a factor entering an aggregate production function through a Baumol/Hulten weakest-link structure, where automating a subset of complementary tasks raises the non-automated tasks' shadow prices and caps the aggregate — the growth effect is bounded by the unautomated residual, not by the automated frontier. My CQ3 P90 of 2.9% is below the historical unconditional 5-year mean of ~3.4%, which is the quantitative statement that demography wins in my distribution's right tail too. 14.

key_drivers: PPP-WEIGHT ARITHMETIC: China is ~30-33% of the OECD-38+China PPP aggregate, so 2A's -2.7pp/yr Chinese aging drag times that weight removes roughly -0.9pp from coupled growth on its own; this single multiplication does more work in my CQ3 than any judgment about AI.

MONOTONIC HISTORICAL TREND IN 5-YEAR GROWTH WINDOWS: OECD+China PPP growth has fallen in every decade since the 1960s (~5% -> ~2.3%), and the decline is mechanically demographic and convergence-driven, so the unconditional 3.4% mean of historical windows is the wrong level anchor even though its ~0.8-1.0pp dispersion is the right spread anchor.

COMPOSITION OF THE OECD-38 GDP-WEIGHTED INFLATION AGGREGATE: Turkey, Mexico, Colombia, Chile and Costa Rica hold the measure 0.5-2.0pp above the G7 core, which makes CQ2's >=2.50% gate and CQ6-C's >=2.70% gate far easier to clear and starves CQ6-D of the <2.00% condition it needs.

REINHART-SBRANCIA RESOLUTION BASE RATE vs 2A's (r-g) PRIOR: the modal historical resolution of >100%-of-GDP public debt is financial repression at low or negative real rates, which fights 2A's upward (r-g) arithmetic and is why my CQ4 band is wide (0.4-3.1%) around a P50 that just equals the starting level and the 1960-2025 unconditional mean.

CONJUNCTION DISCIPLINE: CQ1, CQ2 and CQ5 are each two-part, and the historical record is that forecasters over-rate conjunctions; two of the four conjuncts I price (direction-specific sector wage divergence 25%, failed bond rally conditional on a 25% equity drawdown 37.5%) are themselves rare-in-direction, which is where most of my downward pressure on CQ1 and CQ5 comes from.

RECESSION OMISSION: a 5-year window carries a ~70-75% chance of containing an OECD-wide contraction and a 10-year window a ~78-80% chance of a >=25% MSCI World drawdown; embedding those hazards rather than forecasting a smooth path is what separates my CQ1 (13) and CQ3 left tail from a trend-extrapolated view.

wave1.coupling_tension: The sharpest tension is with AI-Q3 (2036 OECD-38+China operational data-centre electricity, ensemble P50 998 TWh against ~365 TWh in 2024). That P50 is a 2.74x increase over twelve years, i.e. ~8.7%/yr compound, sustained OECD-wide. The outside-view reference class for sustained electricity-demand growth of that rate in mature OECD grids is the 1950s-1960s build-out, and nothing since: OECD electricity demand grew ~1%/yr 1990-2019 and was roughly flat 2010-2023. More to the point, once demographics are endogenous the build is rate-limited by exactly the inputs 2A makes scarce — electricians, linesmen, substation and transformer crews, interconnect queues, turbine and switchgear fabrication labour — and my own CQ1 conjunct-2 reasoning is that a physical-trades wage premium is the live possibility precisely because that labour is short. AI-Q3's P50 and a +10pp physical-trades real wage divergence cannot both sit comfortably: either the build happens and trades wages explode (which then feeds CQ6-C's cost-push), or trades scarcity caps the build. Direction: coupling implies AI-Q3's P50 should be marked DOWN roughly 10-15% (toward ~860-900 TWh) with a fatter left tail, since the labour and equipment constraint binds before the capital constraint does. Two further directional implications, both of which the standalone exogenous-demographics framing gets wrong in opposite directions. AI-Q1 (TFP lift >= +0.50pp, 23.0%) and AI-Q2 (firm adoption >= 50%, 21.3%) are each biased LOW once aging is endogenous: labour scarcity and a rising wage signal are a demand pull for automation, and the historical base rate is that labour-scarce economies adopt labour-saving capital faster (postwar Japan, 1920s US after immigration restriction). I would nudge both up ~3-5pp — though not far, because a Baumol weakest-link structure caps the TFP translation even when adoption is high, which is the standard reason adoption and measured TFP decouple. Conversely AI-Q5 (cognitive labour compensation share of J+K+M GVA falls >= 3.5pp, 38.2%) is biased HIGH: the share is a ratio, and aging shrinks the cognitive labour SUPPLY denominator at the same time, so retirements of high-earning incumbents and a thinner entry cohort hold compensation per head up and partially offset the displacement effect on the share. I would mark AI-Q5 down ~5pp. Finally, 2A's own internal arithmetic is in tension: the IMF WEO healthy-aging offset (+0.4pp/yr to global growth) and the -1.1pp/yr aging drag are quoted over 2025-2050 while 2A's OECD per-capita figure (1.0% -> 0.6%, a -40% cut) is a 2036 figure, so the two cannot be added; I used the per-capita figure for the OECD leg and the -2.7pp figure for the China leg and did not double-count the healthy-aging offset, which is part of why my CQ3 P50 sits at 1.9% rather than above 2.1%.

wave1.lens_self_description: Fermi Structural Decomposer: I built every answer as explicit arithmetic — growth-accounting sums with published PPP weights, conjunct-by-conjunct multiplication with a stated conditional, and an r* + term-premium − repression-wedge ladder for yields — and I was forbidden from appealing to base rates or historical frequencies as evidence (where I needed an event frequency, e.g. CQ5's drawdown leg, I rebuilt it from the locked $1.4T/$300B/$650B capital structure and the AI complex's index weight instead of from the 54-year drawdown record).
wave1.cq1_reasoning:
DECOMPOSITION. Conjunct C1 (OECD-38 harmonized unemployment averages <=5.5% over 2032-36). Arithmetic: structural rate today ~4.9-5.0%; the locked 2A labour-force contraction is Okun-favourable (with 20-64 headcount falling ~-0.3%/yr, even 1.1%/yr GDP absorbs the entrants), which I score as -0.2pp on the structural rate; against that, AI-Q5's cognitive displacement and AI-Q4's 66% capex digestion add a mismatch/slack term. A 5-year average has little room: 5.0 baseline + ~0.4pp of averaged cyclical slack = 5.4, inside the threshold but with <0.2pp of headroom. Marginal C1 = 0.55.
Conjunct C2 ((F+Q) minus (J+K+M) cumulative real MEDIAN hourly wage growth >= +10.0pp over 11 years) = a sustained +0.87pp/yr differential, against a 2010-2024 differential of the OPPOSITE sign. Three arithmetic objections. (i) Q is fiscally administered: care-worker median pay is a budget line in exactly the budgets 2A says are squeezed (net interest 2%->3% of GDP, China-style pension subsidy arithmetic in OECD form). Scarcity therefore clears by RATIONING — vacancies, waiting lists, unfilled rosters — not by the median wage. Q is ~55-60% of F+Q hours, so even F at +1.8%/yr real and Q at -0.1%/yr gives F+Q ~ +0.7%/yr, and you still must subtract J+K+M. (ii) Composition: if AI displaces the LOWER tail of J/K/M employment, the surviving MEDIAN in those sectors mechanically RISES, moving the differential the wrong way — the test is on medians, not on wage bills, and this is the single most under-priced term. (iii) To clear +10.0pp you need J+K+M real median growth at or below ~-0.1%/yr for 11 straight years, i.e. an 11-year real wage decline in the OECD's highest-paid sectors. Marginal C2 = 0.14.
CORRELATION: positive. The world that moves physical medians by 10pp is a tight-labour, physical-scarcity world, which also holds unemployment down. I set P(C1|C2) = 0.78 vs 0.55 unconditional.
MULTIPLICATION: 0.14 x 0.78 = 0.109 -> 11.
SIM REFUSAL: the adapter self-reports CQ1 as "not representable - no unemployment, no ISIC sectors, no sectoral median wage." No number here is model-derived.
wave1.cq2_reasoning:

JONES/BAUMOL WEAKEST LINK, quantified. CES across automatable (share 0.8) and non-automatable (0.2) task bundles, sigma=0.5 (rho=-1): Y = 1/(0.8/A + 0.2/N). hypothesis_critique.a: The failing word is "smoothly", with "supply" close behind. The plank asserts a transfer function between two labour pools that share almost no attribute. Arithmetic of the mismatch: displaced J/K/M workers are median-age ~42-48, metro-located, with a reservation wage 1.8-2.6x the F+Q care median; care work requires 6-24 months of licensure, is physically demanding, and its demand is located where retirees are, not where cognitive jobs were. Timing is also mismatched: displacement is cyclical and lumpy (clustered in an AI-Q4 digestion phase), care demand is a smooth secular ramp. Even granting full substitutability of PERSONS, the wage cannot clear, because Q's price is administered by the same budgets 2A says are being squeezed - so the market that would do the "supplying" is not a market. And the premise is itself only 38.2% likely (AI-Q5). Replace "smoothly" with "after a decade of licensure reform, wage subsidy and large unfilled-vacancy stocks" and it becomes defensible; as stated it is near-false.
hypothesis_critique.b: Two failing words, "blocks" and "severely", plus a conflation the brief's own scope lock separates. AI attacks the VIRTUAL channel - seat-priced IT services, voice BPO, back office - where the Philippines' ~1.7M BPO seats and India's services exports are genuinely exposed, and that part is right. But AI does not touch PHYSICAL labour migration, and the 2A demographics make it MORE valuable: an OECD-38 with an old-age ratio at 39-41% and a care-hours weakest link is a rising bid for migrant care and construction labour, in Gulf and OECD destinations alike. For the Philippines, remittances from physical migration exceed virtual-services value added, so the net demographic coupling is plausibly POSITIVE. "Blocks" is wrong even on the virtual channel: AI-Q2's 21.3% says most OECD firms will not be using AI in production by 2036, and the integration labour that closes that gap is exactly what Indian services firms sell - partial substitution with a simultaneous complementary demand pull, not a block. India additionally has a large domestic absorber. "Severely" is wrong at the national level and right at the segment level (Philippine voice BPO).
hypothesis_critique.c: The failing word is "then" - the implied sequencing. The plank imports a cyclical shape (overshoot, then mean-reversion) into a structurally worsening problem. Every upward inflation driver in 2A INTENSIFIES into the 2030s rather than fading: net interest climbing 2% -> 3% of GDP, debt past 100% by 2029, the old-age ratio reaching 39-41% with its labour-scarcity wage signal, Baumol care and construction prices, and the datacenter electricity bid. The disinflationary forces, by contrast, are front-loaded: the capex boom's supply, the AI-Q4 digestion, and imported Chinese deflation. So the plank has the time derivative backwards. It gets partial credit because one live branch does deliver its shape - a 2027-32 capex bust producing a disinflationary 2030s is my regime D at 15% - and because my own CQ2 arithmetic (central case 2.39%) says inflation does not in fact "run hot" in the first leg either, so the plank is wrong at both ends but for opposite reasons.
hypothesis_critique.d: Two failing words: "eventually" and "wins". "Eventually" is unfalsifiable and specifically evades the Dec 31 2036 horizon - a plank that resolves at an unstated date is not a forecast. "Wins" smuggles an aggregate-level claim into what the question's own CQ6 bands measure as a growth RATE against a threshold, with no stated counterfactual: outrunning population decline in LEVELS (output rises) is compatible with losing badly in RATES (growth below 2.6%, which is my 87% case). "Exponential" is the third error: under Jones/Baumol task complementarity, exponentiating one subset of tasks produces a BOUNDED aggregate, not an exponential one - my own CES arithmetic (sigma=0.5, automatable share 0.8) gives an asymptotic level cap of 5x and a marginal growth rate that decays toward the non-automated tasks' rate. The plank is directionally right about the sign of AI's contribution (+0.31pp probability-weighted) and wrong about its functional form and its arrival time.

key_drivers: China's PPP weight times its aging drag: 0.38 x (-2.7 pp/yr) = -1.03 pp of coupled growth from Chinese demographics alone, plus 0.62 x (-0.4) = -0.25 pp from OECD, for -1.28 pp total. This single product is the largest term in CQ3 and the main reason my answer sits ~1.1 pp below the simulation's.

The locked OECD potential anchor (0.6%/yr per capita + ~0.2%/yr population = ~0.80 pp aggregate) set against a probability-weighted AI TFP lift of only +0.31 pp computed off AI-Q6's own regime means (0.162x0.75 + 0.472x0.35 + 0.365x0.07). The offset is a third of the drag, not a multiple of it.

The 2036 weakest link is HV interconnection / transformer / switchgear capacity and licensed care hours - NOT compute and NOT energy - and both clear by RATIONING (multi-year queues, unfilled vacancies, waiting lists) rather than by price, because care prices are fiscally administered and interconnection is queue-allocated. This is why real scarcity coexists with CQ1 failing.

Diffusion, not substitution elasticity, is what caps 2036. My CES arithmetic (sigma=0.5) shows the Baumol level cap is hard (5x) but binds in the 2040s-50s, costing only ~0.15-0.30 pp/yr by 2036; AI-Q2's 21.3% adoption marginal does the real capping.

AI-Q4 at 66%: a capex digestion/impairment phase landing inside the 2032-36 window withdraws BOTH the capital-deepening growth contribution (halving my +0.14 pp gross to +0.07 pp) and the r* support (reducing the AI/grid capital-demand term in CQ4 to +0.15 pp), which is why CQ4 turns out to be a term-premium story with a net-zero r*.

Whether the flight-to-quality bid survives: this single switch drives CQ5's second conjunct, CQ4's P90, and the entire C-versus-D split in the asset matrix. Levered basis-trade absorption and eroding convenience yields raise P(failure | drawdown) above its structural prior, but the most likely drawdown cause in my own distribution (an AI capex bust = a growth/deflation shock) is the cause least likely to break the bid - a tension I resolved at 0.38 rather than 0.50.

wave1.coupling_tension: The sharpest tension is between AI-Q2 (21.3%) and AI-Q3 (P50 998 TWh), and it propagates into AI-Q4. Direction of the inconsistency: AI-Q2's firm-adoption marginal is too LOW once demographics are endogenous, by roughly 10 points. A shrinking 20-64 cohort is the best-documented driver of firm-level automation adoption (the labour-scarcity wage signal), so holding demographics exogenous strips out the main adoption forcing variable; endogenous, AI-Q2 should sit near 32%, not 21.3%. But the joint distribution is where the real problem is: a 2.7x rise in OECD-38+China datacenter electricity (365 -> 998 TWh) alongside fewer than half of firms using AI in production forces nearly all of that load into a narrow frontier-lab and hyperscaler slice - which is internally coherent only in AI-Q6-B's "rent concentration" branch, and which mechanically implies that net external AI revenue CANNOT cover compute D&A, because the paying customer base is too narrow. That is AI-Q4's second resolution criterion. So the three locked marginals are jointly coherent only at AI-Q4 near 0.75, above the locked 0.66 - the locked AI-Q4 is, if anything, too low, in the direction of more impairment rather than less. A second, opposite-signed tension: AI-Q5 (38.2%) is too HIGH once demographics are endogenous. Aging raises the relative price of ALL labour including cognitive labour, because the scarcity is in bodies as much as in skills, so the J/K/M compensation share falls by less than an exogenous-demographics model implies; coupled, AI-Q5 belongs near 30%. These two corrections push CQ6 mass in the same direction (out of A and into B and D) even though they move the underlying marginals oppositely, which is why my CQ6-B sits at 54.
