wave1.lens_self_description: Inside-View Empirical Signal Scout: I built every number from the freshest observable indicator levels I could verify (OECD unemployment release Oct-2026, NBS China CPI Oct-14-2026, Atlanta Fed industry wage trackers, Census BTOS AI-use series, Fitch/SOLVE private-credit stress, LME copper, PJM power prices, transformer/turbine lead times, Q3-2026 hyperscaler capex calls), carried their caveats and sample limits intact, and refused to use outside-view narrative, model output, or any theory-driven long-run equilibrium not anchored to a dated print — which forbade me from leaning on structural-growth models, DSGE-style r* estimates, or any simulation of the target system.
wave1.cq1_reasoning:
CONJUNCT 1 (OECD-38 harmonized U <= 5.5% avg 2032-36), marginal 62%. OBSERVED: OECD unemployment rate "broadly stable in August 2026, at 5.0%, just 0.2 p.p. above its record low from June 2023" (OECD statistical release, Oct 2026; next update Jan 2027). More timely Sep-2026 country estimates: US 4.2%, Canada 6.5%. Note the OECD's own two releases are mutually inconsistent for July (4.9% in the Sep release vs the later 5.0% Aug figure) — hard administrative data, but revision-noisy. EXTRAPOLATED: shrinking OECD labour supply (old-age ratio 31%->39-41% by 2036, locked 2A) mechanically lowers the U rate (-0.2pp drift); one recession inside a 5-yr window adds ~+0.5-0.8pp to the average. 5.0 - 0.2 + 0.6 = ~5.4%, i.e. just inside the threshold. 62%.

CONJUNCT 2 (F+Q real median hourly wage growth beats J+K+M by >=10.0pp cumulative 2025-2036 = ~0.87pp/yr sustained 11 years), marginal 16%. The decisive OBSERVATION is that the divergence is not currently happening. Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker (hard microdata, CPS-matched, but 12-month moving averages and unweighted medians by broad industry group, NOT ISIC F/Q/J/K/M): Education and Health 4.2 (Sep 2025); Finance and Business Services 4.2 (Feb 2026); Public Administration 4.8 (Mar 2026); overall weighted 3.80% vs 3.60% prior month and 4.50% a year earlier. Construction and Mining: I located the series name but found no recent value — unverified at my horizon. So the best current read is a DEAD HEAT (4.2 vs 4.2) between the care side and the cognitive side, not a +0.87pp/yr physical premium. Second decisive observation, Stanford "Canaries" (Brynjolfsson/Chandar/Chen, ADP payroll microdata): employment for workers aged 22-25 in the most AI-exposed jobs fell ~6%, 13% relative decline after controlling for firm-level shocks, while older workers in those jobs GAINED 6% to 9%; the authors state the adjustment runs through "hiring volume rather than pay cuts". Caveats preserved verbatim-in-substance: the paper dates from Aug-2025, covers late-2022 to Jul-2025, is US-only and ADP-panel-only; sources in circulation give inconsistent magnitudes (6%, 13%, 13-16%, ~20% for software/customer service) which are different measures and must not be pooled. Yale Budget Lab (Oct-2025) finds "the broader labour market has not experienced a discernible disruption since ChatGPT's release 33 months ago" and explicitly warns widespread effects "will take longer than 33 months to materialize" — i.e. the white-collar wage effect this conjunct needs is, on the best current evidence, statistically indistinguishable from zero at the aggregate level. Two mechanical forces work against the conjunct: (i) COMPOSITION — if J+K+M adjusts on headcount (juniors not hired), the surviving J+K+M workforce is more senior, so its MEDIAN hourly wage mechanically rises; (ii) ADMINISTERED PRICES — Q (health/social care) wages are reimbursement-set, and the locked 2A fiscal block (net interest 2%->3% of GDP, China pension subsidies already ~2.9T RMB / ~10.1% of fiscal expenditure) is precisely the constraint that converts care scarcity into unfilled vacancies and waiting lists rather than into real median wages. 16%.

CORRELATION: positive, ~+0.25. A tight labour market is the same state that would generate physical-sector wage pressure, so P(C2|C1) ~ 0.20 vs 0.16 unconditional. JOINT = 0.62 x 0.20 = 0.124 -> 12.
wave1.cq2_reasoning:
CONJUNCT A (OECD-38 GDP-weighted core >= 2.50%/yr avg 2027-2036), marginal 50%. OBSERVED, hard statistical-agency data: US core CPI "rose to 2.6% in September 2026 from a five-year low of 2.4% in August, slightly exceeding the expected 2.5%"; euro area core 2.5% in Sep-2026, up from 2.4% in Aug-2026 (Oct-2026 flash due 4 Nov 2026, not yet published — unverified at my horizon). US core PCE: sources conflict — one puts Aug-2026 at 3.1% "higher than the previous value of 3.0%", the Sep-2026 print was due 29 Oct 2026 with a 3.1% forecast; I did NOT verify the Sep actual, so treat 3.0-3.1% as the Aug level and the Sep level as unverified. Caveat flagged: one aggregator gave euro area Sep headline HICP at 3.8%, which does not square with 2.5% core and I do not trust it. INFERRED: a GDP-weighted OECD-38 core today is ~2.6-2.8% (US ~half the weight at 2.6-3.1%, euro area 2.5%, Japan ~2%). So the series starts ABOVE the threshold. ARITHMETIC: if 2027-29 averages 2.6%, the 2030-36 average must still be >=2.46% for the 10-yr mean to clear 2.50% — i.e. a persistent ~0.5pp overshoot of target for seven years. Upward: IMF Oct-2026 WEO flags "energy price pressures" and global inflation 4.7% in 2026 easing to only 4.1% in 2027 (AE 3.1%); PJM wholesale power +76% in Q1 2026; retail electricity +~7% YoY nationally and +16% YoY in Illinois; LME grade-A copper cash settlement US$14,751/t on 14 Oct 2026 after a record US$14,822 on 12 Oct (single secondary roundup, unconfirmed by a major outlet — treat as approximate); generator step-up transformer lead times "surpassed 160 weeks by the first quarter of 2026, compared with an average of 143 weeks in 2024"; gas turbine lead times "stretched to five years". Downward: credible central banks, post-capex-bust excess capacity. 50%.

CONJUNCT B (China headline CPI avg < 1.50%/yr 2027-2036), marginal 58%. OBSERVED, NBS primary release of 14 Oct 2026: September CPI +0.9% y/y and +0.2% m/m, up from 0.8% in August and 0.5% in July; core (ex food and energy) 1.0% y/y, unchanged from August and reported as the first 1.0% in 19 months; PPI +5.0% y/y, accelerating from +3.8% in August. Trading Economics notes the CPI print was "slightly below market expectations of 1%". Caveat: one iTiger item reported -0.3% y/y for September but its details match the Oct-2025 release and I discarded it. The reflation evidence (PPI +5.0%, core at 1.0%) is the strongest single argument AGAINST this conjunct and is why I am at 58% not 70%. Against reflation: population -60M over 2026-2035, worker-to-retiree 4.4->2.8, high precautionary saving, pension subsidy burden (locked 2A) — a structurally demand-deficient price level. Recent realized averages: 2022-2026 ~0.4%, 2019-2026 ~1.0%, 2015-2024 ~1.6%. 58%.

CORRELATION: mildly NEGATIVE, ~-0.15. The joint demands a DIVERGENCE, but the live drivers are common-global (energy, copper at records, China PPI +5.0% feeding tradable goods prices) and a China demand deficit exports goods disinflation to the OECD. The offsetting positive-correlation channel is the coherent bifurcation story (OECD labour-scarcity services inflation + Chinese excess capacity). JOINT = 0.50 x 0.58 x 0.90 = 0.261 -> 26.
wave1.cq3_reasoning:
REFERENCE CLASS: 5-year PPP-weighted realized growth averages for the OECD+China bloc, anchored on the current observed run-rate and walked forward by the locked demographic deltas.

PPP WEIGHTS CARRIED EXPLICITLY. 2025 world PPP shares: OECD-38 ~46-47%, China ~19.5%. Within the bloc: OECD 0.705 / China 0.295 today; by 2032-36 China's share drifts up to ~0.32 because it still grows faster. I use 0.68 / 0.32.

CURRENT OBSERVED RUN-RATE: IMF Oct-2026 WEO puts global growth at 3.1% for 2026 (raised 0.1pp) rebounding to 3.4% in 2027, with US growth "expected to remain at 2.3 percent" and EU/euro area "subdued". Caveat: sources disagree on whether the 2027 figure was revised +0.2pp or left unchanged, and I found NO October-2026-edition figure for China or for the AE aggregate — the 4.5% China number in circulation comes from the January-2026 update, not October. So the bloc run-rate is INFERRED: 0.68 x ~1.7 + 0.32 x ~4.6 = ~2.6%/yr.

WALK-FORWARD, OECD-38 LEG. Locked 2A: aging cuts baseline OECD real GDP per capita growth ~40%, 1.0%->0.6%/yr by 2036. Add OECD-38 population growth ~+0.2%/yr (US +0.3-0.4% on lower immigration, EU ~0, Japan/Korea negative) = 0.8%/yr absent productivity offsets. AI offset: expected PPP-weighted TFP lift from the locked 2B regime masses = 0.162 x ~0.75 + 0.472 x ~0.35 + 0.365 x ~0.07 = +0.31pp/yr. JONES/BAUMOL WEAKEST-LINK HAIRCUT: pass-through to measured output is at most 1:1 and plausibly less, because the binding tasks are observably the non-automated physical ones. Where the cap binds is directly measurable TODAY: transformer lead times >160 weeks (vs 143 weeks average in 2024), gas turbine lead times five years after 43 GW of 2025 orders (strongest in two decades), ERCOT large-load interconnection queue ~410 GW in April 2026 (about five times the grid's total generating capacity — caveat preserved: "developers seek to hedge their bets due to lengthy and uncertain electricity interconnection queues", so queues are padded with duplicates and this number overstates real load), lead time to power 36 months in Pittsburgh to 84 months in Columbus, Ohio. A task that cannot be energized before 2032 cannot contribute TFP by 2036. Also subtract: the capex-level growth contribution goes to ~zero or negative in 2032-36 given the locked 66% AI-Q4 impairment/revenue-shortfall prior, plus fiscal drag (net interest 2%->3% of GDP) and crowding out at a 2.60% US 10y real yield. OECD-38 P50 = 1.25%/yr (1.7 today, -0.45pp).

WALK-FORWARD, CHINA LEG — this is where the PPP weight does the work. Locked 2A: -2.7pp/yr aging drag, population -60M over 2026-2035 (7.92M births in 2025 vs deaths rising toward ~15M/yr, so roughly -0.5%/yr headcount and -1.0 to -1.3%/yr working-age), worker-to-retiree 4.4->2.8, pension/social-security subsidies ~2.9T RMB (~10.1% of fiscal expenditure). China is also the world's largest automation adopter, so the labour-scarcity DEMAND PULL partially offsets. From ~4.6% today to P50 2.8%/yr in 2032-36, i.e. -1.8pp realized against a -2.7pp gross aging drag, with ~0.9pp recovered through capital deepening and automation. 0.32 x 2.8 = 0.90pp of the bloc answer — China alone contributes half the total.

COMBINED P50 = 0.68 x 1.25 + 0.32 x 2.8 = 0.85 + 0.90 = 1.75%, rounded to 1.8%/yr. This is the key coupled finding: the locked 2A demographic block MECHANICALLY delivers a bloc P50 below 2%, roughly 0.8pp below the current observed run-rate, before any AI-pessimism is added.

P10 = 0.8: requires a capex bust (66% prior) landing inside the window plus a China hard landing plus two sub-zero OECD years; 5-year averages smooth, so one -1% year with 2% elsewhere still gives ~1.4%, and 0.8 needs two.
P90 = 2.7: requires TFP breakout AND China holding ~4.0% AND OECD ~2.0% (0.68 x 2.0 + 0.32 x 4.0 = 2.64). Distribution left-skewed (P50-P10 = 1.0 vs P90-P50 = 0.9) to respect the locked impairment prior.
wave1.cq4_reasoning:
OBSERVED ANCHOR (locked, treated as given fact): US 10y TIPS real yield ~2.60%, FRED DFII10, 30 Oct 2026. That is the highest sustained US real yield since 2008 and it is the single most important number in this question.

NON-US LEGS ARE WHERE I HAVE TO ADMIT IGNORANCE. G7 GDP weights (nominal USD): US ~0.50, Japan ~0.11, Germany ~0.11, UK ~0.08, France ~0.08, Canada ~0.065, Italy ~0.055. What I could verify: US 10y nominal 4.44% on 18 June 2026 (stale); 10y JGB "rose to a 30-year high" on 1 Sep 2026 per Reuters, level not given in the excerpt — unverified at my horizon; a 10y JGB print of 2.06% described as a 26-year high in Dec-2025; a 2.635% bund level that is UNDATED and which I therefore will not rely on. Current November-2026 levels for any G7 benchmark other than the locked US TIPS print are unverified at my horizon.

INFERRED CURRENT LEVEL (clearly separated from observation): using the locked 2.60% US print plus my best estimates of the others (Japan ~0.0-0.3% real, Germany ~0.3-0.8%, UK ~1.5-2.0%, France ~1.0-1.3%, Italy ~1.5%, Canada ~1.5%), the G7 GDP-weighted 10y real yield today is ~1.80%. The US contributes 1.30pp of that 1.80pp, so this question is ~72% a US question.

WALK-FORWARD TO 2032-36. Pushing UP, all from the locked block plus live telemetry: global (r-g) worsens ~+1.0pp even where a frictionless r* eases; gross public debt crosses 100% of GDP by 2029, ~142% US and ~127% China by 2031; net interest 2%->3% of GDP; 3-year P95 Debt-at-Risk ~117% of GDP, +2.4pp more under a 20% AI-led equity valuation shock; eroding sovereign convenience yields; retiree dissaving; and an enormous verified real-capex claim on savings (hyperscaler 2026 capex forecast $803-828B with executives pledging more in 2027, Amazon "meaningfully more in 2027", Alphabet 2026 raised to $180-190B and 2027 to increase "significantly", Moody's at ~$785B this year closing on $1T in 2027 — note the $803-828B and the earlier ~$725B Big-4 figures use different company sets and dates and are not directly comparable). Pushing DOWN: the BIS AER 2026 Box C aggregate-demand-shortfall channel, post-bust excess capacity, slower g, and financial repression (regulatory captive demand for sovereigns).

P50 = 2.1%: a modest further rise from the inferred 1.80%, driven mostly by Japan and Germany normalizing off near-zero real yields rather than by the US going much above 2.60%. P10 = 1.2% (D-regime: demand shortfall plus repression pulls the weighted real yield back toward the 2010s). P90 = 3.1% (C-regime term-premium spike). Five-year averages compress tails, which is why I do not go above 3.1 or below 1.2.
wave1.cq5_reasoning:
CONJUNCT A (ICE BofA MOVE averages >= 105 over 2027-2036), marginal 32%. OBSERVED, and this is poorly sourced — flagged as vendor/aggregator data throughout: the most recent level I am confident in is 70.9 on 17 Jul 2026 (ICE BofA via Yahoo Finance, a third-party aggregator, not checked against ICE); a dated commentary piece gives 103.01 on 26 Mar 2026; another gives ~75.4 against "above 170 during the April 2025 hedge-fund basis-trade stress"; an undated Convex page shows 66. These cannot all be current and the latest reading is unresolved. The November-2026 MOVE level is unverified at my horizon. REFERENCE CLASS: MOVE decade averages — ~90 since 1988, ~80-90 in 2003-07, ~75 in 2010-19, ~120 in 2022-24. A >=105 ten-year mean requires a 2022-23-style regime to dominate the decade. Structural support: MOVE is normalized basis-point vol and scales with the rate level, and the locked 2.60% real yield starting point is a far higher-rate world than the 2010s; plus fiscal dominance and basis-trade leverage, described in secondary commentary as "typical gross leverage in the 20-50x range" such that "a 1% drop in Treasury prices can therefore translate into a 20-50% hit to equity" — commentary, NOT Fed/OFR/ICE primary data, and no source confirms a RECORD in basis-trade leverage. A Fed-linked analysis cited secondhand notes TIC data "likely understate the amount of U.S. government debt held through offshore financial centers", so the true exposure size is uncertain. 32%.

CONJUNCT B (at least one MSCI World -25% peak-to-trough in which G7 GDP-weighted 10y nominals fail to fall >=50bp, or rise >=25bp, during the drawdown window). Decomposed.
B1, a -25% MSCI World drawdown somewhere in a 10-year window: base rate 2000-02, 2007-09, 2020 (-34%), 2022 (~-25/-27% USD) = ~4 episodes in 26 years = one per 6.5 years, so P(>=1 in 10y) = 1 - exp(-10/6.5) = 78%. Raise to 82% for the observed concentration: the IMF GFSR Oct-2026 stress case is itself a 20% AI-led equity valuation shock, and the circular ~$1.4T of vendor/cloud/chip commitments backed by ~$300B equity and ~$650B debt is a correlated-repricing structure. Live 2026 telemetry of exactly this kind of air-pocket, all vendor/press: a "Morgan Stanley Technology Momentum Long Index" AI proxy "fell 19% through the quarter" with the fall "as high as 37% from its June peak to the July trough" while MSCI ACWI gained 1.2% over three months; MSCI EM fell 2.6% to 1,620.66 on 17 Jul 2026 into correction territory; MSCI emerging Asia -3.5% by early Oct 2026; one undated report of >$1T of market value erased in a week. I found NO MSCI World October-2026 drawdown figure — unverified at my horizon; the MSCI October factsheet would settle it. OBSERVE that the AI complex has already had a 37% peak-to-trough while the broad index did not break: that is evidence the correlated-shock transmission is not yet complete.
B2, conditional on B1, yields failing to rally: the flight-to-quality bid WORKED in 2008, 2020 and 2000-02 (yields fell far more than 50bp); 2022 is the single counterexample (equities ~-25% while yields ROSE 200bp+), so ~1 in 4-5 historical episodes = ~22% unconditional. I mark it UP to 38% for three reasons: (i) the threshold is lenient — merely failing to fall 50bp counts, and fast drawdowns often produce sub-50bp yield moves; (ii) the measure is G7 GDP-weighted and the 10y JGB is in a structural RISING regime (30-year high, Sep 2026), which drags the weighted number up during any global equity event; (iii) fiscal dominance at 100%+ debt/GDP with eroding convenience yields. The offsetting force is decisive and is why I do not go higher: the MODAL large drawdown in this window is an AI-capex bust (locked 66% prior), and an AI capex bust is DISINFLATIONARY, so the bid works precisely in the most likely scenario.

CORRELATION: strongly positive between A and B — both are "rates are the shock" worlds. P(B1|A) = 0.88; P(B2|B1,A) = 0.58; P(B|A) = 0.51. JOINT = 0.32 x 0.51 = 0.163 -> 16. Most forecasters will over-rate this conjunction because each leg individually feels live; the binding constraint is that a 10-year MOVE mean of 105 is above every decade average on record except 1987-94 and 2022-24.
wave1.cq6_reasoning:
Built by integrating my own CQ3 distribution under the lexical priority lock, step by step, using GDP-weighted OECD-38 core inflation over 2032-36 as the second axis.

My CQ3: P10 0.8 / P50 1.8 / P90 2.7, approximately normal with right-side sigma ~0.70 and a fatter left tail.

STEP 1, A if growth >= 2.6%. P(X >= 2.6) = P(Z >= (2.6-1.8)/0.70 = 1.14) = 12.7%. Rounded to 12. CROSS-CHECK AGAINST LOCKED 2B: standalone Transformative Breakout is 16.2%. My coupled A at 12 is DELIBERATELY BELOW it, and must be: A requires not merely a TFP breakout but coupled real GDP growth >= 2.6%/yr delivered against China's -2.7pp aging drag at a 0.32 PPP weight and the OECD per-capita growth cut to 0.6%. Endogenizing demographics makes A strictly harder than the exogenous-demographics breakout. A = 12.

STEP 2, else C if OECD core >= 2.7% AND growth < 2.0%. P(growth < 2.0) = P(Z < 0.286) = 61%, lifted to 63% for the fat left tail. P(OECD-38 core >= 2.7% averaged 2032-36) = 26-27%: my CQ2 conjunct A gave 50% for a >= 2.50% average over 2027-36, and this is a higher threshold over a LATER window, where the near-term observed momentum (US core CPI 2.6% Sep-2026, euro core 2.5% Sep-2026, US core PCE ~3.0-3.1% Aug-2026) has less weight and central-bank convergence has more. Correlation: the supply-constrained low-growth world (grid/care walls; 160-week transformers, five-year turbines, copper at ~$14.7k/t) and the demand-deficient low-growth world roughly offset, so I take P(core>=2.7 | growth<2.0) ~ 0.26 unchanged. 0.63 x 0.26 = 0.164. C = 16.

STEP 3, else D if growth < 1.7% AND core < 2.0%. P(growth < 1.7) = P(Z < -0.143) = 44%, lifted to 46% for the fat left tail. P(core < 2.0 | growth < 1.7) = 0.42 (unconditionally ~0.35; raised because the low-growth state is disproportionately the post-capex-bust / BIS-labour-income-deficit state, and because my own CQ4 locked prior puts 66% on impairment or revenue shortfall). 0.46 x 0.42 = 0.193. D = 19.

STEP 4, B = residual = 100 - 12 - 16 - 19 = 53.

EXPLICIT CONSISTENCY CHECK AGAINST MY OWN CQ3: my P50 is 1.8%, which falls inside B's 1.7-2.5% band, so B must be modal and A must be small — satisfied (B 53, A 12). The lock's rule 4 also hands B the low-growth/moderate-inflation leftover cell (e.g. growth 1.4% with core 2.3%), which is a substantial chunk of my left tail, so B exceeding the standalone Jagged Diffusion mass of 47.2% is required, not an error. A at 12 is below the standalone 16.2% breakout, as the coupling demands.

EXPLICIT CONSISTENCY CHECK AGAINST MY OWN CQ2: I put 50% on OECD-38 core averaging >= 2.50% over 2027-36. C requires >= 2.70% over the 2032-36 subwindow, which must be a strict subset in probability — my 26-27% is comfortably below 50%. Multiplying by the growth condition gives 16, so C cannot be inflated past what my CQ2 inflation marginal supports. Conversely D requires core < 2.00%, and 1 - 0.50 = 50% is my upper bound on sub-2.5% core; my D inflation leg at 0.42 conditional sits inside that. No contradiction.

SUM = 12 + 53 + 16 + 19 = 100.

hypothesis_critique.a: The failure word is SMOOTHLY, and secondarily SUPPLY. There is no observed transmission mechanism — occupational, geographic, licensing, or wage — connecting a displaced cognitive worker to a care vacancy, and the live telemetry says the adjustment channel is the wrong one: Stanford/ADP 'Canaries' finds the labour market 'is adjusting through hiring volume rather than pay cuts', with 22-25 year olds in the most AI-exposed jobs down ~6% (13% relative after firm controls) while older workers in those same jobs GAINED 6% to 9% (caveats: Aug-2025 paper, late-2022 to Jul-2025, US-only, ADP panel; circulating magnitudes of 6/13/13-16/~20% are different measures and must not be pooled). Hiring-volume adjustment means no wage signal is generated to pull anyone into care, and the people NOT displaced are the mid-career workers who could plausibly retrain. On top of that, care pay is administered: Atlanta Fed shows Education and Health wage growth at 4.2 (Sep 2025) and Finance and Business Services at 4.2 (Feb 2026) — a dead heat, no reallocation premium. Yale Budget Lab (Oct-2025) finds no 'discernible disruption' 33 months after ChatGPT, i.e. the labour-saving stock the plank wants to redeploy is, at the aggregate level, statistically indistinguishable from zero today. 'SUPPLY' also smuggles in the assumption that the binding constraint is bodies rather than money; the locked 2A fiscal block says it is money.
hypothesis_critique.b: The failure word is BLOCKS, with SEVERELY doing secondary damage. The plank collapses the two channels my scope lock requires me to keep apart. AI compresses the VIRTUAL channel (cross-border services exports, seat-priced IT-BPO) but cannot substitute for a body in a care home or on a construction site, so the PHYSICAL labour-migration channel is made MORE valuable by exactly the OECD aging the question locks in (old-age ratio 31%->39-41% by 2036). The Philippines is disproportionately a physical-migration and remittance economy (nurses, care aides, seafarers); its exposure is the opposite sign to the plank's claim. India's IT-BPO is genuinely exposed, but India has repriced up the value chain through every prior automation wave, and India's measured growth is dominated by its own domestic demographic dividend, not by services exports to the OECD. 'BLOCKS' asserts a binary closure where the observable effect is a margin compression in one channel alongside a tightening in the other. 'SEVERELY' then overstates the net.
hypothesis_critique.c: The failure word is THEN — the implied clean sequencing — with FALLS carrying the rest. The plank gets the timing backwards relative to the coupling. The near-term disinflationary risk is a capex bust (locked 66% prior on impairment or revenue shortfall by 2032), while the bottleneck-driven price pressures peak INSIDE the 2030s, not before: generator step-up transformer lead times already 'surpassed 160 weeks by the first quarter of 2026, compared with an average of 143 weeks in 2024'; gas turbine lead times 'stretched to five years' after 43 GW of 2025 orders, the strongest in two decades; LME copper at a record ~US$14,822/t cash settlement on 12 Oct 2026 (single secondary source, unconfirmed by a major outlet); PJM wholesale power +76% in Q1 2026; US retail electricity +~7% YoY, +16% YoY in Illinois (caveat preserved from the RBC note: 'the sharpest increase in prices occurred before data center construction really began to accelerate', so data centres are contributing but are not the only driver). The care-wage Baumol channel also arrives in the 2030s, not now. And the plank ignores the bifurcation my CQ2 scores: the live divergence is OECD core at 2.5-3.1% against China CPI at 0.9% with core at 1.0% (NBS, 14 Oct 2026), so there is no single global 'inflation' to run hot and then fall. It scores 30 rather than lower only because a near-term plateau followed by partial mean reversion is genuinely one of the live paths.
hypothesis_critique.d: Two failure words. EVENTUALLY makes the plank unfalsifiable and in particular unresolvable at the 31 Dec 2036 horizon — it is a resolution-date dodge, and a forecast that cannot be scored is not a forecast. WINS is undefined: growth of what, measured how, accruing to whom (the BIS AER 2026 Box C warning about aggregate-demand shortfalls if displaced labour income lags capital-concentrated output is precisely the case where output 'wins' and nothing else does). EXPONENTIAL is the substantive error: under Jones/Baumol weakest-link production, exponential capability gains in a subset of tasks yield bounded aggregate gains because the non-automated tasks' shadow prices rise to absorb them — which is observable right now as 160-week transformer waits, 84-month lead-times-to-power in Columbus Ohio, and an ERCOT large-load queue of ~410 GW against roughly a fifth of that in actual capacity (queue padded with duplicate requests, so overstated). At the actual resolution date it does not outrun: my CQ3 P50 of 1.8%/yr is BELOW the ~2.6% the bloc is running today. The score is 14, not 2, only because the direction of travel for the back half of the century is not something the 2036 horizon can refute.

key_drivers: China's ~0.32 PPP weight inside the bloc multiplied by its locked -2.7pp/yr aging drag: China alone supplies ~0.90pp of my 1.75pp coupled CQ3 P50, so the single largest determinant of the growth answer is a demographic fact, not an AI fact.

The physical weakest link, observable today and dated: generator step-up transformer lead times >160 weeks (vs 143 weeks average in 2024), gas turbine lead times five years after 43 GW of 2025 orders, 36-84 month lead-times-to-power by US metro, LME copper cash settlement ~US$14.75-14.82k/t in mid-Oct 2026, PJM wholesale power +76% in Q1 2026. These cap the realized TFP contribution and simultaneously raise the impairment probability.

AI labour adjustment runs through HIRING VOLUME, not PAY (Stanford/ADP Canaries: 'adjusting through hiring volume rather than pay cuts'). This single empirical regularity breaks CQ1's second conjunct, breaks hypothesis plank (a), and dampens the locked AI-Q5 compensation-share story.

The fiscal channel converts care scarcity into vacancies rather than real median wages: administered reimbursement prices plus net interest rising 2%->3% of GDP plus China's ~2.9T RMB pension subsidy at ~10.1% of fiscal expenditure. Scarcity without a price is invisible to every wage-based resolution criterion in this question set.

The starting real-rate level: US 10y TIPS 2.60% (FRED DFII10, 30 Oct 2026) while hyperscaler capex is still ACCELERATING ($803-828B forecast for 2026, 'meaningfully more in 2027'). The buildout's binding constraint is the discount rate, not demand — which is what makes CQ4 high, CQ6-B's 'steep real term premia' the modal regime, and long nominal bonds a poor 2026-2030 holding.

wave1.coupling_tension:
Three places where coupling makes a locked 2B marginal inconsistent, with directions.

(1) AI-Q1 (2032-36 PPP-weighted TFP lift >= +0.50pp, 23.0%) is internally two different questions once demographics are endogenous, and the locked single number cannot be right for both. On the PPP-weighted measure as written it is TOO HIGH: China carries ~a third of the bloc's PPP weight, its locked aging drag is -2.7pp/yr, and shrinking-workforce economies reallocate capital toward labour substitution with falling marginal product and toward pension-financing claims, which depresses MEASURED TFP in a third of the weight regardless of frontier capability. On an OECD-38-only cut it is TOO LOW: aging is a demand pull, and labour scarcity is the most reliable historical accelerant of adoption. Net on the question as literally posed: down to roughly 18-20%. Direction: DOWN.

(2) AI-Q5 (cognitive-sector labour compensation share of GVA falls >= 3.5pp, 38.2%) has the right sign but the wrong mechanism once demographics are endogenous, and the mechanism change moves the number DOWN. With exogenous demographics the fall comes from displacement of a fixed workforce. With endogenous demographics, OECD cognitive-sector headcount declines substantially through retirement and non-replacement — the Stanford/ADP result is precisely that 22-25 year olds are not hired while 'older workers in those jobs' gain 6% to 9%. A sector that loses juniors and retains seniors has a RISING average wage, so the compensation share falls by less than the employment decline implies, and some of the apparent AI effect is simply the demographic pipeline narrowing. Direction: DOWN, to roughly 32-34%, with the caveat that the Stanford finding is US-only ADP panel data from late-2022 to Jul-2025 and the Yale Budget Lab's contemporaneous read is that the aggregate effect is statistically indistinguishable from zero.

(3) The sharpest tension is between two locked marginals that cannot both sit comfortably once the physical constraint is coupled in: AI-Q3's data-centre electricity P50 of 998.2 TWh/yr by 2036 and AI-Q4's 66.0% impairment probability. The observed physical ceiling — generator step-up transformer lead times surpassing 160 weeks by Q1 2026 against a 143-week 2024 average, gas turbine lead times stretched to five years after 43 GW of 2025 orders, lead-time-to-power of 36 to 84 months depending on metro, an ERCOT large-load queue of ~410 GW that is itself padded with duplicate hedging requests — does two things AT ONCE and in opposite directions for these two questions. It caps realized 2036 operational load, which pushes AI-Q3's P90 of 1,573.8 TWh down hard (the high tail requires energizing capacity that physically cannot be energized on that schedule), and it simultaneously RAISES AI-Q4, because the ~$1.4T of circular commitments backed by ~$300B equity and ~$650B debt is being committed against capacity with a 3-7 year energization lag, which is the textbook generator of both impairment and of net external AI revenue falling below compute D&A. So coupling moves AI-Q3's upper tail DOWN and AI-Q4 UP, and those two moves are driven by the same observable and are therefore not independent — an ensemble that treats them as independent marginals will understate the joint probability of the 'strandedbuildout' state that my CQ6-D at 19 is partly pricing. Secondary note on CQ6-A: it must be scored BELOW the standalone Transformative Breakout mass of 16.2%, because A demands coupled growth >= 2.6%/yr against the demographic drag rather than merely a TFP breakout; any panelist placing A at or above 16.2% has failed to couple.

wave2.coupling_tension:
PRIMARY TENSION, AI-Q4 (66%) IS TOO LOW, AND THE REASON IS A COUPLING MY EFFORT OWNS. Impairment is not primarily a demand question; it is a discount-rate-times-useful-life question. AI compute has a 3-6 year book life, so the hurdle rate on a 2026-2030 build is roughly (real discount rate + 1/life). Couple that to the demographic/fiscal block: old-age dissaving (+0.35pp to r*), public dissaving at >100% debt/GDP (+0.25pp), eroding convenience yields and leveraged basis-trade absorption (+0.40pp real term premium) — i.e. 2A's own arithmetic says the real discount rate that the ~$1.4T of circular commitments must clear STAYS at or above the locked 2.60% US TIPS level rather than reverting to the 2010s. At a ~2% G7-weighted real yield and a 5-year life, the required gross revenue yield on AI compute is ~22-25%/yr of capex, which is not plausibly cleared by a customer base that AI-Q2 (21.3%) says is fewer than half of OECD firms. Endogenous demographics therefore RAISE AI-Q4, to roughly 0.74. Direction: UP. This is the one place where aging-as-fiscal-constraint and aging-as-demand-pull do NOT offset: the demand pull raises adoption (AI-Q2 up) while the saving/fiscal channel raises the cost of capital faster, so the buildout gets both more wanted and less financeable, which is precisely the impairment state.
SECOND TENSION, AI-Q3's UPPER TAIL. The P90 of 1,573.8 TWh requires ~12%/yr compound OECD-38+China operational datacentre load for twelve years. The Signal Scout's dated telemetry (generator step-up transformer lead times >160 weeks in Q1 2026 vs a 143-week 2024 average; gas turbine lead times at five years after 43 GW of 2025 orders; 36-84 month lead-time-to-power by US metro) means capacity that is OPERATIONAL in 2036 must be queued by roughly 2031-32, and the equipment order book is already a binding constraint. Direction: AI-Q3's P90 DOWN ~15-20% (toward ~1,280-1,340 TWh), P50 down modestly to ~920-950, with a fatter left tail. Note the dependence the ensemble will miss: the SAME observable moves AI-Q3's tail down and AI-Q4 up, so treating them as independent marginals understates the joint mass on the stranded-buildout cell. That cell is what my CQ6-D at 14 and my regime-D asset numbers (AI complex -9.0%/yr, power/grid -3.0%/yr, private credit -7.0%/yr) price.
THIRD TENSION, AND IT CUTS AGAINST MY OWN CQ6 ORDERING. AI-Q4 at 66% is a disinflationary-bust prior. Taken alone it implies D > C. I nonetheless report C 26 > D 14, and the entire reason is the composition arithmetic of the OECD-38 GDP-WEIGHTED core inflation measure (Turkey, Mexico, Colombia, Chile, Costa Rica hold the aggregate 0.5-2.0pp above the G7 core), which starves D of its <2.00% condition. I flag this explicitly as the load-bearing non-AI assumption in my CQ6: if that composition claim is wrong, C and D roughly swap, long nominal sovereigns go from my worst regime-conditional holding (-6.5%/yr in C) to my best (+5.5%/yr in D), and the whole asset matrix inverts. This is a measurement-definition risk, not a macro-forecasting risk, and the ensemble should treat it as the single highest-variance input in my payload.
wave2.cq1_reasoning:
PRIOR ADOPTED: the Historian's 13 (conjunct C1 0.40, conjunct C2 0.25, rho +0.35, P(C2|C1)=0.32). I update the CONJUNCTS separately rather than the joint, to avoid applying evidence to a number that already contains it.
C1 (OECD-38 harmonized U <= 5.5% avg 2032-36). Prior 0.40. EVIDENCE 1: OECD release, unemployment "broadly stable in August 2026, at 5.0%, just 0.2 p.p. above its record low from June 2023"; the OECD's own two releases disagree on July (4.9% vs 5.0%), so the print is revision-noisy. LR for "stable 5.0% near record low" | C1 true vs false = roughly 1.2 — BELOW 2:1, so DISCOUNTED to 1.1. EVIDENCE 2 (structural, from the Fermi seat, not evidence): a shrinking 20-64 denominator is Okun-favourable, worth about -0.2pp on the structural rate; this is arithmetic and it reshapes the conditional rather than updating it. Posterior C1 = 0.47 (prior odds 0.667 x 1.1 = 0.733, plus the Okun structural adjustment that moves the Historian's 0.40 toward the Fermi 0.55).
C2 ((F+Q) minus (J+K+M) cumulative real MEDIAN hourly wage growth >= +10.0pp, i.e. +0.87pp/yr for 11 years). Prior 0.25. EVIDENCE 3, the highest-LR signal in this question: Stanford/ADP "Canaries" finds the AI labour adjustment runs through "hiring volume rather than pay cuts", with 22-25 year olds in exposed jobs down ~6% (13% relative) while older workers in the same jobs GAINED 6-9%. P(hiring-volume-not-pay adjustment observed | a +10pp median-wage divergence is coming) / P(same | not coming) = about 0.5, and I keep it because it is above 2:1 in the negative direction and because it is mechanistically decisive: a sector that stops hiring juniors and retains seniors has a MECHANICALLY RISING median, which moves the tested differential the wrong way. Caveats preserved: US-only, ADP panel, late-2022 to Jul-2025, and circulating magnitudes (6%, 13%, 13-16%, ~20%) are different measures that must not be pooled; the Yale Budget Lab's contemporaneous read is that the aggregate effect is statistically indistinguishable from zero at 33 months. EVIDENCE 4: Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker shows Education and Health 4.2 against Finance and Business Services 4.2 — a dead heat, not a +0.87pp/yr physical premium. LR about 0.6, but the series is 12-month-moving-average unweighted medians by broad industry group and NOT ISIC F/Q/J/K/M, and Construction/Mining is unverified at the horizon; I cannot justify it above 2:1, so DISCOUNTED to 0.8. EVIDENCE 5, the only amplifier: dated physical-scarcity prints (transformer lead times >160 weeks vs a 143-week 2024 average, gas turbine lead times five years, PJM wholesale +76% in Q1 2026, LME copper ~US$14.75-14.82k/t mid-Oct 2026). Raw LR for C2 maybe 1.6-1.8, but the Fermi structural finding is that this scarcity clears by RATIONING (queues, unfilled rosters, waiting lists) and not by a median wage, because Q is reimbursement-set and interconnection is queue-allocated; below 2:1 and structurally blunted, so DISCOUNTED to 1.25.
POSTERIOR C2: odds 0.333 x 0.5 x 0.8 x 1.25 = 0.1665 -> 0.143. Take 0.15.
CORRELATION: +0.35 retained. P(C2|C1) = 0.15 x 1.28 = 0.19.
JOINT: 0.47 x 0.19 = 0.089 -> 9.
DIRECTION: AMPLIFIED downward, -4 points off the Wave-1 Historian prior of 13 (and below all three Wave-1 seats, 13/11/12). The amplification is carried almost entirely by one signal, Evidence 3, which is the only one in the set I can justify above 2:1, and it attacks the measure (medians) rather than the phenomenon (scarcity). Real physical scarcity and a failing CQ1 are fully compatible, which is the finding.
wave2.cq2_reasoning:
PRIOR ADOPTED: the Historian's 41 (conjunct A 0.70, conjunct B 0.65, rho -0.10, P(B|A) 0.60).
CONJUNCT A (OECD-38 GDP-weighted core >= 2.50%/yr avg 2027-2036). Prior 0.70. The three Wave-1 seats span 0.70 / 0.42 / 0.50, and the entire spread is one identification question: does the OECD-38 GDP-weighted aggregate carry Turkey, Mexico, Colombia, Chile and Costa Rica at material weight? This is arithmetic, not judgment, so I resolve it structurally rather than by LR: Turkey alone at ~2% of OECD GDP running a 10-20% core contributes +0.3 to +0.5pp, and the OECD-wide aggregate historically ran 0.5-2.0pp above the euro-area/US core for exactly this reason (OECD aggregate CPI ~1.8-2.2% in 2015-2019 against euro-area core ~1.0%). The Fermi bottom-up build of 2.39% books "rest 0.13 x 2.5%", which understates the EM members; I therefore adopt the Historian's composition and REJECT the Fermi central case. EVIDENCE: US core CPI 2.6% Sep-2026 (up from a five-year low of 2.4% in Aug), euro area core 2.5% Sep-2026, US core PCE ~3.0-3.1% Aug-2026 (the Sep actual unverified). The series starts AT OR ABOVE the threshold. LR about 1.5 for A, below 2:1 so DISCOUNTED to 1.25; and most of its content is already inside the Historian's 0.70. Posterior A = 0.72.
CONJUNCT B (China headline CPI avg < 1.50%/yr 2027-2036). Prior 0.65. THE MATERIAL SIGNAL, and the one that justifies this seat existing: NBS primary release of 14 Oct 2026 gives September CPI +0.9% y/y and +0.2% m/m, up from 0.8% in August and 0.5% in July, core (ex food and energy) 1.0% y/y and reported as the first 1.0% in 19 months, and PPI +5.0% y/y accelerating from +3.8% in August. Raw LR: P(this reflation signature | China 10-yr average >= 1.5%) / P(same | < 1.5%) looks like 2.2-2.5, because PPI acceleration of that size has historically led CPI by two to four quarters. I CANNOT SUSTAIN THAT LR. The 2021 episode is the counterexample inside the same regime: Chinese PPI reached roughly +13% while CPI stayed near 1%, because PPI is commodity-and-export-price driven and has been structurally decoupled from the household price level since the property bust. That precedent cuts the LR to about 1.5, below my 2:1 bar, so I DISCOUNT it to an effective 1.4 against B. Posterior: prior odds 1.857 / 1.4 = 1.326 -> 0.570; I set B = 0.62, because the threshold arithmetic is demanding in the other direction — failing B needs roughly 2.0%+ sustained from 2028 off a 2023-2026 run rate of ~0.0-0.9%, against -60M population over 2026-35, worker-to-retiree 4.4 -> 2.8, and pension subsidies already ~2.9T RMB or ~10.1% of fiscal expenditure, with the fiscal space for a reflationary household transfer being consumed by the pension transfer that will not reflate.
CORRELATION: mildly negative, rho about -0.10, retained. Chinese deflation is exported disinflation into OECD tradables (1998-2004, 2014-2016), partially offset by a shared commodity shock. P(B|A) = 0.62 x 0.92 = 0.57.
JOINT: 0.72 x 0.57 = 0.410 -> 41, less a one-point conjunction haircut = 40.
DIRECTION: essentially UNMOVED, -1 point off the Historian prior of 41. This is the honest result: the two material LRs point opposite ways and cancel. The China reflation print moves B down roughly 3 points; the observed OECD core prints starting above the threshold move A up roughly 2 points. Note that my 40 sits well above the Fermi 30 and the Scout 26, and the whole gap is the OECD-38 composition identification, not a different view of inflation dynamics.
wave2.cq3_reasoning:
PRIOR ADOPTED: the Historian's 0.8 / 1.9 / 2.9.
PPP WEIGHT, RESOLVED FIRST BECAUSE IT DOMINATES. The three Wave-1 seats disagree materially: Fermi 0.38 China, Historian 0.33, Scout 0.32. Fermi's 0.365-0.38 rests on OECD-38 PPP GDP of ~$73T against China ~$42T; that OECD figure is too low. Rebuilt: world PPP GDP ~$195T, China ~19.5% = ~$38T; OECD-38 sums to ~41% (US 14.8, Japan 3.2, Germany 3.0, UK 2.2, France 2.1, Turkey 2.0, Italy 1.8, Mexico 1.8, Korea 1.7, Spain 1.4, Canada 1.3, Poland 0.9, Australia 0.9, rest ~4) = ~$80T. China share of the pair = 38/118 = 0.322 at the 2026 start, drifting to ~0.34-0.35 by the 2034 midpoint. I use 0.335 / 0.665. This is a ratio and so deflator-base invariant; I ADOPT the Fermi seat's reasoning that a weight is identified while rejecting its level.
THE HEADLINE PRODUCT: 0.335 x (-2.7pp China aging drag) = -0.90pp of coupled growth from Chinese demographics alone; 0.665 x (-0.4pp OECD per-capita drag) = -0.27pp; total -1.17pp/yr. Against that, the probability-weighted AI TFP lift computed off AI-Q6's own regime means (0.162 x 0.75 + 0.472 x 0.35 + 0.365 x 0.07) = +0.31pp, net about +0.25pp after the aging-demand-pull plus (+0.05), fiscal-crowding-out minus (-0.05) and incremental Baumol reallocation (-0.06) adjustments. The offset is roughly a fifth of the drag. No Bayesian update changes this; it is the structure.
LEGS: OECD-38 = 0.80pp locked aggregate baseline (0.6% per capita + ~0.2% population) + 0.25pp net AI + 0.07pp net capital services (gross +0.14 halved for the AI-Q4 digestion phase landing inside the window) - 0.08pp damages/energy-cost = 1.04%; cross-checked by composition at 1.11%; I take 1.15%, a touch above Fermi, because the Scout's 1.25% carries the observed 2026 run-rate correctly. China = 2.8%.
COUPLED P50 = 0.665 x 1.15 + 0.335 x 2.80 = 0.765 + 0.938 = 1.70%, plus ~0.05pp of within-window weight drift = 1.75%.
UPDATES, WITH LRs.
(1) IMF Oct-2026 WEO: global 3.1% in 2026 (raised 0.1pp) rebounding to 3.4% in 2027, US "expected to remain at 2.3 percent", EU subdued; no Oct-2026-edition China or AE figure was verifiable, and the 4.5% China number in circulation is from the January-2026 update. Implied bloc run-rate ~2.6%. LR for "2026-27 run-rate 2.6%" | (2032-36 >= 2.2%) vs (< 2.2%) is about 1.3 — the autocorrelation of five-year growth windows at a six-year lag is weak for aggregates this large. BELOW 2:1, DISCOUNTED to 1.15. Worth +0.05pp on P50 and nothing else.
(2) PHYSICAL BOTTLENECK, the strongest signal: generator step-up transformer lead times surpassing 160 weeks by Q1 2026 against a 143-week 2024 average; gas turbine lead times stretched to five years after 43 GW of 2025 orders, the strongest in two decades; lead-time-to-power 36 months in Pittsburgh to 84 months in Columbus; ERCOT large-load queue ~410 GW in April 2026 (caveat preserved verbatim in substance: developers hedge across queues, so the figure is padded with duplicates and overstates real load). LR: P(these lead times | the 2032-36 realized TFP contribution is capped below ~+0.35pp) / P(same | uncapped) = about 2.5. ABOVE 2:1, KEPT. The logic is a date, not a theory: capacity operational in 2032-36 must be queued by 2029-32, so the marginal project in the window is equipment-constrained today. Worth -0.08pp on P50 and, more importantly, a hard cut to P90.

hypothesis_critique.a: The failure word is "smoothly", and it is doing two jobs, both of which fail. First, SMOOTHLY presumes a transfer mechanism between two labour pools that are separated by licensure, credentialing and reimbursement, not by a wage gradient. Second, and decisively, the Stanford/ADP Canaries result is that the AI adjustment runs through "hiring volume rather than pay cuts": the people not being employed in cognitive work are 22-25 year olds who were never hired, not mid-career workers released with transferable savings, while "older workers in those jobs" GAINED 6-9%. A cohort that never entered white-collar work is not a stock of "labour savings" that can be redeployed; it is an entry-cohort that chose differently. The plank also quietly assumes the receiving sector can pay, and the Q wage bill is a fiscally administered budget line in exactly the budgets 2A squeezes (net interest 2% -> 3% of GDP), so the care shortage clears as vacancies and waiting lists rather than as hires. Even "eventually and painfully" would be a stretch; "smoothly" is not close. Caveats on the evidence preserved: Canaries is US-only ADP panel data, late-2022 to Jul-2025, and the Yale Budget Lab's contemporaneous read is that the broader labour market shows no discernible disruption at 33 months.
hypothesis_critique.b: Two words fail, and in opposite directions. "BLOCKS" fails because the scope lock names TWO channels — cross-border VIRTUAL services exports and PHYSICAL labour migration — and AI touches only the first. The 2A demographic block is a demand pull on the second: an OECD-38 old-age ratio going to 39-41% with licensed care hours as a binding constraint is a standing bid for physical migrant labour, so the aggregate export of labour is not blocked, it is RECOMPOSED from virtual to physical. "SEVERELY" fails on timing and magnitude: the locked AI-Q2 at 21.3% says fewer than half of OECD firms even use AI directly in production by 2036, and the locked AI-Q4 at 66% says the compute that would do the displacing is likely to be impaired or revenue-short inside the window, so BPO substitution at a severity that dominates India's domestic demand growth is not a 10-year story. I hold 14 rather than lower because the direction is right for the virtual channel specifically and because the Philippines is far more concentrated in exactly the voice and back-office tasks that go first, so "severely" is defensible for one of the two named economies and one of the two named channels.
hypothesis_critique.c: The failure word is "then", the sequencing claim, and specifically what the plank assumes about the MEASURE. On the OECD-38 GDP-weighted core basis the question actually locks, the aggregate carries Turkey, Mexico, Colombia, Chile and Costa Rica, which have historically held it 0.5-2.0pp above the euro-area and US core (OECD aggregate CPI ~1.8-2.2% in 2015-2019 against euro-area core ~1.0%). My own CQ2 posterior puts 0.72 on that aggregate averaging >= 2.50% across all of 2027-2036 and about 0.37 on >= 2.70% in the LATER 2032-36 subwindow — so the "falls in the 2030s" half is the half that fails, not because dynamics do not mean-revert but because composition does not. A secondary failure: "hot for the next few years" understates the starting point, since US core CPI at 2.6% in Sep-2026 and US core PCE at ~3.0-3.1% in Aug-2026 are an overshoot that is already moderate rather than hot. The plank would score far higher if it specified G7 core or euro-area core; at 27 I am pricing mostly the chance that the measure is read the plank's way.
hypothesis_critique.d: Two words, and the second is the fatal one. "EVENTUALLY" is unfalsifiable at a Dec 31 2036 resolution horizon — it exempts the claim from the very window being scored, which is a category error in a dated question, and the Fermi CES arithmetic confirms the exemption is doing real work: the Baumol weakest-link LEVEL cap is hard (Y_max about 5x) but binds in the 2040s-50s and costs the OECD only about 0.15-0.30pp/yr by 2036. "WINS" is undefined and, on the only quantitative reading available (the lock's A gate of coupled growth >= 2.6%/yr), my own answer is 11. The arithmetic is the critique: the coupled aging drag is -1.17pp/yr (0.335 x -2.7 for China plus 0.665 x -0.4 for the OECD) against a probability-weighted AI TFP lift of +0.31pp computed off AI-Q6's own regime means, i.e. the offset is roughly a fifth of the drag, not a multiple of it. "Exponential" is also wrong about the binding margin in this window, which is DIFFUSION (AI-Q2 at 21.3%) and physical energization (transformers at >160 weeks, turbines at five years), neither of which compounds at a capability rate.

key_drivers: THE LOCKED 2.60% US 10y TIPS PRINT AS EVIDENCE, NOT COINCIDENCE. wave2.coupling_tension:
THE DECISIVE COUPLING ERROR IS NOT IN 2B, IT IS IN HOW 2A's DRAG FIGURES WERE APPLIED, AND IT IS SHARED BY ALL THREE WAVE-1 SEATS. 2A's -2.7 pp/yr China figure and -1.1 pp/yr global figure are IMF WEO Apr-2025 Ch.2 drags over 2025-2050 measured against a NO-AGING counterfactual. All three panelists subtracted them (or most of them) from China's CURRENTLY OBSERVED ~4.5-5% run-rate. But that observed run-rate is already produced by an economy whose working-age population peaked in 2013 and whose total population has fallen since 2022 — a large part of the 2025-2050 average drag is ALREADY IN THE PRINT. Panelist 2 made the double-count explicit and visible: his China leg of 2.70% implies a "no-aging counterfactual of ~5.4%/yr" which he called "internally coherent" — it is the opposite; it asserts that China's 2026 growth contains ZERO realized aging drag while its dependency ratio has been deteriorating for a decade. The drag is also back-loaded: the worker/retiree ratio collapse from 2.8 accelerates into the 2040s, so the INCREMENTAL 2026->2036 drag is roughly -1.0 to -1.3 pp, not -1.8 or -2.7. Correcting the double-count alone lifts coupled CQ3 by ~+0.25 to +0.30 pp, which is most of my gap to the Wave-1 centre.

SECOND: AI-Q4 at 66% was mistranslated into a real-economy deduction. Panelist 2 halved his capital-services contribution (+0.14 -> +0.07 pp) "because AI-Q4 puts an impairment/digestion phase inside the window"; panelist 3 took the capex growth contribution "to ~zero or negative". An impairment is a BOOK-VALUE event. A written-down GPU still computes and a written-down substation still delivers electrons; neither measured GDP, measured capital services, nor measured TFP falls because a balance sheet was marked. AI-Q4's second limb (external AI revenue < 0.5x compute D&A) is a transfer-pricing and depreciation-schedule fact, not an output fact. So AI-Q4 can be high (I would mark it UP, to ~0.72, for the reason panelist 2 identified: narrow paying base against 998 TWh of load) AND coupled growth can be intact. The impairment belongs in CQ5, CQ4's term premium and the private-credit/AI-complex rows of the asset matrix, NOT in CQ3. Direction: Wave 1 biased CQ3 DOWN by ~0.10-0.15 pp through this category error.

THIRD, ON 2B PROPER: AI-Q2 (21.3%) is too LOW once demographics are endogenous — labour scarcity is the best-documented firm-level automation forcing variable (postwar Japan, 1920s US post-Quota) and holding demographics exogenous strips it out; endogenous it belongs near 33%. AI-Q5 (38.2%) is too HIGH, but not for the reason Wave 1 gave: all three cited the Stanford/ADP junior-hiring result, which is a US-only ADP panel to Jul-2025 with magnitudes that sources report inconsistently (6% / 13% / 13-16% / ~20%) and must not be pooled; the robust coupling point is simply that a sector shedding juniors and retaining high-paid seniors has a RISING compensation-per-head, so the GVA share falls less. Mark to ~31%.

FOURTH, A TENSION WITH MY OWN ANSWER THAT I WILL NAME RATHER THAN HIDE: my CQ2 at 48 rests on the OECD-38 PPP-GDP-weighted aggregate being structurally 0.4-0.9 pp above a G7 core because Turkey, Mexico, Colombia, Chile and Costa Rica are members. That same composition fact makes CQ6-D nearly unreachable (sub-2.0% on that aggregate requires G7 core near 1.5% AND Turkish disinflation to single digits), which is why my D is 6 against Wave 1's 11-19 — and it simultaneously makes CQ6-C's >=2.7% gate easy. If the resolver instead uses a market-FX-weighted or G7-proxy aggregate, my CQ2 drops to ~32, C drops to ~0.17 and D rises to ~0.13. That is the single largest resolution-criterion risk in my payload and it is an accounting-basis question, not a forecasting one.

STEP 2 - else C if OECD-38 core >= 2.7% AND growth < 2.0%. P(growth < 2.0) = P(z < -0.12) = 0.45. INFLATION LEG FROM MY OWN CQ2: I put P(core >= 2.50% over 2027-36) = 0.78 on PPP-GDP weights with the five EM members carried explicitly. Raising the gate to 2.70% and narrowing to 2032-36 (mean reversion down, fiscal dominance up, Turkish composition persistent): P(core >= 2.7% in 2032-36) = 0.55. Positive dependence — my own binding constraints (administered care prices, HV interconnection and transformer rationing, 160-week lead times, copper at ~$14.7k/t) are SUPPLY-side and therefore stagflationary: P(core >= 2.7 | growth < 2.0) = 0.60. C = 0.45 x 0.60 = 0.27 -> 27. CONSISTENCY: C at 27 sits strictly below 100 x 0.55, so it cannot exceed what my CQ2 inflation marginal permits.

STEP 3 - else D if growth < 1.7% AND core < 2.0%. P(growth < 1.7) = P(z < -0.47) = 0.32. P(core < 2.0 | growth < 1.7) = 0.18. This is where I depart hardest from Wave 1's 11/15/19. Sub-2.00% on a PPP-GDP-weighted OECD-38 core requires the G7 block near 1.5% AND Turkiye in single digits AND Mexico near 3% simultaneously — the composition that carries my CQ2 conjunct A starves D of its inflation condition. Panelist 1 identified this exact point ("the single most under-appreciated arithmetic fact in the CQ6 lock") and then set the conditional at 0.28; panelist 3 set it at 0.42 on a disinflationary-bust argument that is about the G7 and silent on the five EM members. D = 0.32 x 0.18 = 0.058 -> 6.

STEP 4 - B = residual = 100 - 25 - 27 - 6 = 42. Sum = 100.

AUDIT OF THE LEFTOVER CELLS. My implied low-growth/moderate-inflation leftover = P(growth < 2.0) - C - D = 0.45 - 0.27 - 0.058 = 0.12, which sits inside B; the remaining 0.30 of B is the 2.0-2.6% growth band plus the growth-2.0-2.6%-with-core->=2.7% cell that rule 2 does not claim (it requires growth < 2.0). My CQ3 P50 of 2.1% falls inside B's band and B is modal at 42, as the lock requires, while A at 25 is exactly P(CQ3 >= 2.6) shaded down 3 points. No mass is double-booked: C requires core >= 2.7 and D requires core < 2.0, so they are disjoint by construction.

hypothesis_critique.a: "SMOOTHLY" is the stated trap and it is the wrong one to focus on - the plank fails on "SUPPLY". Even granting a large white-collar labour saving, there is no transfer mechanism: the Stanford/ADP evidence (US-only, ADP panel, late-2022 to Jul-2025, magnitudes inconsistently reported across sources as 6%, 13%, 13-16% and ~20% - different measures, not poolable) says the adjustment runs through HIRING VOLUME, not separations, so no stock of mid-career cognitive workers is released at all. What exists is a thinner entry cohort of 22-25 year olds who never entered J/K/M - and they do not become licensed care workers either, because Q's constraint is licensure, clinical placements and an administered wage below the displaced cohort's reservation wage. The flow is a non-event in both directions. A second failure: AI savings accrue to firms and capital owners while care demand is a public fiscal claim, so even a real saving does not finance a care wage bill (the BIS Box C point). 4.
hypothesis_critique.b: "BLOCKS" carries the failure, and "SEVERELY" carries a second one. AI compresses the PRICE of routine virtual services export; it does not block the EXPORT of labour, and the coupled demographic block creates enormous demand for exactly the labour AI cannot automate - bedside care, construction trades, logistics. The Philippines' comparative advantage migrates from BPO seats to nursing, caregiving and seafaring, which is a PIVOT, not a block; the OECD old-age ratio going to 39-41% by 2036 is a demand shock in its favour. On "severely": India's IT-BPO is roughly 7-8% of GDP and a smaller share of employment, so even a hard hit to it is a growth-rate event, not a development reversal, and India's domestic demand and its own position as an AI delivery platform both cut the other way. The plank also quietly assumes the virtual and physical channels are substitutes when the question's own scope lock separates them. 14.
hypothesis_critique.c: "THEN FALLS" is the failing clause - the sequencing is backwards, not the level. The hot phase IS front-loaded (power prices, PJM +76% in Q1 2026, retail electricity, copper at records, tariff pass-through) and the plank gets that right. What it gets wrong is that the 2030s ADD two inflation legs rather than removing them: fiscal dominance as net interest goes 2% -> 3% of GDP at 100%+ debt/GDP, and the Baumol grid-and-care supply wall whose scarcity clears partly through administered price increases once rationing becomes politically untenable. And on the measure that actually resolves (GDP-weighted OECD-38, with Turkiye, Mexico, Colombia, Chile and Costa Rica inside it at PPP weights), the aggregate does not fall below 2.5% even if the G7 converges to target. The plank is a G7-shaped claim applied to an OECD-38 measure. 26.
hypothesis_critique.d: TWO WORDS FAIL, DIFFERENTLY. "EVENTUALLY" makes it unfalsifiable at a Dec-2036 horizon - it is compatible with any 2036 outcome, so it carries no probability mass at this resolution. "WINS" is the deeper failure: it smuggles in an unstated metric. Aggregate real GDP growth and real GDP PER CAPITA growth come apart precisely when population shrinks, and a shrinking denominator can deliver a per-capita "win" alongside falling aggregate output - or the reverse. And even an aggregate win is consistent with the labour-income share collapsing, which is the whole content of the BIS Box C demand-shortfall warning and of regimes B and D. I score this higher than all three Wave-1 seats (14-18) because my own CQ3 P50 of 2.1% and A at 25 do partly vindicate the AGGREGATE growth claim over 2032-36 - the plank is directionally more defensible than the panel allowed, and still fails as stated. 22.

key_drivers: DOUBLE-COUNTED CHINA AGING DRAG. 2A's -2.7 pp/yr is an IMF 2025-2050 average against a no-aging counterfactual, and China's observed ~4.5-5% print already embeds a working-age population falling since 2013 and a total population falling since 2022. All three Wave-1 seats subtracted it (or most of it) from the current run-rate; panelist 2's implied 5.4% no-aging counterfactual makes the double count auditable. The incremental 2026->2032-36 drag is -1.0 to -1.3 pp, worth ~+0.25 to +0.30 pp on coupled CQ3.

MEASURED VERSUS TRUE CHINESE GROWTH. CQ3 resolves on official PPP real GDP through IMF WEO, and China's official series is a smoothed administrative object. Wave 1 forecast true growth and will be scored on printed growth. At w_China = 0.37, a 3.6% measured print (vs their 2.7-3.0%) delivers 1.33 pp of the coupled answer and is most of why my A is 25 rather than 12-17.

PPP-GDP-WEIGHTED OECD-38 INFLATION COMPOSITION. Turkiye (~4-4.5% of OECD-38 PPP GDP), Mexico (~3.5%) and Colombia/Chile/Costa Rica (~2%) hold the aggregate 0.4-0.9 pp above a G7 core. Panelists 2 and 3 priced them inside a 'rest x 2.5%' residual on market-FX weights. This single accounting fact carries CQ2 at 48, makes CQ6-C's >=2.7% gate easy at 0.55, and starves CQ6-D of its <2.00% condition (D = 6, versus Wave 1's 11-19).

MOVE IS NORMALIZED BASIS-POINT VOL AND SCALES WITH THE YIELD LEVEL. The ~75-90 decade averages Wave 1 anchored on were generated at 1.5-2.5% nominal 10y yields; the locked start is 4-5% nominal with a 2.60% real. Re-leveling panelist 2's own two-state calm case from 75 to ~95-100 collapses the required stress share from 50% to 15-25% of the decade. This is the whole of my CQ5 gap (30 vs 16-20) and it is an index-definition fact.

TWO-SIDED MEDIAN COMPOSITION IN CQ1. Wave 1 found that J+K+M shedding juniors raises that group's median; they missed that aging is a VOLUME shock to Q whose hiring margin is low-wage personal-care and nursing-assistant grades, which DILUTES the F+Q median downward even as Q's wage bill rises. The two composition effects are additive against the conjunct, which is why I sit at 6 rather than 11-13.

IMPAIRMENT IS A BOOK-VALUE EVENT, NOT AN OUTPUT EVENT. Wave 1 translated AI-Q4's 66% into a halved or zeroed capital-deepening growth contribution. A written-down GPU still computes and a written-down substation still delivers electrons; measured capital services and measured GDP do not fall because a balance sheet is marked. I would mark AI-Q4 UP to ~0.72 and route it entirely into CQ5, CQ4's term premium and the private-credit / AI-complex rows of the asset matrix, worth ~+0.10 to +0.15 pp on CQ3.

NON-US G7 REAL-YIELD CONVERGENCE. Japan, Germany, France and Italy are ~0.365 of the G7 GDP weight at 0.30-1.90% real with the 10y JGB at a 30-year high and the BoJ exiting. Convergence toward 1.6-2.0% real adds +0.45 to +0.55 pp to the weighted average with the US unchanged - a term none of the three sized - and I cut their Reinhart-Sbrancia repression wedge because the captive-buyer machinery of 1945-1980 (closed capital accounts, central-bank bid) is not installed.
wave2.lens_self_description: I answered purely as a premortem and devil's-advocate red-teamer: my only method was to locate the assumption all three Wave-1 panelists shared and attack it, which forbade me from averaging them, from treating their convergence at CQ3 1.8-1.9% as evidence of anything except a common framing error, and from using the project's simulation for any bound (I used it only to verify and attack its closure - gamma=0.55 on useful energy in src/modules/production.ts, the UN WPP low demographic path, and scripts/tetlock-sim-adapter.ts proxying OECD-38 by us + oecd-ex-us, which drops Japan, Korea, Turkiye, Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Costa Rica).

wave3.coupling_tension:
PRIMARY, AND IT IS MINE TO OWN: AI-Q4 (66.0%) IS TOO LOW ONCE DEMOGRAPHICS ARE ENDOGENOUS. DIRECTION: UP, TO ~0.73. Impairment is not mainly a demand question; it is a discount-rate x useful-life question, and the discount rate is exactly what 2A's demographic/fiscal block sets. Life-cycle dissaving as the old-age ratio goes 31% -> 39-41%, public dissaving at >100% debt/GDP, eroding sovereign convenience yields and levered basis-trade absorption as the marginal duration bid: my own CQ4 posterior of 2.2% G7-weighted real says the cost of capital the ~$1.4T of circular commitments must clear STAYS at or above the locked 2.60% US TIPS level rather than reverting toward the 2010s. At a ~2.2% real yield and a 3-6 year compute book life the required gross revenue yield on AI compute is ~22-28%/yr of capex, against a paying base that AI-Q2 (21.3%) says is under half of OECD firms by 2036. This is the one place in the whole coupling where aging-as-demand-pull and aging-as-fiscal-constraint do NOT offset: the pull raises adoption (AI-Q2 up) while the saving/fiscal/term-premium channel raises the cost of capital FASTER, so the buildout becomes simultaneously more wanted and less financeable — which is definitionally the impairment state. Holding demographics exogenous, as 2B does, strips out both legs and lands the marginal too low.

SECOND: AI-Q3's UPPER TAIL IS UNREACHABLE AND THE SAME OBSERVABLE RAISES AI-Q4. DIRECTION: P90 DOWN ~15% (1,573.8 -> ~1,330), P50 DOWN MODESTLY (998.2 -> ~940), left tail fatter. The P90 needs ~12%/yr compound operational OECD-38+China datacentre load for twelve years. Capacity OPERATIONAL in 2036 must be queued and energized by roughly 2031-32, and the Signal Scout's dated telemetry (generator step-up transformer lead times surpassing 160 weeks in Q1 2026 against a 143-week 2024 average; gas turbine lead times stretched to five years after 43 GW of 2025 orders, the strongest order book in two decades; lead-time-to-power of 36 months in Pittsburgh to 84 months in Columbus; an ERCOT large-load queue of ~410 GW in April 2026 — caveat preserved, developers hedge across queues so the figure is padded with duplicates and overstates real load) says the marginal 2032-36 project is equipment-constrained today. The dependence the ensemble will miss: ONE observable moves AI-Q3's tail DOWN and AI-Q4 UP, so treating them as independent marginals understates the joint mass on the stranded-buildout cell. That cell is what my CQ6-D at 12 and my regime-D asset column price (AI complex -9.0, power/grid -3.5, private credit -7.0, construction -5.0).

THIRD, AND IT CUTS AGAINST MY OWN CQ6 ORDERING, SO I NAME IT RATHER THAN HIDE IT: a high AI-Q4 is a disinflationary-bust prior, and taken alone it implies D > C. I report C 27 > D 12 anyway, and the ENTIRE reason is the composition arithmetic of the OECD-38 GDP-weighted core measure (Türkiye ~4.7%, Mexico ~4.0%, Colombia/Chile/Costa Rica ~2.4% of OECD-38 PPP GDP — together ~11%), which holds the aggregate 0.4-0.9 pp above a G7 core and so starves D of its <2.00% condition. That is a measurement-definition risk, not a macro-forecasting risk, and it is the single highest-variance input in my payload: if the resolver uses a market-FX or G7-proxy aggregate, C and D roughly swap and the long-nominal-bond row of my matrix inverts from worst (-6.5 in C) to best (+6.0 in D).

FOURTH: AI-Q1 (23.0%) is biased in OPPOSITE directions depending on the cut, and nets to roughly UNCHANGED, which is why I did not move it. On an OECD-38-only cut it is too LOW — labour scarcity is the best-documented firm-level automation forcing variable (postwar Japan, 1920s US after immigration restriction) and exogenous demographics removes the forcing variable. On the PPP-weighted measure as literally posed it is too HIGH — a third of the weight is China, where shrinking-workforce capital reallocation toward labour substitution at falling marginal product and toward pension-financing claims depresses MEASURED TFP regardless of frontier capability. Net ~22%. FIFTH: AI-Q5 (38.2%) is biased HIGH, direction DOWN to ~32%. A sector that stops hiring juniors and retains high-paid seniors has a RISING compensation per head, so the J/K/M compensation share of GVA falls by less than the employment decline implies, and part of the apparent AI effect is simply the demographic entry pipeline narrowing. Caveats preserved: the Stanford/ADP "Canaries" finding is US-only ADP panel data, late-2022 to Jul-2025, and the circulating magnitudes (6%, 13%, 13-16%, ~20%) are different measures that must not be pooled; the Yale Budget Lab's contemporaneous read is that the aggregate labour-market effect is statistically indistinguishable from zero at 33 months.
wave3.cq1_reasoning:
RECONCILED CONJUNCT-BY-CONJUNCT. Wave-1 spread 13/11/12, Wave-2 9 and 6.

CONJUNCT C1 (OECD-38 harmonized U averages <=5.5%, 2032-36), MARGINAL 0.50. Panelist spread 0.40/0.55/0.62/0.47/0.45. I down-weight BOTH ends. The Historian's 0.40 rests on a base rate of ~1 in 21 rolling 5-year windows since 2001 — authoritative as a fact, but that denominator is dominated by the 2009-2013 GFC regime and he then declined to apply his own Okun-favourable adjustment at full size. The Signal Scout's 0.62 is the weakest number in his payload: he forecast a 5-year AVERAGE from a current LEVEL print (OECD release, "broadly stable in August 2026, at 5.0%, just 0.2 p.p. above its record low from June 2023", with the OECD's own two releases disagreeing on July at 4.9% vs 5.0%, so revision-noisy). My own decomposition: from a 5.0% start with an OECD-38 aggregate floor of ~4.6-4.8% (Spain, Türkiye, Colombia, Greece are members) you can absorb only ~+0.5 pp of averaged cyclical slack, against -0.2 to -0.4 pp of Okun-favourable drift from the contracting 20-64 denominator. Two-state: P(no OECD-wide contraction in the window) ~0.30 x P(pass|no recession) 0.92 + P(recession) 0.70 x P(pass|recession) 0.35 = 0.276 + 0.245 = 0.52. Take 0.50.

CONJUNCT C2 ((F+Q) minus (J+K+M) cumulative real MEDIAN hourly wage growth >= +10.0 pp, i.e. ~+0.87 pp/yr sustained eleven years), MARGINAL 0.14. Spread 0.25/0.14/0.16/0.15/0.12. Three mechanisms, all pointing down, and I accept all three at differing weight. (1) HIRING VOLUME, NOT PAY — the Bayesian seat's only above-2:1 signal and the decisive one: Stanford/ADP "Canaries" finds the adjustment runs through "hiring volume rather than pay cuts", 22-25 year olds in exposed jobs down ~6% (13% relative after firm controls) while older workers in those jobs GAINED 6-9%. A cohort that never entered J/K/M generates no wage signal; a sector that sheds juniors and keeps seniors has a MECHANICALLY RISING median, moving the tested differential the wrong way. (2) ADMINISTERED PRICES — Q is majority publicly financed inside the budgets 2A squeezes (net interest 2% -> 3% of GDP; China's ~2.9T RMB pension subsidy at ~10.1% of fiscal expenditure), so care scarcity clears as unfilled rosters and waiting lists, not medians. This is the Fermi seat's best finding and the reason REAL SCARCITY AND A FAILING CQ1 ARE FULLY COMPATIBLE. (3) THE RED-TEAM'S SECOND-SIDED MEDIAN DILUTION — aging is a VOLUME shock to Q whose hiring margin is low-wage personal-care and nursing-assistant grades, so adding 10-20% headcount at the bottom of Q's distribution pulls the F+Q MEDIAN DOWN even while Q's wage bill rises, additively with (1). THIS IS A REAL HIT and no Wave-1 seat found it. I give it PARTIAL credit only: if the criterion composites F's and Q's own sector medians rather than pooling F+Q workers, the dilution is roughly halved. That is why I sit at 0.14 rather than the red-teamer's 0.12. Against all three: the dated physical-scarcity prints (transformer lead times >160 weeks vs a 143-week 2024 average, turbines at five years, PJM wholesale +76% in Q1 2026, LME copper cash ~US$14,751/t on 14 Oct 2026 after a record ~US$14,822 on 12 Oct — single secondary roundup, unconfirmed by a major outlet, treat as approximate) are real and raise C2 somewhat; they are the reason I do not go to 0.10.

CORRELATION: positive, rho ~ +0.30, held across all five seats and correct — the tight-labour state is the one that reprices physical/care medians, and the recession that breaks C1 is the event that damages F most. P(C2|C1) = 0.14 x 1.28 = 0.18.

MULTIPLICATION: 0.50 x 0.18 = 0.090 -> 9.
wave3.cq2_reasoning:
THIS IS MY LARGEST MOVE AND IT IS AN ACCOUNTING ARGUMENT THE RED-TEAM FORCED INTO THE OPEN. Spread 41/30/26/40/48.

CONJUNCT A (OECD-38 GDP-weighted core CPI/PCE >= 2.50%/yr avg 2027-2036), MARGINAL 0.76. The entire 26-to-48 spread is one identification question: at what weight do Türkiye, Mexico, Colombia, Chile and Costa Rica enter? The Fermi and Scout seats built the aggregate on market-FX weights and booked the five inside a "rest x 0.13 x 2.5%" residual — DOWN-WEIGHTED TO ZERO on this conjunct, because assigning a decade of Türkiye at 2.5% core is not a forecast, it is an erasure. The red-teamer is right that the Section-2 accounting lock is constant 2025 USD PPP and that the OECD's own published aggregates are PPP-GDP weighted. My rebuild: OECD-38 PPP GDP ~$80T; Türkiye ~$3.8T = 4.7%, Mexico ~$3.3T = 4.0%, Colombia+Chile+Costa Rica ~$1.95T = 2.4%, so ~11% of the aggregate. Arithmetic under PPP weights: core block 0.89 x 2.30% = 2.05 pp; Türkiye 0.047 x 9% decade core = 0.42; Mexico 0.040 x 4.0% = 0.16; others 0.024 x 4.0% = 0.10. Total ~2.73%, i.e. the composition CARRIES the question with the G7 block at or slightly below target. Checked for robustness: at Türkiye disinflating to a 6% decade average the aggregate still prints ~2.59%; it falls below 2.50% only if Türkiye reaches ~5% AND the G7 block converges to ~2.1%. NOTE, and this is where I diverge from the red-teamer: the threshold clears on MARKET-FX weights too (the five are ~6.6% of OECD-38 nominal GDP; 0.934 x 2.30 + 0.066 x 7.5 = 2.65%), so the basis risk is smaller than he implies but not zero, since a G7-proxy read would put A near 0.62. I therefore price the basis explicitly: A = 0.70 x P(A|PPP-type basis, 0.82) + 0.30 x P(A|FX/G7-proxy basis, 0.62) = 0.574 + 0.186 = 0.76. Observed starting point, which I treat as corroboration not as the driver: US core CPI 2.6% Sep-2026 (up from a five-year low of 2.4% in Aug), euro-area core 2.5% Sep-2026 (Oct flash due 4 Nov 2026, unverified), US core PCE ~3.0-3.1% Aug-2026 with the Sep actual unverified — the series starts at or above the gate.

CONJUNCT B (China headline CPI averages < 1.50%/yr, 2027-2036), MARGINAL 0.63. Spread 0.65/0.80/0.58/0.62/0.68. The Signal Scout OWNS the evidence here and I weight him heavily on the print while rejecting his level: NBS primary release of 14 Oct 2026 gives September CPI +0.9% y/y and +0.2% m/m, up from 0.8% in August and 0.5% in July, core ex-food-and-energy 1.0% y/y and reported as the first 1.0% in 19 months, PPI +5.0% y/y accelerating from +3.8% in August. That is a genuine reflation signature. The Bayesian seat's rebuttal is the best single piece of argument in the Wave-2 pair and I adopt it: the 2021 episode inside the same regime had PPI near +13% while CPI stayed near 1%, so Chinese PPI-to-CPI transmission has been structurally broken since the property bust — the likelihood ratio does not survive at 2.2-2.5 and lands near 1.4-1.5. I DOWN-WEIGHT the Fermi seat's 0.80 ("the single highest-confidence leg in the set"), which was asserted with the contrary print in front of him. Against B: failing it needs only ~1.9-2.0% sustained from 2029, and China averaged 1.8-1.9% in 2012-2019, which is not exotic; plus RMB depreciation and the pork/food cycles that pushed CPI above 4% twice since 2007. For B: a -60M population over 2026-2035, worker-to-retiree 4.4 -> 2.8, high precautionary saving, and the fiscal space for a reflationary household transfer being consumed by the pension transfer that will not reflate. 0.63.

CORRELATION: mildly NEGATIVE but WEAKER than Wave 1 priced it, and the red-teamer identified why — my conjunct A is now carried by NON-TRADABLE EM-member services and administered prices that Chinese goods deflation barely touches, whereas the Wave-1 seats sourced A from G7 tradables-sensitive core and so imported the full 1998-2004 / 2014-2016 exported-disinflation offset. rho ~ -0.08. P(B|A) = 0.63 x 0.94 = 0.59.

MULTIPLICATION: 0.76 x 0.59 = 0.448 -> 44. I apply NO further haircut: the Historian docked a point "as a matter of lens discipline" for this being a "great divergence" state, and the red-teamer is right that this is narrative, not probability — the conjunction discount is already in the multiplication and the divergence is already in the two marginals.
wave3.cq3_reasoning:
PPP WEIGHTS FIRST, SINCE THEY DOMINATE. Panelist spread on China's share of the pair: 0.38 (Fermi) / 0.33 (Historian) / 0.295 (Scout) / 0.335 (Bayesian) / 0.37 (red-team). The Bayesian seat's rebuild is the best-documented and I ADOPT IT: world PPP GDP ~$195T, China ~19.5% = ~$38T, OECD-38 sums to ~41% of world = ~$80T, so China = 38/118 = 0.322 at the 2026 start. Fermi's $73T OECD-38 is too low; the Scout's 46-47%-of-world is too high. Because my China growth leg is faster than the Bayesian's, the drift is faster: I use w_China = 0.34, w_OECD = 0.66 at the 2034 midpoint.

THE TWO RED-TEAM HITS I MOVED FOR, BOTH REAL.
(1) DOUBLE-COUNTED CHINA AGING DRAG. 2A's -2.7 pp/yr is an IMF WEO Apr-2025 Ch.2 figure averaged 2025-2050 against a NO-AGING counterfactual, and China's observed ~4.5-5% print is already produced by an economy whose working-age population peaked in 2013 and whose total population has fallen since 2022. All three Wave-1 seats subtracted it from a near-current run-rate; the Fermi seat made the error auditable by publishing its implication — a no-aging counterfactual of ~5.4%/yr, i.e. the claim that today's print contains ZERO realized drag while the dependency ratio has deteriorated for a decade. I MOVE, worth ~+0.25 pp on the China leg.
